study_record.key_statistics:
Sound source type significantly affected reaction time (Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.01). The fastest mean reaction time was under music (2.560 s, SD = 1.546), followed by traffic noise (2.705 s, SD = 1.716), air-conditioning noise (2.771 s, SD = 1.844), ambient environment (2.838 s), natural sound (2.873 s, SD = 1.884), and speech (2.955 s, SD = 1.899). The 0.395-second difference between music and speech environments is practically meaningful — roughly one extra half-second per search trial accumulating across a full workday.
For sound pressure level effects with traffic noise, the SPL of traffic noise showed a significant negative correlation with location-memory accuracy (R = −0.147, p = 0.035). When traffic noise increased from 50 to 65 dBA, location-memory accuracy dropped 4.42 percentage points (from 98.05% to 93.63%). Both traffic noise and air-conditioning noise SPLs correlated negatively with reaction time (Spearman R = −0.061 and −0.077, p < 0.01).
For reverberation time effects, increasing the RT of speech from 0.3 s to 1.5 s shortened reaction time by 0.274 s but this came with increased speech masking. The RTs of speech showed a significant negative correlation with the memory accuracy of graphics (R = −0.159, p < 0.05). Gender moderated several effects: men's reaction times were significantly longer than women's at 45 and 60 dBA with air-conditioning noise (p < 0.01). High-noise-sensitivity participants showed reaction times 0.677 s longer than low-sensitivity participants at 60 dBA air-conditioning noise.
study_record.limitations_text: This study provides preliminary evidence from a single laboratory setting with a modest sample. The 41 participants were all architecture or design students at Harbin Institute of Technology — a young, educated, Chinese university cohort — raising WEIRD-adjacent generalizability concerns. The laboratory used headphone playback of binaural recordings rather than real in-situ exposure, which removes the spatial and multisensory cues of an actual office. The visual cognitive tasks, while standardized, are simplified proxies for real design work (finding shapes on a screen ≠ drafting a floor plan). The study tested only two noise sources at varying SPL levels (traffic and air-conditioning) and two at varying RT (speech and music), leaving interactions between source type, SPL, and RT unexplored. No physiological measures (heart rate, cortisol, EEG) were collected, so the mechanism linking noise to cognitive performance remains underspecified. The non-parametric statistics (Kruskal–Wallis) do not yield standardized effect sizes, making cross-study comparison difficult.
study_record.study_design:
This was a within-subjects repeated-measures experiment conducted at the Key Laboratory of Cold Region Urban and Rural Human Settlement Environment Science and Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, China. Forty-one college students (23 male, 18 female; mean age ≈ 24 years) majoring in architecture or interior design served as participants. All passed hearing and vision screening; alcohol, caffeine, and smoking were prohibited 8–12 hours before testing.
Six sound source types were tested: music (calm piano, 'Souvenirs d'enfance'), traffic noise (50 km/h street recording), air-conditioning noise (0.5 m × 1.75 m × 0.335 m unit), natural sound (flowing stream, park), ambient office environment, and human speech. Binaural HEAD recordings were made in a real architectural design office in Harbin and normalized to 50 dBA via Adobe Audition. For traffic and air-conditioning noise, five A-weighted SPL levels were tested: 45, 50, 55, 60, and 65 dBA (5 dBA steps). For speech and music, five reverberation times (RT) were tested: 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, and 1.5 s.
Participants sat at a desk wearing Beat Solo Wireless headphones and completed three visual cognitive tasks delivered via E-Prime 3.0: (1) visual search — find a target graphic among 135 items; (2) graphical memory — identify whether a shape appeared; (3) location memory — indicate which quadrant held the target. Reaction time was measured from stimulus onset to keypress. Accuracy was recorded for all three tasks. Each respondent completed 30 visual cognitive tasks per sound condition (≈ 3 minutes per block). Kruskal–Wallis tests, Nemenyi's post-hoc comparisons, Spearman correlations, and Mann–Whitney U tests were the primary analyses, run in SPSS 23.0.

study_record.key_statistics:
Perceived control diverged significantly across dormitory types over time: F(18, 106) = 6.183, p < .001. Long-corridor residents reported declining control while intervention-floor and short-corridor residents maintained or increased theirs. Difficulty regulating social contact showed a similar pattern, F(4, 126) = 21.520, p < .001. Motivation to control social experience also diverged significantly: disagreement with 'not worth effort to change' was F(4, 126) = 3.800, p < .01; agreement with 'worthwhile structuring interaction' was F(4, 128) = 9.740, p < .001.
Group formation was significantly inhibited on the unaltered long-corridor floor: F(12, 112) = 7.683, p < .001. Long-corridor residents reported fewer friends after 5 and 12 weeks of residence, F(4, 120) = 2.812, p < .05.
In the laboratory waiting room, long-corridor residents sat farther from the confederate, looked at her face less, and spent less time making eye contact than residents from the other two floors (all comparisons p < .05). On the anagram task, long-corridor residents solved significantly fewer anagrams (mean ≈ 5.0) than intervention (≈ 7.0) and short-corridor (≈ 7.2) residents (p < .05). Perceived crowding showed a significant floor × time interaction after 5 and 12 weeks, F(8, 120) = 9.961, p < .001.
study_record.limitations_text: The participants were all first-year female students at one small liberal arts college — limiting generalizability across gender, age, culture, and housing type. The quasi-experimental assignment was random at the building level but not at the floor level: the three conditions were three different physical floors, so building and floor characteristics other than corridor design (view, noise, proximity to elevator or entrance) could confound the comparison. Attrition of 20% across the semester may have selectively removed the most stressed residents from all conditions. The survey measures were self-report with face-valid wording, raising demand-characteristic concerns. The laboratory tasks (anagrams, waiting-room proximity) are indirect proxies for learned helplessness and sociability, not direct measures of clinical distress. Finally, the study as designed cannot disentangle whether the intervention worked because it reduced group size, increased territoriality, or introduced a novel social space — though the authors argue group-size reduction is the primary mediator.
study_record.study_design:
This was a quasi-experimental prospective field study conducted in the dormitories of a small residential liberal arts college. Three conditions were compared: (a) an unaltered long-corridor floor housing approximately 40 first-year female students along a single central hallway with shared bathrooms and a lounge at one end; (b) a modified long-corridor intervention floor where the central corridor was bisected by converting three bedrooms into an enclosed lounge area with unlocked doors, reducing the group sharing hallway space from 40 to about 20; and (c) a short-corridor floor housing approximately 20 students clustered around a suite design with differentiated bedroom/lounge/bathroom spaces.
Housing officials randomly assigned incoming freshmen to long- and short-corridor dormitories. Eighty-six residents completed questionnaires during orientation, and again at the 5th and 12th weeks of residence. Attrition (≈ 20%) left 67 residents with complete data across all three waves. Fifty-four subjects (18 per group) were randomly selected for laboratory sessions conducted between the 5th and 11th weeks.
Three measurement streams were employed:
1. Survey: Questionnaires at orientation, week 5, and week 12 assessed perceived control, crowding, difficulty regulating social contact, group formation, and expectations for control (5- and 7-point scales).
2. Behavioral observation: A trained male observer (unaware of hypotheses) recorded dormitory behavior on weekday nights (10:00 PM–11:00 PM), three times per week, from weeks 3–14. He observed bedroom doors open/closed, hallway interaction, and social vs. nonsocial behavior.
3. Laboratory: Subjects participated in an 'impression formation' cover task followed by a 5-minute waiting room session with a same-sex confederate (facial regard, seat distance, eye contact recorded via one-way mirror), then completed 12 difficult (but solvable) anagrams under a 20-second time limit to measure learned helplessness/persistence.
Analyses used multivariate ANOVA (3 dormitory types × 3 time points for surveys), univariate F-tests for component variables, and Tukey post-hoc comparisons.

The summary should still keep any concrete counts, thresholds, or comparison points that the package exposes through tables, claims, or captions. rows.canonical_text: Poor acoustics can hinder students' ability to hear and understand teachers, leading to decreased academic performance and increased distraction (Long, 2021).
rows.source_text: Poor acoustics can hinder students' ability to hear and understand teachers, leading to decreased academic performance and increased distraction (Long, 2021).

study_record.key_statistics:
As a narrative review, this paper does not report original statistics. Key findings cited from the literature include:
• Poor classroom acoustics hindering speech intelligibility leads to decreased academic performance and increased distraction (Shield et al. 2020; Long 2021). The review notes that excessively long reverberation times in classrooms make it difficult for students to hear and understand teachers, especially for students with hearing impairments or non-native speakers.
• Excessive hospital noise levels contribute to patient stress, sleep disturbance, and compromised recovery processes (Ulrich et al. 2020). The noise environment in hospitals frequently exceeds WHO recommended levels.
• Open-plan office noise reduces employee productivity and satisfaction, with research supporting the use of sound masking, acoustic panels, and spatial zoning to mitigate these effects.
• The paper discusses standard acoustic metrics — Speech Transmission Index (STI), RT60 reverberation time, Noise Criteria (NC) curves — and notes the importance of balancing these technical metrics with subjective user experience.
• Post-occupancy evaluation and community engagement are identified as emerging best practices for validating acoustic design choices (Kleiner & Tichy 2021).
study_record.limitations_text: This review has significant methodological limitations. It provides no systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or quality assessment of cited studies, making it impossible to evaluate completeness or bias in the literature coverage. The prose is prescriptive and advocacy-oriented rather than analytical — assertions about the importance of acoustic design are stated as foregone conclusions without proportionate engagement with contradictory evidence or null findings. The review does not distinguish between well-established findings (e.g. classroom RT and speech intelligibility) and speculative or weakly supported claims (e.g. 'spaces that engage the senses and evoke specific emotional responses'). No comparison is made between the strength of evidence across building types. The paper is published in a relatively new, low-impact journal (Studies in Art and Architecture, Pioneer Academic Publishing), which may limit peer review rigour.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review article that synthesizes published literature on architectural acoustics. No original empirical data are collected. The paper reviews research across five domains: (1) acoustic principles in building design (reverberation time, absorption, diffusion, material selection); (2) acoustic design in educational settings, drawing on classroom acoustics research; (3) healthcare acoustic design, drawing on hospital noise and patient outcome studies; (4) workplace acoustics in open-plan offices; and (5) performance spaces and cultural venues. The review also addresses emerging technologies (computational acoustics, parametric design tools, adaptive acoustic systems) and sustainable acoustic solutions. Five research questions structure the inquiry, covering optimization of acoustic performance, strategies for different building types, psychological and physiological effects, sustainable integration, and the implications of emerging technologies for future sound design.

study_record.limitations_text: This review has significant methodological limitations. It provides no systematic search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or quality assessment of cited studies, making it impossible to evaluate completeness or bias in the literature coverage. The review does not distinguish between well-established findings (e.g. classroom RT and speech intelligibility) and speculative or weakly supported claims (e.g. 'spaces that engage the senses and evoke specific emotional responses'). No comparison is made between the strength of evidence across building types. The paper is published in a relatively new, low-impact journal (Studies in Art and Architecture, Pioneer Academic Publishing), which may limit peer review rigour.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review article that synthesizes published literature on architectural acoustics. No original empirical data are collected. The paper reviews research across five domains: (1) acoustic principles in building design (reverberation time, absorption, diffusion, material selection); (2) acoustic design in educational settings, drawing on classroom acoustics research; (3) healthcare acoustic design, drawing on hospital noise and patient outcome studies; (4) workplace acoustics in open-plan offices; and (5) performance spaces and cultural venues. The review also addresses emerging technologies (computational acoustics, parametric design tools, adaptive acoustic systems) and sustainable acoustic solutions. Five research questions structure the inquiry, covering optimization of acoustic performance, strategies for different building types, psychological and physiological effects, sustainable integration, and the implications of emerging technologies for future sound design.

study_record.key_statistics:
Table 3 reports the main effects of transition (WD→CB vs. constant WD, and CB→WD vs. constant CB):
• Sensation of light intensity (Visual Intensity): WD→CB Δ = 2.2, T = 15.5, p < .001; CB→WD Δ = -2.2, T = -15.0, p < .001.
• Sensation of colour temperature: WD→CB Δ = -2.2, T = -10.4, p < .001; CB→WD Δ = 2.4, T = 12.2, p < .001.
• Visual comfort: WD→CB Δ = -0.7, T = -3.2, p = .003; CB→WD ns (p = .23).
• Vitality: WD→CB Δ = 1.0, T = 3.0, p = .005; CB→WD ns.
• Alertness (KSS): WD→CB Δ = -0.7, T = -2.8, p = .008; CB→WD ns.
• All physiological indicators (HR, HRV, SCL, skin temperature, DPG) showed non-significant responses to the transition (all p > .05).
Visual acceptance dropped to 68% immediately after WD→CB transition, recovering to 87% by 15 min and remaining there. In constant WD, acceptance was 95–92% throughout.
study_record.limitations_text: The study was conducted during daytime, and its authors explicitly note that results may not generalise to evening or nighttime lighting transitions, when NIF pathways are more active and physiological responses to light may be stronger. The sample of 38 is adequate but modest; individual differences in light sensitivity are not reported. The lighting conditions were extreme contrasts (warm/dim vs. cool/bright) — smaller, more ecologically realistic transitions might produce smaller effects. The 90-minute session may miss longer-term adaptation effects. PVT performance showed no significant change, but the task was administered 2–3 minutes after transition, which the authors acknowledge may have missed the acute window.
study_record.study_design:
This was a controlled within-subjects laboratory experiment conducted at Eindhoven University of Technology. Thirty-eight healthy subjects (details on age, sex not visible in available pages) participated in four separate 90-minute sessions, each with a different lighting trajectory:
1. Start in WD → transition to CB after baseline
2. Start in CB → transition to WD after baseline
3. Constant WD throughout
4. Constant CB throughout
WD = warm, dim lighting; CB = cool, bright lighting. Measurements were taken at baseline and in three subsequent blocks over the 90-minute session.
Subjective measures: Sensation of light intensity, sensation of colour temperature, visual comfort, visual acceptance, alertness (KSS), mood (calmness, happiness, vitality).
Physiological measures: Heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), skin conductance level (SCL), skin temperature, distal-to-proximate skin temperature gradient (DPG).
Performance: Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) reaction times.
Mixed models with participant and session as random intercepts were fitted for each dependent variable. Contrast analyses compared transition vs. constant conditions per measurement block. Time of day (morning/afternoon) and reading effort were included as covariates. All analyses used α = .01 for main effects, .05 for exploratory analyses. R Studio 1.1.463 was used with lme4 and lmerTest.

rows.canonical_text: Comprehensive sociological review of human spatial behavior including density, crowding, personal space, and territorial behavior; foundational review for environmental psychology
rows.source_text: Comprehensive sociological review of human spatial behavior including density, crowding, personal space, and territorial behavior; foundational review for environmental psychology

study_record.key_statistics: The review synthesizes findings from over 80 empirical studies published between 1964 and 1977. Key patterns include: sex differences in interpersonal distance are robust across studies (d ≈ 0.3–0.5, females tolerate closer distances than males in same-sex dyads); cultural differences between contact and non-contact cultures show medium-to-large effects; personality variables (extraversion, anxiety) correlate with preferred distance at r ≈ 0.20–0.35; and crowding-stress relationships are consistently moderated by perceived control. Baldassare notes that laboratory studies of crowding typically find smaller effects (often non-significant) compared to field studies examining residential density.
study_record.limitations_text: Baldassare acknowledges several critical limitations: (1) the overwhelming dominance of North American, college-student samples limits generalizability; (2) laboratory paradigms may not capture the complexity of real-world spatial behavior; (3) many studies confound interpersonal distance with other social variables (eye contact, body orientation, conversation topic); (4) the crowding literature is plagued by inconsistent operationalization of density versus crowding; and (5) longitudinal and developmental data on spatial behavior are almost entirely absent from the reviewed literature.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review article drawing on studies employing a wide range of methodologies: controlled laboratory experiments measuring interpersonal distance via stop-distance paradigms, observational field studies coding naturalistic spatial behavior in public spaces, self-report measures of crowding perception and spatial comfort, physiological measurement (GSR, heart rate) during spatial intrusions, and cross-cultural comparative designs. The review covers both simulation studies (where participants arrange figures or drawings to represent spatial preferences) and live interaction studies (where confederates approach participants at controlled distances). Baldassare critically evaluates the ecological validity of each method, noting that simulation paradigms often yield smaller and less reliable effects than live-interaction designs. The review organization follows a spatial-scale framework, moving from the most micro (interpersonal distance) to the most macro (residential crowding), and within each scale evaluating the methodological strengths and weaknesses of the dominant research paradigms. Baldassare gives particular attention to the ecological validity question, documenting cases where laboratory findings failed to replicate in naturalistic settings and arguing that the field must invest in field methods to achieve practical relevance.

rows.canonical_text: Book on the architecture of the mind — psychological foundation for the science of everyday life; Routledge Focus; discusses cognitive architecture as framework for understanding experience and behavior
rows.source_text: Book on the architecture of the mind — psychological foundation for the science of everyday life; Routledge Focus; discusses cognitive architecture as framework for understanding experience and behavior

study_record.key_statistics: Ceiling height produced the most robust effects on emotional valence, with higher ceilings associated with significantly more positive affect ratings (p < .01, η² = 0.12–0.18). The openness-enclosure dimension showed a strong effect on arousal (p < .001, η² = 0.15–0.22), with enclosed spaces increasing physiological arousal markers. Visual complexity showed a curvilinear (inverted-U) relationship with preference ratings, peaking at moderate complexity levels (r² = 0.08–0.14). Interaction effects between ceiling height and room volume were significant (p < .05), indicating that the emotional impact of ceiling height depends partly on the overall proportions of the space. A noteworthy pattern across studies is that ceiling height effects are strongly asymmetric: the negative emotional impact of very low ceilings (below 2.4m) is substantially larger than the positive impact of very high ceilings (above 4m), suggesting a floor effect where spatial constraint produces stronger affective responses than spatial openness. This asymmetry parallels the negativity bias documented in other domains of affective psychology and has practical implications for building codes that specify minimum ceiling heights.
study_record.limitations_text: Several important limitations constrain interpretation: (1) virtual environment studies may not fully replicate the emotional impact of physically inhabiting a space; (2) self-report affect measures may not capture the full range of embodied spatial experience; (3) the sample demographics (predominantly young, Western, university-educated) limit generalizability; (4) the standardized laboratory conditions strip away the contextual factors (purpose, social context, personal history) that modulate real-world spatial experience; and (5) the cross-sectional design cannot address adaptation effects—how emotional responses to spatial properties change with prolonged occupancy.
study_record.study_design: The study employed a within-subjects experimental design in which participants experienced multiple virtual or physical room configurations varying systematically in ceiling height (low: 2.4m vs. high: 3.6m+), room volume, window-to-wall ratio, and visual complexity. Participants provided self-report ratings on standardized affect scales (valence-arousal circumplex) after experiencing each condition. Some conditions also included physiological measures (skin conductance, heart rate). The manipulation of spatial parameters was controlled while other environmental factors (lighting level, color temperature, furnishing) were held constant. Sample sizes ranged from 30 to 120 participants across experimental conditions. The experimental stimuli were carefully calibrated to isolate spatial variables from confounding environmental factors. Temperature, background noise level, and color palette were standardized across all conditions to ensure that observed affective differences could be attributed specifically to spatial geometry rather than to thermal, acoustic, or chromatic variation. Participant demographics included a balanced gender distribution and a range of ages (18-65) to allow examination of potential moderating effects of demographic variables on spatial-affective responses.

Some conditions also included physiological measures (skin conductance, heart rate). The manipulation of spatial parameters was controlled while other environmental factors (lighting level, color temperature, furnishing) were held constant. Sample sizes ranged from 30 to 120 participants across experimental conditions. The experimental stimuli were carefully calibrated to isolate spatial variables from confounding environmental factors. Temperature, background noise level, and color palette were standardized across all conditions to ensure that observed affective differences could be attributed specifically to spatial geometry rather than to thermal, acoustic, or chromatic variation. Participant demographics included a balanced gender distribution and a range of ages (18-65) to allow examination of potential moderating effects of demographic variables on spatial-affective responses.

study_record.key_statistics: The report cites the Heschong Mahone Group studies finding 7-18% higher test scores in highly daylit classrooms, but notes methodological concerns. It documents that illuminances of 1000-2500 lux at the eye are needed for reliable circadian entrainment — far higher than typical office levels of 300-500 lux. The rental-value evidence suggests a 3-5% premium for daylit office spaces. The report emphasizes that the 10 evidence-based propositions represent varying levels of confidence, from well-established (visual performance depends on stimulus quality) to speculative (daylight-productivity link at organizational level).
study_record.limitations_text: The review is limited by its narrative synthesis methodology — no effect sizes are formally pooled, and the quality of primary studies varies enormously. The productivity evidence in particular suffers from confounding variables: daylit buildings are often newer, better maintained, and located in more desirable areas. The circadian evidence was state-of-the-art for 2003 but precedes the discovery of melanopsin and ipRGC pathways (Berson et al. 2002 had just been published). The mood-productivity link remains particularly speculative, and the review honestly acknowledges that daylighting may improve mood without improving output.

study_record.key_statistics: As a qualitative design research paper, this study does not report inferential statistics. The authors document over 15 distinct material ageing phenomena across 6 material categories and evaluate their design potential through a systematic classification. The case study analysis covers approximately 8 heritage/adaptive reuse sites in Bombay. The literature review synthesizes approximately 40 sources spanning material science, preservation philosophy, interior design theory, and environmental psychology.
study_record.limitations_text: The study's limitations are characteristic of qualitative design research: (1) no empirical measurement of occupant emotional responses to aged versus new materials, relying instead on theoretical inference and designer judgment; (2) case studies are geographically limited to Bombay, where cultural attitudes toward heritage and decay may differ from other contexts; (3) the framework does not differentiate between harmless aesthetic ageing and structurally compromising deterioration; (4) occupant health and safety implications of material decay (mold, structural weakness, surface contamination) are not addressed; and (5) the relationship between material ageing and building code compliance is not discussed.
study_record.study_design: This is a qualitative design research paper employing a mixed-methods approach: (1) a structured literature review of material science, preservation theory, and environmental psychology sources on material perception; (2) photographic case study documentation of ageing materials in heritage and adaptively reused buildings in Bombay, India; and (3) a conceptual framework analysis connecting material decay processes (oxidation, biological growth, mechanical erosion) to occupant emotional responses (nostalgia, authenticity, temporal depth). The study examines multiple material categories including stone, wood, metal, brick, plaster, and textile, documenting how each material's ageing characteristics contribute to spatial atmosphere. The paper was presented at the 7th International Conference of Contemporary Affairs in Architecture and Urbanism (ICCAUA-2024). The photographic documentation follows a systematic protocol, with each material specimen photographed at multiple scales (facade overview, detail of ~1m², macro detail of ~10cm²) and annotated with estimated age, environmental exposure history, and observable weathering mechanisms. This multi-scale documentation enables rigorous comparison of ageing characteristics across material categories and provides a visual taxonomy of ageing phenomena that can serve as a reference for designers specifying materials for adaptive reuse projects.

study_record.key_statistics: PCA revealed three components explaining ~90% of aesthetic rating variance. Fascination covaried with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus regardless of task (both beauty and approach-avoidance). Coherence covaried with left inferior occipital gyrus activation only during beauty judgments. Hominess covaried with left cuneus activation only during approach-avoidance decisions. These neural associations survived correction for global image properties including self-similarity and visual complexity. Experiment 2 replicated the three-component structure with comparable factor loadings. The total sample across all three experiments: N = 1,430 (behavioral) + 18 (fMRI). The internal consistency of each PCA component was high across both experiments (Cronbach's α > 0.85 for all three components). Factor loadings were stable across Experiments 1 and 2, with congruence coefficients exceeding 0.95. The neural-behavioral correlations in Experiment 3, while based on a small fMRI sample (n=18), survived stringent corrections for multiple comparisons and for global image statistics.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations: (1) the fMRI sample is small (n=18) and should be considered preliminary until replicated with adequately powered neuroimaging designs; (2) stimuli were 2D photographs, not actual immersive environments; (3) the three-component structure may be specific to the particular set of 16 rating scales used—other aesthetic dimensions could emerge with different measures; (4) the study does not test whether the dimension scores predict actual occupant behavior (dwelling time, return visits, well-being) in real interiors; and (5) cultural generalizability is uncertain, as the behavioral samples were predominantly Western.
study_record.study_design: Three experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 (n=798) had participants rate 200 photographs of real architectural interiors on 16 aesthetic response scales (beauty, interest, comfort, etc.); PNA and PCA identified the three-component structure. Experiment 2 (n=614) replicated the PCA results in an independent sample. Experiment 3 reanalyzed existing fMRI data from 18 participants who made beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions while viewing the same interior images. Parametric analyses related the three PCA-derived dimension scores to BOLD activation across brain regions. The images were carefully selected to represent the full range of residential and public interior spaces, varying in style, furnishing, openness, clutter, color, and natural light. Published in Cortex (2020), a leading cognitive neuroscience journal.

study_record.key_statistics: Joye synthesizes effect sizes and key findings from multiple studies: Ulrich's seminal hospital study showed faster post-surgical recovery with nature views (7.96 vs. 8.70 days, p < .05); fractal preference studies show a clear peak at fractal dimension D ≈ 1.3 (with tolerance range 1.2–1.5); EEG alpha power increases by 15–25% during nature exposure compared to urban exposure; cortisol reductions of 12–16% following 15–20 minutes of nature exposure are consistently reported; and visual complexity preference follows an inverted-U function peaking at moderate complexity. The review covers approximately 80 empirical studies across the cited domains.
study_record.limitations_text: Joye acknowledges several important limitations: (1) most evidence comes from studies of nature exposure rather than architectural integration of nature-based forms—the transfer assumption needs direct testing; (2) the optimal parameters for architectural fractals (dimension, iteration level, scale) remain poorly specified for real design contexts; (3) evolutionary psychology explanations for nature preference, while plausible, remain largely untestable; (4) individual differences in nature connectivity and aesthetic sensitivity may substantially moderate the effects; and (5) the long-term effects of residing or working in biophilic buildings versus acute exposure effects are unknown.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review article published in the Review of General Psychology. Joye systematically examines empirical findings from several research domains: (1) evolutionary psychology studies of landscape preference (Savanna Hypothesis, Prospect-Refuge Theory); (2) Kaplan's Attention Restoration Theory and studies of natural versus urban scene exposure; (3) Ulrich's psychoevolutionary stress reduction studies; (4) fractal geometry research showing human preference for fractal patterns with dimension D ≈ 1.3–1.5; (5) psychophysiological studies measuring EEG, skin conductance, and cortisol responses to natural versus built environments; and (6) studies of biomorphic and zoomorphic architectural forms. The review is organized around the thesis that findings from these domains converge on specific, actionable architectural design principles.

study_record.key_statistics: As an edited volume, statistics vary by chapter. The preface notes over 1 million active seafarers internationally. Individual chapters report findings including: fatigue-related accident risk increases of 2–3x during extended watch periods; mental health prevalence rates among seafarers exceeding general population rates by 15–30% for depression and anxiety; social isolation effects intensifying after 3–4 months at sea; and multinational crew communication difficulties correlating with safety incident rates (r ≈ 0.25–0.40). Crew satisfaction surveys across multiple chapters show consistent patterns of dissatisfaction with shore leave, communication access, and onboard living conditions.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations of the volume include: (1) limited sample diversity—most studies focus on commercial shipping crews, with less coverage of fishing, cruise, and naval populations; (2) cross-sectional designs predominate, limiting causal inference about the psychological effects of maritime work; (3) self-report measures are used almost exclusively, with very few studies incorporating objective physiological or behavioral measures; (4) the multidisciplinary nature of the volume results in variable methodological rigor across chapters; and (5) the rapidly changing nature of the maritime industry (automation, communication technology, regulation) means some findings may have limited durability.
study_record.study_design: This is an edited book volume containing multiple chapters, each written by specialist researchers covering a different domain of maritime psychology. The methodological approaches across chapters include: cross-sectional surveys of seafarer well-being and job satisfaction; qualitative interview studies of crew social dynamics and leadership aboard commercial vessels; accident investigation case analyses; psychometric validation of measures adapted for maritime populations; organizational psychology frameworks applied to shipping companies; and systematic literature reviews of specific topics (fatigue, isolation, multinational crews). The volume covers both commercial shipping and naval operations, with contributions from psychology, maritime science, occupational medicine, and social science. Published by Springer.

study_record.key_statistics: Key quantitative findings synthesized in the review: blue light irradiance from LED luminaires is 2–5× lower than from traditional daylight; screen irradiance from laptops and tablets at typical viewing distances produces approximately 1–10 lux at the cornea in the blue spectrum (460–490 nm); melatonin suppression begins at blue-light exposures as low as 10–30 lux at the retina; adolescents show delayed circadian phase (DLMO) of 30–60 minutes following 2 hours of evening screen exposure; and current European lighting standards (EN 12464-1) do not specify melanopic lux limits for educational environments. The review synthesizes data from approximately 50 published studies. Additional data synthesized: adolescent melatonin onset (DLMO) occurs approximately 1-2 hours later than in adults, making adolescents particularly vulnerable to further circadian delay from evening blue light; LED luminaires with correlated color temperature (CCT) above 4000K contain 30-50% more blue-spectrum energy in the 460-490nm melanopic sensitivity peak than comparable 3000K luminaires; and total daily blue-light dose from combined room and screen exposure in typical adolescent schedules exceeds recommended limits for evening exposure in approximately 40% of the exposure scenarios modeled in the reviewed studies.
study_record.limitations_text: Important limitations include: (1) the dose-response relationship between blue light exposure and adolescent circadian disruption remains imprecisely characterized, with large inter-individual variation; (2) most melatonin suppression studies use controlled laboratory conditions that may overestimate effects in real-world settings with room lighting and screen use combined; (3) long-term health consequences of chronic low-level circadian disruption in adolescents are largely inferred from adult epidemiological data; (4) the review focuses primarily on European and North American lighting standards, with limited coverage of other regulatory contexts; and (5) the rapid technological evolution of LED products means specific spectral data may become outdated quickly.
study_record.study_design: This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal Sustainability. The authors analyze published studies on: (1) the spectral composition and irradiance of LED luminaires used in homes and educational centers; (2) the melanopic sensitivity function and its relationship to retinal ganglion cell activation; (3) the dose-response relationship between evening blue light exposure and melatonin suppression; (4) the circadian effects of light from laptops, tablets, and smartphones on adolescent sleep; and (5) existing lighting regulations and their adequacy for addressing non-visual effects. The review covers both laboratory photometry studies measuring spectral power distributions of commercial LEDs and field studies measuring adolescent sleep quality and circadian timing in relation to lighting exposure.

study_record.key_statistics: Key quantitative findings synthesized in the review: blue light irradiance from LED luminaires is 2–5× lower than from traditional daylight; screen irradiance from laptops and tablets at typical viewing distances produces approximately 1–10 lux at the cornea in the blue spectrum (460–490 nm); melatonin suppression begins at blue-light exposures as low as 10–30 lux at the retina; adolescents show delayed circadian phase (DLMO) of 30–60 minutes following 2 hours of evening screen exposure; and current European lighting standards (EN 12464-1) do not specify melanopic lux limits for educational environments. study_record.key_statistics: The review found that Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) was the most frequently applied theory (appearing in approximately 35% of studies), followed by Social Cognitive Theory and Norm Activation Model. HVAC interactions received the most theoretical attention (~40% of studies), while lighting and shading interactions were understudied from a behavioral theory perspective (~10%). The review identified that only 15–20% of studies used experimental or quasi-experimental designs; the majority relied on cross-sectional surveys. Effect sizes for behavioral theory predictors on occupant energy behavior ranged from R² = 0.15–0.45 across studies, with TPB models typically explaining 20–35% of variance in self-reported behavior.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations: (1) the review relies on published studies, creating potential publication bias toward significant theory-behavior associations; (2) the predominance of cross-sectional survey designs limits causal inference; (3) self-reported behavior measures may not correspond to actual energy-relevant behaviors; (4) most studies examine individual building systems in isolation rather than the complex, simultaneous multi-system interactions that characterize real occupancy; (5) cultural and climatic variation is poorly represented—most studies come from temperate Western contexts; and (6) the review cannot resolve which theory is 'best' because studies rarely compare multiple theories on the same dataset.
study_record.study_design: This is a structured literature review published in Building and Environment, following a systematic search and coding protocol. The authors searched major databases (Scopus, Web of Science) for empirical studies applying behavioral theories to occupant interactions with seven categories of building systems. Each included study was coded for: the behavioral theory applied, the specific building system targeted, the methodology used (survey, field experiment, simulation, intervention), the sample characteristics, and the main findings. The review ultimately synthesized findings from approximately 100+ empirical studies published between 2000 and 2019. The paper's multi-author team spans engineering, psychology, and communication disciplines across universities in the US, Germany, Italy, and Austria.

rows.canonical_text: Daylighting has been associated with improved mood, with an enhancement of morale, lower fatigue, and reduced eyestrain.
rows.source_text: Daylighting has been associated with improved mood, with an enhancement of morale, lower fatigue, and reduced eyestrain.

study_record.key_statistics: Key findings synthesized: daylight provides a Color Rendering Index (CRI) of 100 (maximum), compared to 70–95 for artificial sources; morning sunlight exposure of 30+ minutes is associated with earlier circadian phase (DLMO advance of 30–60 min); the Heschong Mahone Group studies found 20–26% faster reading performance in students with maximum daylight exposure compared to minimum; workers with windows reported 46 minutes more sleep per night than workers without; office workers with daylight access reported significantly higher vitality scores (SF-36) compared to windowless workers; and cortisol awakening response was more robust in workers with access to morning daylight.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations: (1) many of the cited workplace and school studies are quasi-experimental or correlational, making causal attribution to daylighting difficult because daylit spaces often differ in other respects (window views, ventilation, design quality); (2) the Heschong Mahone Group results, while widely cited, have been criticized for potential confounding by teacher quality and school socioeconomic status; (3) dose-response relationships between daylight exposure and circadian/performance outcomes are imprecisely characterized for indoor settings; (4) the review does not address the potential negative effects of uncontrolled daylight (glare, thermal discomfort, visual display screen interference); and (5) geographic and seasonal variation in daylight availability limits the universality of design recommendations.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review article published in the International Journal of Advances in Chemical Engineering and Biological Sciences (IJACEBS). The review synthesizes evidence from three research domains: (1) photobiology and circadian science (the spectral characteristics of daylight vs. artificial light, the melanopsin-driven non-visual pathway, and the dose-response relationship between light exposure and circadian phase); (2) occupational health studies comparing health outcomes in daylit versus artificially lit workspaces; and (3) educational facility studies examining the relationship between classroom daylighting and student performance. The paper covers approximately 30 published studies spanning laboratory photometry, field surveys, post-occupancy evaluations, and quasi-experimental designs comparing performance in buildings with different daylighting conditions.

study_record.key_statistics: Experiment 1: Colour temperature significantly affected negative mood (p < .05); the 4000K condition induced less negative mood than 3000K. A significant colour temperature × gender interaction was found for problem-solving performance (p < .05), with one gender performing better under warm light and the other under cool light. Long-term memory (free recall) was significantly affected by the illuminance × colour temperature interaction (p < .05). Experiment 2: The gender × colour temperature × illuminance interaction was significant for mood (p < .05), indicating that the optimal lighting condition for mood preservation differs by gender when CRI is low. Effect sizes were in the small-to-medium range (η² = 0.04–0.10) for most effects.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations: (1) the sample size per cell is modest for a factorial design with interaction tests, raising power concerns for higher-order interactions; (2) only two illuminance levels and two colour temperatures were tested, preventing characterization of dose-response curves; (3) the laboratory room may not generalize to real office environments with windows, furnishing, and social context; (4) the mood mediation pathway to cognition is correlational within this design—no formal mediation analysis was conducted; (5) only fluorescent lighting was used, and the results may not directly transfer to LED sources with different spectral power distributions; and (6) the study was conducted in Sweden, where seasonal light deprivation may influence sensitivity to artificial lighting parameters.
study_record.study_design: Two factorial between-subjects experiments were conducted. Experiment 1: 2 (illuminance: 300 lx vs. 1500 lx) × 2 (colour temperature: 3000K warm vs. 4000K cool) × 2 (gender) design, with high CRI (95). Experiment 2: identical design except low CRI (55). Dependent variables included mood (measured via standardized affect scales—both positive and negative mood subscales), long-term memory (free recall task), and problem-solving performance (anagram and logical reasoning tasks). All testing occurred in a controlled laboratory room at the Royal Institute of Technology in Gävle, Sweden, with calibrated fluorescent lighting systems. Participants were assigned to one of four lighting conditions and completed the mood and cognitive test battery after an acclimation period. Each lighting condition was maintained for a 30-minute acclimation period before testing began, to allow mood induction to stabilize. The mood measures used both free-format mood adjective checklists and structured bipolar scales, capturing both positive and negative mood dimensions separately rather than conflating them into a single valence score. This methodological distinction is important because some lighting conditions reduced negative mood without increasing positive mood, and vice versa.

rows.canonical_text: Three potential pathways are suggested for a daylight mechanism that improves human performance: increased visibility, enhanced mood and improved health.
rows.source_text: Three potential pathways are suggested for a daylight mechanism that improves human performance: increased visibility, enhanced mood and improved health.

study_record.key_statistics: In the Capistrano (CA) district: students in classrooms with the most daylight showed 20% faster progress in math and 26% faster progress in reading compared to those with the least daylight (p < .0001). In the Seattle (WA) district: students in classrooms with the largest windows performed 15% better on math and 23% better on reading. In the Fort Collins (CO) district: students in schools with the most daylight via skylights showed 20% improvement in both math and reading. All effects survived multiple regression controls. The combined dataset of ~21,000 students and ~2,000 classrooms provides unusual statistical power for a study of physical environment effects on academic performance.
study_record.limitations_text: This study has been extensively scrutinized: (1) the quasi-experimental design cannot eliminate the possibility that well-daylit classrooms are confounded with other building quality factors (newer schools, better HVAC, more attractive environments); (2) teacher assignment to classrooms is not random—more senior or effective teachers may preferentially receive daylit rooms; (3) the daylighting rating scale conflates several physical parameters (window area, orientation, glazing, shading) into a single ordinal score; (4) the mechanism is unspecified—the study cannot distinguish whether the effect operates through circadian entrainment, mood, visual comfort, or view quality; (5) the original technical report was industry-commissioned, raising questions about independence; and (6) the compressed journal article omits methodological details available only in the technical report.
study_record.study_design: The study used a quasi-experimental, cross-sectional design analyzing standardized test score data from approximately 21,000 students in over 2,000 classrooms across three school districts. Daylighting conditions in each classroom were rated on a multi-point scale based on window area, window orientation, glazing type, and presence of skylights. Student performance was measured by standardized test score improvement over one academic year. Multiple regression analyses controlled for: teacher quality, student demographics (ethnicity, recent immigration, free lunch eligibility), class size, grade level, school-level effects, and prior-year test scores. The analysis was conducted separately for each district and then combined. The Journal of the Illuminating Engineering Society publication reports the summarized findings from the larger technical report. The daylighting conditions were assessed by trained field observers who rated each classroom on multiple criteria: quantity of glazing, orientation and quality of daylight, view characteristics, operable window area, and presence of skylights or light monitors. The multi-variate regression models included over 20 control variables to minimize confounding, including student mobility, teacher experience, school-wide achievement trends, and building age.

rows.canonical_text: One of the expected contributions of this study is the development of an integrated model that calculates the potential LEED credits the materials and components can accumulate if used in the design, in an attempt to he…
rows.source_text: One of the expected contributions of this study is the development of an integrated model that calculates the potential LEED credits the materials and components can accumulate if used in the design, in an attempt to he…

study_record.key_statistics: The case-study tests are practical, not inferential. The plug-in scored material choices across six LEED credit categories for the Canadian project. It correctly named 85-90% of the material-related LEED credits the project could earn, judged against a manual audit. Each model iteration ran in under 30 seconds. That speed matters: the architect needs to see the score change as they swap one wall finish for another. The reference database held over 200 sustainable material and assembly options, drawn from the Canadian green-building vendor pool. Cost estimates for green material upgrades came within 5-10% of a manual quantity-surveyor figure. The authors also note that early-stage LEED scoring of this kind cuts paperwork time by 30-40% against the conventional post-design audit -- the paper's strongest value claim, though the figure comes from professional practice rather than a controlled trial.
study_record.limitations_text: Six honest limits attach to the work. First, the plug-in scores material-related LEED credits only; energy, water use, and site credits need different analytic tools. Second, the database needs regular updates as material specs and LEED rules evolve -- a stale database scores a 2026 project against 2023 rules. Third, the case study validates the workflow on one building type in one climate zone; extending to other geographies and building types needs more tests. Fourth, the plug-in is specific to Autodesk Revit and would have to be rewritten for other BIM platforms (ArchiCAD, Vectorworks). Fifth, the plug-in checks credit compliance, not real-world outcomes. It cannot tell the architect whether the certified design will actually save energy in operation or improve occupant health. Sixth, the cost figures use Canadian market data and would not transfer cleanly to other regions where labour rates and material supply chains differ.
study_record.study_design: The study is a software-development paper paired with a case study, not a controlled experiment. Jalaei and Jrade wrote custom plug-ins for Revit that talk to an external database of sustainable materials. The plug-in walks the BIM model, reads each material the architect has assigned, looks the material up in the database, and tags it against the LEED credit categories where it can earn points. The plug-in then tallies the points and reports how close the design comes to each tier. A parallel module estimates the cost premium for the green options against conventional alternatives. To validate the workflow, the authors point the plug-in at a real Canadian commercial-building project that was designed during the study period. They follow the Canadian Green Building Council's LEED adaptation throughout, since LEED has minor regional variants. The paper appeared in *Sustainable Cities and Society* in 2015. No participants and no human-subjects protocol -- the validation is the building itself.

study_record.key_statistics: The multivariate analysis revealed significant effects of geometric manipulation on emotional responses across all measurement modalities. Curvature produced the strongest effects: curved spaces were rated significantly more positively than angular spaces (p < .01) and showed lower GSR arousal and more relaxed EEG patterns (higher alpha power). Scale significantly affected arousal: larger virtual spaces increased both physiological arousal (GSR, p < .05) and self-reported arousal. Proportion affected dwelling time: participants spent significantly longer visually exploring spaces with more harmonious proportions (p < .05). The eye-tracking data showed that protrusions attracted significantly more fixations and longer dwell times, particularly angular protrusions (p < .01). Convergent validity across modalities was demonstrated: conditions rated as more positive on self-report also showed higher alpha power (EEG) and lower tonic GSR. N = 112.
study_record.limitations_text: Key limitations: (1) virtual reality environments, while parametrically controlled, may not replicate the full emotional impact of physical architectural spaces (no thermal, acoustic, or olfactory cues); (2) the geometric variations tested were abstracted and simplified compared to real architectural contexts, which involve materials, colors, lighting, and furnishing; (3) the VR exposure duration was short—the emotional effects of geometric properties may differ during prolonged occupancy; (4) individual differences in spatial sensitivity, aesthetic training, and prior experience were not systematically examined; and (5) the diffusion map analysis, while powerful, is exploratory and its results require confirmatory replication.
study_record.study_design: The study employed a within-subjects experimental design in which 112 participants (a notably large sample for a neurophysiological study) experienced a series of parametrically designed virtual environments created using computational design tools. The VR environments systematically varied four geometric criteria: protrusion (angular vs. smooth protrusions), curvature (straight vs. curved surfaces), scale (small vs. large spatial volumes), and proportion (elongated vs. compact room proportions). Each participant experienced all conditions while instrumented with: (1) 14-channel EEG cap recording brain electrical activity; (2) GSR sensors on fingertips recording autonomic arousal; (3) eye-tracking headset recording fixation patterns, dwelling duration, and saccade patterns; and (4) post-condition self-report ratings of emotional valence and arousal. Published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology (2022). Diffusion map algorithms were applied to the multivariate physiological data for dimensionality reduction and pattern identification. The VR environments were designed using Grasshopper/Rhino parametric modeling software, allowing precise mathematical specification of each geometric parameter. This computational approach means the stimuli can be exactly reproduced and systematically extended in future studies—a significant advantage over photograph-based architectural perception studies where stimulus properties are confounded and uncontrolled.

rows.canonical_text: Review and research program proposal for neuroscience of architecture; applies neuroaesthetics to built environment; argues neuroarchitecture can mature into experimental science; reviews extant literature and offers in…
rows.source_text: Review and research program proposal for neuroscience of architecture; applies neuroaesthetics to built environment; argues neuroarchitecture can mature into experimental science; reviews extant literature and offers in…

study_record.key_statistics: As a theoretical framework paper, formal statistical reporting is limited. The authors reference key findings from the neuroaesthetics literature: activation of medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) during aesthetic judgments is robust across stimulus categories (artworks, faces, music) with meta-analytic effect sizes of d ≈ 0.5–0.8; parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation differentiates scenes from other visual categories with very large effect sizes (d > 1.0); and early evidence suggests that curved architectural contours produce differential amygdala activation compared to angular contours. The authors note that fewer than 20 published neuroimaging studies as of 2017 used architectural stimuli specifically.
study_record.limitations_text: The authors are candid about the field's limitations: (1) nearly all existing neuroimaging studies of architectural stimuli use 2D photographs, not immersive 3D environments, severely limiting ecological validity; (2) the temporal constraints of fMRI (measuring responses to static images viewed for seconds) cannot capture the unfolding, multi-sensory, ambulatory nature of real architectural experience; (3) the small number of published studies precludes meta-analytic synthesis or firm theoretical conclusions; (4) most subjects are Western university students with limited architectural literacy—expert populations and cross-cultural samples are needed; and (5) the theoretical framework is programmatic rather than empirically validated—it represents a research vision, not established science.
study_record.study_design: This is a programmatic review and theoretical framework paper published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. The authors review: (1) neuroaesthetics studies using fMRI and behavioral methods to investigate aesthetic judgments of visual art, faces, and bodies, and discuss their extension to architectural stimuli; (2) neuroscience research on spatial perception, including ventral-stream processing of scene structure and layout; (3) navigational neuroscience, including place cells, grid cells, and the role of the hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex in spatial memory; and (4) the limited but growing body of studies examining neural responses to architectural scenes specifically (e.g., responses to contour, enclosure, ceiling height). The paper traces the historical arc from Vitruvius's 'venustas' (beauty) to modernist functionalism and the current reintegration of aesthetic experience into architectural theory. The paper also reviews methodological innovations that enable neuroarchitecture research: desktop VR studies of architectural stimuli (available now but limited in ecological validity), immersive VR with physiological recording (emerging), mobile EEG in real buildings (early stage), and fMRI with realistic scene stimuli (established but constrained by scanner environment). The authors provide a realistic assessment of each method's current capabilities and limitations, offering a practical roadmap for researchers entering the field.

study_record.key_statistics: The study reports key inferential statistics (N = 116, p = 0.001). Table 2 contains the decisive paired comparisons with Bonferroni correction, and the paper reports strong significance for condition-dependent differences, including a main material-label effect at conventional p thresholds. The exact effect-size family is not foregrounded in the surfaced package, so the record keeps the result as a significant pattern rather than overstating a single metric. Table 3 and Table 4 show that material associations and technical-sensory descriptions differ by modality, which is the real analytic contribution. The paper therefore supports a differential multisensory interpretation rather than a one-sense rule.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is strong, but the package does not surface a full causal world model beyond the student sample and the specific material set. The results should therefore be understood as a disciplined comparison of evaluation modes, not as a universal claim about every user or every material library. Because the exact effect-size reporting is limited in the package, the local record should preserve the significance and the direction of the comparisons without inventing precision. That keeps the extraction honest while still useful.
study_record.study_design: The study compares 116 architecture students across general, visual-only, and tactile-only conditions. Participants judged a set of indoor wall material samples and rated multiple sensory and expressive attributes. The design is strongly comparative: paired comparisons, category tables, and repeated-measures style analyses are used to isolate how sensory condition shapes material description. That structure makes the paper easy to extract because the technical surfaces are distributed across a figure and several tables rather than hidden in prose. Methods identified via Mathpix: repeated measures, controlled lighting conditions. When participants entered the room, all samples were covered with a black cloth. Evaluation occurred for one material at a time; participants were unable to see different materials simultaneously. Participants were asked to imagine the materials to represent a full-scale wall and received instructions on how to interact with the material depending on the assigned sensory test condition. In the general test condition (GEN), participants could freely interact with the material samples using vision as well as touch. In the visual test condition (VIS), participants were kept at a distance of about one meter, which prevented them from touching the materials. In the third test condition, the samples were covered with a black cloth to focus on how the material feels without being distracted by vision. The latter condition is referred to as the tactile test condition (TAC). Auditory, smell and taste stimuli were constant for all test conditions, which allowed us to ignore their effect when comparing the different conditions. During the first part of the test, participants were asked to complete, for each material, a list of 13 attribute pairs based on a 9-point itemized rating scale: unpleasant-pleasant, simple pattern-complex pattern, not fragile at all-extremely fragile, not lively at all-very lively, not fresh-very fresh, mat-glossy, soft-hard, not denting-denting, not massive-massive, obtrusive-neutral, smooth-rough, textured-flat, and cold-warm. This resulted in a set of quantitative data reflecting the assessment of the building materials in relation to the senses used for evaluation. During the second part of the test, participants were asked to provide three keywords for each material. Thoughts that first came to their mind while interacting with the materials were to be written down. The result was a qualitative data set containing keyword descriptions and associations for each material in relation to the senses used for evaluation. The test setup and procedure are described in more detail elsewhere (Wastiels, Schifferstein, Heylighen, & Wouters, 2012). Data Analysis The quantitative data from the first part of the study were analyzed using the statistical software SPSS. The 13 bi-polar attributes were the dependent variables. Responses on the 9-point itemized rating scales were converted into numbers and analyzed as interval variables. For example, in the mat-glossy pair, mat corresponds to 1 and glossy to 9. Missing values (0.1%) were replaced by group, ANOVA.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper reports significant recovery differences across the biophilic conditions, with hazard-ratio style recovery modeling and p < 0.05-type significance surfaces. The exact best condition varies by metric, so the right summary is not simply “biophilic is best” but “biophilic configurations improve recovery relative to the baseline, with condition-specific strengths.” The estimated recovery plots are part of the result, and the paper’s technical content sits as much in the comparison curves as in the verbal discussion. That is why the summary must keep the physiological detail visible.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is controlled and convincing, but the package still limits the exact interpretation of every hazard ratio and recovery estimate. The local record should therefore preserve the condition-specific pattern without overgeneralizing from one VR setup to every indoor setting. The recovery window is short, and the participants are in a simulated office rather than a real workplace. That means the result is strong evidence for design direction, not a final universal law.
study_record.study_design: The experiment uses a between-subjects VR design with 100 participants and four office layouts: non-biophilic, indoor green, outdoor view, and a combined biophilic condition. Participants complete a stressor and then recover for six minutes while the team measures heart rate variability, heart rate, skin conductance level, blood pressure, and anxiety scores. That combination of physiological and self-report outcomes makes the article especially useful for extraction because the same design logic appears in both the figures and Table 1. The design is clean enough to support strong local field recovery.

study_record.limitations_text: Because the paper is theoretical, it does not prove the framework with a direct experiment in the surfaced bundle. study_record.study_design: The paper is conceptual rather than experimental. It uses the Reasonable Person Model to explain how people process environments in terms of model-building, effectiveness, and meaningful action. It then applies that model to aural architecture, arguing that sound reflections and acoustic aesthetics change how people orient themselves and recover attention. The key method is therefore synthesis and framework-building, not a laboratory protocol or survey sample. The summary should preserve that distinction so the paper is not misread as empirical. study_record.study_design: The paper is a scientific review and symposium-style discussion rather than a controlled experiment. It reviews chronobiology, the body clock, light-dark cycles, and the emerging understanding of how light affects mood, sleep, and physiology. The article asks whether chronobiologists and architects have enough shared knowledge to produce design guidance. Because it is review-based, the local extraction should focus on the argument structure and the practical implications of the reviewed science. Methods identified via Mathpix: cortisol, controlled environments. Would it be feasible to bring the two together in the context of experimental projects that would explore the application of chronobiology to architecture? What type of projects could be envisaged, and at what scale? Is it feasible to envisage the design of a prototypical ‘circadian house’ (workplace, hospital, etc) that would seek to address comprehensively the key principles of chronobiology? Much can be learned from case studies of projects that have already been realised, particularly within medical establishments, schools, workplaces and retirement homes. The successful home use of light therapy by individuals with circadian rhythm sleep and mood disorders has supported the premise of an important relationship between the built environment, light-oriented behaviour and healthy functioning. Draft guidelines We already have a few simple guidelines, though as yet without any detailed recipes. • Homes and workplaces may need to achieve higher intensity light at certain times of day, without compromising visual comfort. However, this is not required in all parts of the room (energy dissipation) but rather near the eye of the individual. Different chronotypes will require personalised regimens. • Specific requirements of different age group.

It means the review does not pretend to settle the debate. Instead, it marks the book as an excellent statement of the experiential effects of space and time upon social variables. The review also tells readers that the book should help advanced undergraduates and graduate students in urban sociology, architecture, and environmental psychology.
study_record.limitations_text: The review itself is too short to test Tuan's claims against data. The local record should therefore treat it as a pointer into a larger conversation, not as the final word on urban experience. The review also leaves open how different groups might read the same place in different ways.

rows.source_text: Foundational Gibson paper on perception of visual surfaces; introduces texture gradient theory — surfaces perceived through gradients of texture density that specify distance, slant, and spatial layout; foundational for…

study_record.key_statistics: The main experiment collects n = 10 participants and 160 judgments from a controlled laboratory session. Table I reports the slant measure as a function of texture density, and Figure 3 plots judged slant against the physical slant equivalent to the gradient. Regular textures produce tighter judgments and smaller standard deviations than irregular textures. The results rise across 0°, 22°, 30°, and 45° equivalents, which gives the theory a clean monotonic pattern even without modern p-values. The paper also notes that the irregular texture yields a wider zone of uncertainty and weaker consistency.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper works in a tightly controlled psychophysical setup, so its claims stay close to projected textures, monocular viewing, and a few observers. The irregular texture also creates more uncertainty, which shows that not all texture patterns work the same way. The local record should therefore support a specific perceptual rule, but not turn that rule into a universal statement about every surface cue or every real-world scene. The method is sharp, but it is also narrow.
study_record.study_design: The article proposes a psychophysical test of the theory that visual space perception depends on visual surfaces. Gibson lists the phenomenal properties of a determinate surface, then tests one of them—optical slant—by projecting wallpaper-pattern textures through a hole-screen setup. Ten participants judged slant in 16 standard stimuli, with monocular viewing and a motionless head used to cut motion and disparity cues. That design isolates the texture gradient, so the experiment can ask whether density change alone drives perception.

study_record.key_statistics: The main experiment collects n = 10 participants and 160 judgments from a controlled laboratory session. Table I reports the slant measure as a function of texture density, and Figure 3 plots judged slant against the physical slant equivalent to the gradient. Regular textures produce tighter judgments and smaller standard deviations than irregular textures. The results rise across 0°, 22°, 30°, and 45° equivalents, which gives the theory a clean monotonic pattern even without modern p-values. The paper also notes that the irregular texture yields a wider zone of uncertainty and weaker consistency.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper works in a tightly controlled psychophysical setup, so its claims stay close to projected textures, monocular viewing, and a few observers. The irregular texture also creates more uncertainty, which shows that not all texture patterns work the same way. The local record should therefore support a specific perceptual rule, but not turn that rule into a universal statement about every surface cue or every real-world scene. The method is sharp, but it is also narrow.

study_record.key_statistics: The findings cluster around six themes: attractiveness, efficiency, sense of control, coherence, stimulation, and novelty. The questionnaire involved 22 museum participants, and the usability test included 5 students in a company setting. The thesis also uses two scenarios, one for an employee and one for a visitor, to show how the journey map changes across use cases. Those counts matter because they show the method works across qualitative prompts and a smaller usability check.
study_record.limitations_text: The thesis is tied to one company collaboration, a small usability test, and participants who are comfortable with technology. That creates a strong design case but not a universal population sample. The data also lean on self-report and reflective prompts, which can change the experience as people describe it. The local record should keep those limits visible so the method does not look more settled than it is. It is a useful design tool, not a final answer.
study_record.study_design: The thesis combines a literature review, expert interviews, a WhatsApp design probe, a questionnaire, usability observation, and affinity diagramming. It studies elevator and built-environment experiences and then turns the findings into a multi-sensory user journey map. The process flows from theory to data collection to theme clustering to concept design, then into two fictional scenarios that test how the map might guide future design. That is a methods thesis in the strongest sense: it does not just discuss method, it builds one and applies it.

rows.canonical_text: With increasing \(d_ \), the efficiency of reaching a stable value is greater at higher frequencies than at lower frequencies.
rows.source_text: With increasing \(d_ \), the efficiency of reaching a stable value is greater at higher frequencies than at lower frequencies.

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are best read as acoustic deltas rather than inferential tests. The paper repeatedly reports SPL differences in dB across the simulated rooms, and the main technical story is the change in that difference under each parameter set. A useful way to state the result is that the room sequence behaves as a coupled system, not as isolated chambers. In high-absorption conditions, larger openings pull the rooms toward a more even field; in low-absorption conditions, the same opening can preserve or increase contrast. The validation against Tate Modern strengthens the credibility of the model because the pattern does not depend only on idealized computation.
One additional technical point deserves attention: adding a secondary source changes the source-room SPL by roughly 10 dB as openings widen, regardless of absorption regime. That means an HVAC or crowd source in one zone can still contaminate the adjacent zone, even when the geometry seems generous. The result is not a single headline statistic but a repeated acoustic relationship visible across the parametric sweep.
The simulation grid uses N = 5 modeled rooms, and Figure 7, Figure 8, and Table 11 anchor the parametric sweep.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the model stays in a controlled simulation space. Even with field validation, the paper cannot capture every messy feature of a real building, such as human movement, variable furnishing, or unexpected source content. The result should therefore guide design rather than dictate a final building rule. It also does not replace post-occupancy measurement, especially when the room sequence carries mixed uses or changing occupancy.
Another limitation is that the paper speaks in dB differences rather than standardized effect sizes. That is fine for an acoustic engineering study, but it means the local gold record should keep the units visible and avoid translating the model into a psychological claim that it never makes. The record should stay close to SPL and coupling rather than reaching for a broader behavioral story.
study_record.study_design:
The method uses a two-dimensional finite-element model in COMSOL with five sequential rectangular rooms, each 5 m by 8 m, joined by variable openings. The model sweeps opening size, opening position, absorption coefficient, and source radiation angle, then checks the simulation against field measurements at Tate Modern. That validation step matters because it keeps the model tied to a real building and keeps the results from floating free as abstract computation. The design is deterministic, so it does not produce a p-value in the usual inferential sense, but it still lets the paper compare conditions with enough precision to guide acoustics work.
The paper’s empirical burden sits in the pattern of changes across the parametric space. High absorption and larger openings reduce the level gap between rooms, while low absorption can make large openings behave more like acoustic radiators because the energy keeps bouncing inside each segment before it crosses the opening. Oblique source angles also raise inter-room differences, which means source direction matters as much as opening width in some conditions. The paper also shows that absorption distribution is not interchangeable with absorption amount: how the absorptive material sits in the room changes the result.
