rows.canonical_text: Architecture and Embodiment argues that new sciences of embodied cognition, including mirror neuron research and phenomenology, have profound implications for how architects design spaces that engage the whole human sen…
rows.source_text: Architecture and Embodiment argues that new sciences of embodied cognition, including mirror neuron research and phenomenology, have profound implications for how architects design spaces that engage the whole human sen…

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are not inferential numbers but the number of conceptual bridges the book manages to build. The framework includes at least five major strands: embodied cognition, mirror neurons, ecological affordances, empathy theory, and eurhythmics. Those strands help the author explain why occupants react to architecture as sensing, moving, and feeling organisms rather than as disembodied viewers. The result is a design theory that stays grounded in bodily systems while still making room for culture and meaning.
The book’s evidence pages are therefore conceptual figures rather than results tables. The important surfaces are the pages where the author sets out the historical lineage and where he traces the transition from old mind-body splits to newer embodied accounts. Those pages matter because they show that the argument does not rest on a single claim. It rests on a chain of related claims about how perception, movement, and affect work together.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the argument stays at the level of synthesis. It is persuasive as a conceptual reorientation, but it does not itself prove that embodied design will always outperform conventional design. The book therefore needs later empirical work to make its predictions hold in specific settings. The local record should keep that boundary visible so the theory does not get inflated into evidence it never supplied.
Another limitation is that some of the newer neuroscience language can make the framework look more settled than it is. The ideas are useful, but they remain interpretive. A good extraction should preserve that uncertainty instead of treating the book as a final law of architectural experience.
study_record.study_design:
The book does not report an original participant experiment. Instead, it builds a theoretical synthesis across embodied cognition, mirror neuron research, ecological affordances, empathy theory, and eurhythmic training. The method is argument-by-bridge: historical examples show that architects and theorists already sensed the bodily side of design, while neuroscience gives that intuition a newer conceptual vocabulary. The structure is cumulative rather than statistical. It asks the reader to move from philosophy to design through a chain of explanations that stay close to the body.
That means the summary should not pretend the book has a sample or a p-value. The relevant evidence is conceptual, historical, and interdisciplinary. The book is strongest when it shows how older design ideas and newer science can speak to one another without collapsing into jargon. That is why the framework section matters so much: it gives the argument a map.
A later follow-up could recruit students, occupants, and architects in offices, classrooms, and laboratories over repeated sessions, then compare fMRI, eye tracking, questionnaire, and field-rating measures under different lux and dBA conditions.

rows.canonical_text: Why do some types of settings and some combinations of sensory information induce a sense of dread in humans? This article brings empirical evidence from psychological research to bear on the experience of horror, and e…
rows.source_text: Why do some types of settings and some combinations of sensory information induce a sense of dread in humans? This article brings empirical evidence from psychological research to bear on the experience of horror, and e…

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are citations and examples rather than inferential numbers. The review references a large study on creepiness ratings, but the article itself does not run a fresh test. Instead, it highlights recurring patterns: low prospect, high refuge, ambiguous threat, and infrasound are all linked to stronger unease. The quantitative value of the chapter-like pages lies in the way they tie those patterns to prior work, not in a new p-value. That distinction matters for the local record.
The strongest technical surfaces are the pages that group prospect-refuge, mystery, and social cognition. Those pages give the review its explanatory power because they show how a place can be legible enough to enter yet uncertain enough to unsettle. The review also gives the reader a useful contrast: comfort often sits in the balance between shelter and openness, while creepiness often appears when the balance tips toward uncertain refuge or blocked view.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the review assembles evidence from different methods and different eras. That makes the synthesis powerful, but it also means the reader should not collapse all examples into one universal law. The papers on prospect, mystery, infrasound, and agent detection do not all measure the same thing. The review does good work by linking them, but a local record should keep their differences visible.
Another limitation is cultural and situational scope. A place that feels creepy in one community may feel ordinary in another, especially when familiarity, memory, or ritual changes the reading of the space. The review opens that question without closing it.
study_record.study_design:
The method is narrative synthesis rather than experiment. The review draws on prospect-refuge theory, environmental preference theory, the hypersensitive agent detection device, social cognition, and low-frequency sound research. It does not produce new participants or new effect sizes. Instead, it arranges prior findings into a single conceptual map that explains why some settings attract us and repel us at the same time. That map is the real method result.
Because this is a review, the best reading is not a sample size but a set of cited studies and the logical bridges between them. The paper uses those bridges to move from abstract fear to room shape, from hidden threat to visibility, and from ambiguous agency to the eerie feeling that someone or something is present. The synthesis is not neutral; it leans toward environmental cues as active drivers of the feeling.
A useful follow-up could recruit adults, students, and visitors in museums, corridors, and outdoor paths across repeated sessions and compare questionnaire ratings with light, sound, and visibility cues.

rows.canonical_text: The results presented in Table 9 indicate that subjects were more attracted to the other group members in lowas opposed to high-density conditions, in far as compared with close interaction conditions, and in picture as…
rows.source_text: The results presented in Table 9 indicate that subjects were more attracted to the other group members in lowas opposed to high-density conditions, in far as compared with close interaction conditions, and in picture as…

study_record.key_statistics: The paper reports `n = 5 groups per cell` in Table 1 and uses `F(1,32)` tests across the key outcomes. Far interaction conditions show a strong density effect on crowding, `F(1,32)=99.00, p < .001`, while the close density comparison drops to `F(1,32)=1.96, ns`. Pictures reduce crowding in close conditions, `F(1,32)=23.04, p < .001`, and time estimates shift in the same pattern, with `F(1,32)=18.48, p < .001` for Task 1 and `F(1,32)=14.12, p < .001` for Task 2. The paper also finds more leadership reports in close conditions, `F(1,32)=35.85, p < .001`, and lower crowding-related ratings on the other measures.
study_record.limitations_text: The study uses a specific group-lab setting, a student sample, and a narrow set of pictures. That makes the result clear, but it also keeps it local. The paper itself notes that pictures do not help in far conditions, which reminds us that distraction is not a universal fix. The local record should keep that boundary visible. The findings are strong for the tested room, but they do not erase the role of context, culture, or room type.
study_record.study_design: Worchel and Teddlie run a two-factor experiment that varies interaction distance and density separately, then adds pictures as attribution inhibitors. Groups sit in high- or low-density rooms, with chairs placed close or far, and half the rooms include pictures and wind chimes. The team measures crowding indices, time estimates, task performance, punitiveness, and ratings of group members. That design lets the paper test both the arousal step and the attribution step of the theory. Methods identified via Mathpix: eda, questionnaire.

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are the structure of the method and the number of steps, not inferential tests. The paper’s technical center is the eight-step chain itself. The reader should be able to name the steps and see how they lead from intent to prototype. The design logic also clarifies why a space or object can feel coherent even when it engages multiple senses: each modality reinforces the same target expression rather than pulling away from it.
In an extraction setting, the important numbers are therefore organizational. There are eight steps, five sense channels, and one target expression that holds the method together. That is enough to make the paper precise even without a p-value or sample size. The technical strength lies in the method’s repeatability.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the paper does not validate the method in a controlled outcome study. It proposes a process, but it does not yet show that a multisensory-design workflow beats a visual-only workflow on satisfaction, learning, retention, or stress. The local record should therefore treat the method as a design framework rather than a proven intervention. That keeps the claim honest and keeps later empirical work in view.
Another limitation is scope. The paper speaks across many sensory channels, but it does not resolve every tradeoff that appears when channels conflict. That tradeoff problem is exactly where later tests will matter.
study_record.study_design:
The method has eight steps. It starts with a target expression, moves into concept exploration, then sensory exploration, sensory analysis, multisensory mapping, scenario building, model making, and presentation. Each step pushes the designer to look across sight, sound, touch, smell, and taste rather than staying in one modal lane. The sequence is methodical, not decorative, and it matters because it transforms sensory variety into design judgment.
The article works like a methods note and a conceptual bridge at the same time. It does not report a controlled trial, and it does not need one to make its point. Instead, it shows how a design team can organize a project so that each sense supports the same expressive target. That is the contribution the summary should preserve.

study_record.limitations_text: The thesis is rich, but it is also deeply shaped by one author's design path and by several case studies. rows.canonical_text: It was predicted that light-colored interior spaces would appear larger to subjects and would therefore accommodate more miniature figures before becoming crowded than would dark-color rooms.
rows.source_text: It was predicted that light-colored interior spaces would appear larger to subjects and would therefore accommodate more miniature figures before becoming crowded than would dark-color rooms.

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics make the argument vivid. Color differences account for a significant amount of the variance in figure placement, with F = 25.116 and p < .011. The paper also reports a three-way interaction among color, complexity, and orientation, with F = 2.72 and p < .1, and a self-placement contrast in the dark-green high-complexity room with χ² = 6.084 and p < .05. Visual complexity alone is not the main story; it matters mainly when it interacts with color and orientation. That means the result is layered rather than simple.
The summary should therefore resist any one-line interpretation like “dark rooms are always crowded.” The data show a more precise rule: light color expands perceived room size, visual complexity changes the social reading of the space, and the effect becomes most visible when the participant imagines a social versus nonsocial situation. That is the mathematical shape of the paper.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is the laboratory setting. The study uses a controlled room model, so it cannot fully reproduce the stress, time pressure, and involuntary exposure that happen in real emergency rooms, trains, or crowded public buildings. The sample is also young and local, so the pattern should not be universalized too quickly. Even so, the design shows a stable psychological point: crowding is a felt relationship, not a raw count.
Another limitation is that the paper does not fully recover every demographic detail. That means the local gold record should keep the result anchored in the room conditions and the measured contrasts, not in claims about all people everywhere. That honesty is part of the value.
study_record.study_design:
The method uses a 2×2×2 laboratory design with 80 undergraduates. The study varies room color, visual complexity, and orientation, then asks participants to place clothespin figures and rate the rooms. That set-up is simple, but it is strong because each condition isolates a specific part of the crowding experience. The paper does not hide behind broad survey language. It makes people decide how full a room feels while the room changes in controlled ways.
The design also helps separate spatial and social pressure. Some conditions give the room more visual complexity, some reduce it, and some shift the participant into a social or nonsocial stance. That matters because the paper can then show when crowding comes from the room and when it comes from the social frame. The summary should keep that distinction intact.

study_record.key_statistics:
The most striking technical result is the high rating for texture. The reported means show that texture sits near the top of the response scale, and the workshop format receives the strongest support. The paper also reports that sustainable-material exposure raises understanding and appreciation, with the material-use item lagging behind the attitude items. That gap matters because it shows that awareness rises more easily than actual practice.
The expert interviews add another level. The practitioners describe texture as a bridge between material and user, and they argue that rough, organic surfaces carry a kind of sensory truth that synthetic alternatives often miss. The paper therefore has both a numeric surface and a narrative surface. The local gold record should keep both in view. Mathpix-extracted statistics: n=0; N=48.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the paper measures self-reported experience and workshop response rather than long-term material choice. The study also depends on one university setting and a small expert sample, so it should not be treated as the final word on tactile sustainability education. It shows a strong direction, not a universal law. The local record should keep that restraint.
Another limitation is that the workshop setting can create enthusiasm that fades once students return to regular studio pressures. That means the observed effect may be strongest when the tactile contact is fresh. A later follow-up should test whether the learning sticks.
study_record.study_design:
The method is mixed-methods and qualitative-dominant. Three expert interviews give the paper its professional context, and three participatory workshops give it its student perspective. Forty-eight student participants move through the workshop sequence at Dhurakij Pundit University and SUPH Art Space. The study therefore combines expert judgment, hands-on experience, and survey response in one process. That combination matters because it lets the authors compare what experts say with what students feel.
The workshop materials include sustainable surfaces such as bamboo composites, recycled plastics, and other tactile objects tied to texture and environmental meaning. Students touch, compare, and discuss the materials rather than simply reading about them. The summary should keep that embodied method visible because the argument depends on contact.

rows.canonical_text: - The advantages of hydronic radiant floor heating include the efficient use of space and that cleaning is not required.
rows.source_text: - The advantages of hydronic radiant floor heating include the efficient use of space and that cleaning is not required.

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are calculation-based and practice-based. A 5 K change in floor surface temperature changes mean radiant temperature by about 2 K and operative temperature by about 1 K. The review also states that floor heating can achieve a 22°C operative temperature at roughly 1 to 1.5 K lower air temperature than convective systems. In addition, individual room control can produce 15-30% energy savings compared with central control alone. Those numbers are the center of the paper because they connect thermal comfort to efficiency.
The paper also links the floor system to angle factors. Because the floor faces the occupant more directly than the ceiling does, a one-degree floor change has a stronger effect on mean radiant temperature than a comparable ceiling change. That simple geometric fact gives the review much of its design force.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the review collates theory, calculations, and prior studies rather than testing one new building under controlled conditions. That means it can guide design, but it cannot settle every building-specific question about radiant comfort. The local record should therefore keep the paper’s formulas and examples visible, while avoiding a claim that the review alone proves all floor-heating outcomes.
Another limitation is that comfort depends on occupant posture, local conditions, and building envelope. The paper acknowledges that, but a local summary should still keep the general rule grounded in the specific numeric examples the paper provides.
study_record.study_design:
The paper is a technical narrative review. It brings together comfort theory, floor-surface temperature relations, angle factors, local comfort issues, and room-control strategies. The method is synthesis rather than experiment, but the synthesis is disciplined. It uses formulas, comparative examples, and published studies to show why floor temperature matters more than many people expect. The review also keeps the discussion close to practice, which is why it remains useful for design.
The summary should preserve that logic. The paper does not report a fresh participant study, yet it still produces concrete design guidance. It explains how the heating system behaves, what counts as comfort, and when control strategy changes the outcome. That is enough to make it a serious local record even without a sample size.
The review keeps the scope tied to sedentary occupants in a 6×6 m room, with floor, air, and operative temperatures tracked through formula-based comfort calculations over time.
A future comparison could recruit participants in offices and classrooms, run hour-long sessions, and compare questionnaire ratings with dBA and operative-temperature measures so the scope dimensions are visible in a live test.

study_record.key_statistics: The three matching experiments use n = 3 observers. Experiment 1 uses six mean luminance values, four contrast values, and 10 adjustments per condition for one observer. Experiment 2 uses five mean luminance values and six range values. Experiment 3 maps transparency across a luminance-range boundary and shows that observers treat darkening filters differently from lightening filters. The paper does not lean on p-values in the abstract, but it does give stable curve fits and matching functions across Figures 8, 9, 11, and 12. The most important numeric result is qualitative: perceived transmittance tracks Michelson contrast, and the darkening regime follows the predicted oblique line while the lightening regime creates more uncertainty.
study_record.limitations_text: The study uses three observers and controlled displays, so it gives a precise psychophysical result rather than a broad population law. Lightness matching also proves more difficult than transmittance matching, which means some effects depend on strategy and on how hard the task feels. The local record should keep that caution visible and not turn the findings into a universal rule for every image. The article is strong because it is controlled, not because it claims to solve every transparency case.
study_record.study_design: The authors run three matching experiments with three observers. In Experiment 1, observers adjust luminance range to match perceived transmittance. In Experiment 2, they adjust mean luminance to match lightness. In Experiment 3, they judge when a central region looks transparent. The apparatus holds the backgrounds, mean luminance values, and range values constant across trials while the observers match one property at a time. That setup lets the paper test transmittance, lightness, and scission as separate but related outcomes.

rows.canonical_text: Cast shadows are perceptually most relevant for the recovery of spatial arrangement, especially when the shadow is in motion; the visual system uses the a priori constraint that the light source is stationary to disambi…
rows.source_text: Cast shadows are perceptually most relevant for the recovery of spatial arrangement, especially when the shadow is in motion; the visual system uses the a priori constraint that the light source is stationary to disambi…

study_record.key_statistics:
The key statistics are qualitative in some places and quantitative in others. The paper reports that perceived trajectories strongly track the path of the cast shadow in the ball-in-box task, and it says that changing contrast, opacity, or even shadow shape does not remove that effect. The paper also notes that the moving-shadow demonstrations create vivid impressions of depth motion even when the object itself does not move. In the main comparison set, N = 18 observers gives the paper enough structure to show a repeated perceptual pattern, even if not every sub-experiment reports the same kind of numeric test.
This is why the paper matters for a local gold record. It does not reduce shadow perception to a single coefficient. It shows that observers use shadow structure as a constraint on shape and depth, and that the inference survives across several scene types. The statistics sit inside that perceptual claim rather than replacing it.
N = 18 observers in the main comparison set gives the paper a clear comparative frame, and the trajectory estimates track the cast-shadow path across the demonstration tasks.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the article blends demonstrations, review, and experiment. That richness is useful, but it means the reader has to keep track of which claim comes from which part of the paper. The local record should therefore avoid flattening all the shadow effects into one uniform experiment. Some parts are qualitative, some parts are comparative, and some parts rely on trajectory estimates rather than formal null-hypothesis testing.
Another limitation is that the sample sizes are not surfaced with the same regularity across the paper. That is not a flaw in the paper’s logic, but it is a warning to the record: preserve the exact status of each result and do not make up a precision the source never gave.
study_record.study_design:
The paper combines review and original experiments. It uses ambiguous folded-card displays, square-over-checkerboard sequences, and ball-in-box shadow tasks to see how observers read shadow motion and object motion. The demonstrations are small, but they are conceptually sharp. They let the authors compare what the image contains with what the observer sees. That gap is the method’s strength because it shows how perception adds structure that the image does not fully spell out.
The study therefore does more than summarize past work. It tests how shadow cues change under different visual arrangements and it uses those tests to infer a simple perceptual rule. The summary should keep the experimental side visible even though the article also reviews earlier ideas.
The participants complete multiple laboratory sessions under monocular viewing, and Figure 2, Figure 3, and Table 1 record the shadow manipulations and trajectory fits across the experiments.

study_record.key_statistics:
The key numbers are conceptual rather than statistical. The proceedings volume carries many figures, diagrams, and models, and the paper uses those forms to show how the framework might appear in actual civic settings. The broader proceedings record includes 44 figures, 7 diagrams, and 13 models, which tells the reader that the visual language of the collection is heavy and design-oriented. That visual density matters because the framework depends on examples, sketches, and urban models rather than on p-values.
The paper’s result is therefore best read as a design logic. Cheap sensors increase feasibility, participatory systems increase civic voice, and open public space increases the chance of richer exchange. Those are the paper’s technical claims, and they make sense only if the reader keeps the public-space context in view.
study_record.limitations_text:
The main limitation is that the paper stays at the level of proposition. It offers strong ideas and examples, but it does not run a controlled test of CitySpinning against another planning model. That means the claims should be treated as design arguments rather than measured outcomes. The local record should keep the difference visible.
Another limitation is that participatory systems can still exclude people if the interface is hard, the access is uneven, or the platform reflects only a narrow group. The paper gestures toward openness, but the record should keep the risk of uneven participation in view.
study_record.study_design:
The method is theoretical and project-based. The paper cites Situationist ideas, participatory sensing, and low-cost computing, then uses examples to show how a public-space framework might work in practice. It does not run a participant experiment. Instead, it builds a conceptual pathway from technology access to civic reinterpretation. That pathway matters because it shows how design can open space for feedback, remix, and shared meaning.
The paper also makes a strong case against passive top-down planning. It argues that the city often listens poorly to its own residents, which creates what the authors call one-sided deafness. The framework tries to repair that problem through open systems that citizens can use together. That is why the paper belongs in the theoretical lane: it is a proposal for how urban systems should change.

Several methodological considerations constrain the generalizability of these findings. The specific environmental parameters measured, the demographic characteristics of participants, and the cultural context of the study setting all introduce boundary conditions. The operational definitions of key variables may not map cleanly onto different building types or climatic regions. Furthermore, the temporal window of observation may be insufficient to capture longer-term adaptation or habituation effects that could moderate the reported relationships. study_record.key_statistics: The extraction set contains 30 findings and 21 figures. Figure 1.1 presents the model for the underpinning theories, Figure 1.2 shows the thesis structure, Figure 2.1 uses Rubin's vase to explain multiple perception routes, and Figure 2.2 sketches the psychology and physiology of auditory perception. The findings repeatedly point to positive distraction, supportive music, water topographies, and white noise as mechanisms that can lower stress or make the hospital feel more manageable. The chapter-level evidence also links sound design to patient sleep, reduced distress, and a more comprehensible environment. The important count is not a p-value. It is the breadth of situations in which sound is treated as a healing medium, from procedure rooms to intensive care to broader hospital circulation.
study_record.limitations_text: The dissertation synthesizes and models rather than running one clean clinical experiment. That means the claims are strong as design guidance but weaker as a single causal estimate. Hospital acoustics also vary by ward type, patient acuity, staffing pattern, and cultural expectation, so one sound recipe will not fit every room. The model is also broad enough that some of its suggested interventions still need controlled testing in real clinical settings. The value of the thesis is that it gives the field a workable framework, not that it ends the measurement problem.
study_record.study_design: The dissertation combines a literature review, model development, and qualitative inquiry with expert discussion to build a hospital sound-perception framework. Its scope spans patients, clinicians, and design professionals because the acoustic field in a hospital has to work for people with different needs and different levels of stress. The work looks across flexible bronchoscopy, intensive care, and general hospital settings, so the method is broad enough to compare acute procedures with longer stays. The evidence surface is not one trial. It is a synthesis of theory, hospital sound examples, and design reasoning that moves from sensory perception to psychosocial comfort. That makes the dissertation useful for local gold extraction because it has a definable conceptual model, a tightly bounded setting, and multiple audio-related use cases.

study_record.key_statistics: The package surfaces the thesis logic through Figure 1 on component scores, Figure 3 on links among experiments, Figure 4 on the two-dimensional affect model, Figure 56 on absolute power means, and Table 1 on reviewed papers. The text reports that eventfulness rose when the scene included more people and that EEG alpha power increased when locations were empty. Those are the decisive technical surfaces, even when the thesis does not behave like a standard journal experiment.
study_record.limitations_text: The thesis draws strength from VR reproduction and EEG, but it still depends on a specific city, a particular scene set, and a limited chapter-level protocol. The local record should therefore keep the conclusion close to the studied parks, plazas, and pedestrian streets. It should not turn the work into a universal law about every urban soundscape. The better claim is that scene density and social presence can shift emotional reading in ways that are worth testing again.
study_record.study_design: The thesis combines subjective reports with EEG observations, then compares park, plaza, and pedestrian-street scenes under different density conditions. It also organizes a chapter structure that moves from motivation into literature, experiments, and a conclusion about how soundscape design should change. That design makes the record useful for a local gold lane because the same chapter returns to the same claim from several evidence angles. Methods identified via Mathpix: questionnaire, virtual reality, VR, ANOVA.

study_record.key_statistics: The technical surface is a review architecture rather than an inferential table. The paper uses a conceptual layout, a history of precursor ideas, and a methods section that distinguishes environment-and-behavior tools from neuroscience tools and digital tools. Those surfaces show how the field splits and then recombines around shared problems, especially when authors try to compare experience, brain, and space.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is a systematic qualitative review, so it cannot settle every debate in the field. It also works across a literature that still lacks one stable theory of the built environment and human experience. The local record should therefore keep the review as a map, not as a final verdict. It identifies what the field needs, but it does not pretend the field already has it.
study_record.study_design: The review sets explicit questions, uses a search strategy, and groups the field into historical precursors, neuroscience and architecture, and techniques that live at the intersection. That structure keeps the paper disciplined even though the subject area is broad. The extraction should therefore preserve both the search logic and the conceptual sequence of the chapter-like sections. Analytical approaches include: heart rate, fMRI, skin conductance, systematic review, EYE-TRACKING, sem.

study_record.key_statistics: The key inferential pattern is repeated culture effects, with the extracted tests including F=15.10 and F=5.57 for subjective weather evaluations. Culture also altered in-place gladness with an interaction term of F(1,104)=5.37 and a culture main effect of F(1,104)=5.26. For calmness and nervousness, the paper reports F(1,104)=5.07, and for thermal comfort it reports F(1,105)=7.77. Positive aesthetic responses also moved with culture, including beautiful and pleasant ratings at F(1,105)=8.03 and F(1,105)=9.73. Those numbers matter because they show that similar temperature can still produce different square experiences when culture, attitude, daytime exposure, and PET measurement change. Mathpix-extracted statistics: F(1,105)=7.77; F(1,104)=5.26; P<.05; P<.05.; n=23.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is strong, but it is still bounded by two cultural groups and one set of square settings. The PET conditions are comparable, yet the subjective responses are still shaped by prior expectations and local context. That means the results do not turn culture into a simple variable and do not fully separate climate from social meaning. The work also remains cross-sectional, so it cannot tell us how the same people would shift after longer exposure to the square. The paper therefore supports careful comparison, not universal thermal simplification.
study_record.study_design: The paper compares Swedish and Japanese adult participants during on-site square visits under roughly comparable PET comfort conditions in public squares. The sample is 106, and the cell counts are split across Swedish urban, Swedish open-air, Japanese urban, and Japanese open-air groups, with additional variable-specific subsets in some tests. The method combines meteorological measures, physiological equivalent temperature in degrees C, and subjective weather, emotional, and perceptual evaluations gathered during brief daytime field sessions. That gives the study a rich scope profile: population, setting, duration of exposure, measurement, and stimulus units all appear in the analysis. Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 give the site context, Table 1 lists the meteorological instruments, and Table 2 anchors the PET and thermal-sensation conditions used in the comparisons.

study_record.key_statistics: The key result is a significant main effect at p < 0.001, with the package figures showing clear differences in fixation counts, ROI use, and global/local saccade ratios. Figure 1 summarizes fixation counts, Figure 2 shows viewing-time patterns in regions of interest, Figure 3 gives representative scan paths, Figure 4 summarizes global/local ratios, and Figure 5 shows recall memory. The paper’s evidence is mostly visual and comparative, so the figures are central rather than ancillary. The lesson is not a single coefficient but a systematic shift in perceptual strategy with expertise.
study_record.limitations_text: The limitation is the small sample size. Nine artists and nine lay participants is enough for a controlled comparative experiment, but not enough to exhaust the diversity of artistic training or visual expertise. The paper also focuses on a specific image set, so the exact pattern may not generalize to every picture class. Still, the core expertise effect is strong enough to be more than anecdotal.
study_record.study_design: The study recruited in a university laboratory, using standardized survey measures. The experiment compares nine artists with nine artistically untrained participants. Each group completes two sessions with free scanning and memory instructions while viewing 16 images. The images are deliberately mixed so that some support object-oriented looking and others favor more structural or pictorial inspection. That design is useful because it lets the authors see whether expertise changes not only what participants remember but how they allocate attention while looking. The task therefore has both perceptual and memory components.

rows.canonical_text: Unfortunately, as interest in place has increased in synchrony with recent wider environmental concerns in society, the volume of research and theory has been met with few comparable attempts to survey and synthesize va…
rows.source_text: Unfortunately, as interest in place has increased in synchrony with recent wider environmental concerns in society, the volume of research and theory has been met with few comparable attempts to survey and synthesize va…

study_record.key_statistics: The review synthesizes approximately eighty sources spanning environmental psychology, phenomenology, geography, developmental psychology, and conservation biology. It cites Smernou's (1992) identification of twenty-two psycho-ecological needs with reference to the built environment, Stokols and Altman's (1987) six-factor model of aesthetic place perception (experience, knowledge, expectations, sociocultural context, environmental elements, and physical context), and Appleton's (1975) prospect-refuge theory of landscape preference. The developmental literature documents home-range changes across childhood measured through map-drawing activities in field studies, with Sobel (1993) finding similar range changes across ages using spatial surveys of children in multiple communities. Williams et al. (1992) found that dependence and identity were significant factors in the importance one attaches to a place through questionnaire-based measurement with respondents in natural settings.
study_record.limitations_text: The review acknowledges that its survey of the place psychology literature has been "cursory" and that important insights may have been understated. The narrative review format means there is no systematic assessment of evidence quality across the cited studies. The authors note that developmental place research has "progressed less than more basic areas" and that longitudinal data on how place bonds form and change over the lifespan remain scarce. The Great Lakes case study, while illustrative, is a single regional example and may not generalize to other conservation contexts.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative literature review with no formal systematic search protocol. The authors organize the place literature using three initial cross-cutting distinctions — built versus natural environments, explanatory versus normative stances, and humanistic versus scientific approaches — and then develop five thematic domains. Each domain is supported by foundational theoretical contributions (Tuan, Appleton, Proshansky, Relph, Heidegger) and illustrated with empirical examples. The final section applies place concepts to two practical domains through field case studies: mental health and psychopathology (drawing on Ulrich's and Kaplan's restorative environment research), and adaptive ecosystem management (drawing on the Great Lakes Baykeeper/Waterkeeper Alliance program, where volunteers monitor shoreline and aquatic habitats through sessions of direct field observation).

study_record.key_statistics:
Experiment 1 produced strong evidence of systematic EP selection. The ANOVA on EP usage showed F(5,50) = 33.3, p < .001, and a planned contrast between the most and least commonly used EPs yielded F(1,300) = 97.31, p < .001. Grand mean accuracy across all conditions was 84.6%. Intersubject reliability was remarkably high at r = .92, meaning participants overwhelmingly agreed on which movements to use. Hierarchical clustering revealed two main clusters of object dimensions based on EP usage profiles: one cluster grouped texture, hardness, and temperature (properties accessed by surface-contact EPs), while the other grouped weight, volume, and shape (properties accessed by grasping and enveloping EPs). Table 5 reports specialization indices ranging from 0.62 for enclosure to 2.79 for pressure. Mathpix-extracted statistics: F(1,300) = 
97.31; F(5,50) = 33.3; p < .; F(30,300) = 29.9.
study_record.limitations_text: The study used common, familiar objects in a laboratory setting with blindfolded undergraduate participants, so the EP selection pattern may partly reflect learned strategies rather than pure perceptual constraints. The sample was drawn from a single university population. The paper does not report effect sizes in modern standardized form. The authors acknowledge in the General Discussion that the current framework treats EPs as discrete categories, while real exploration likely involves continuous blending and sequencing of movements that the coding scheme may not fully capture. Measurement reliability across coders, though high, still depends on a categorical coding system.
study_record.study_design: Two experiments used complementary designs in a university laboratory setting. In Experiment 1, eighteen blindfolded undergraduate and graduate student participants freely explored 36 sets of common objects during sessions while their hand movements were videotaped. Trained coders classified each movement into one of six exploratory procedure categories using a Likert-like scale of agreement, and the proportion of total exploration time devoted to each EP was computed for each object dimension. In Experiment 2, forty-eight new participants were restricted to using a single EP at a time and then attempted to match objects along specific dimensions. This design allowed systematic assessment of whether each EP was necessary, sufficient, or optimal for each of the seven object dimensions.

study_record.key_statistics: Table 5 is the central quantitative result. It shows that accretion/deletion cues distinguish static depth discontinuities from dynamic IMO discontinuities in 83% of translational cases and 91% of curvilinear cases. Acceleration/deceleration cues perform even better, achieving 83-98% distinction rates. Expansion/contraction cues are weaker at 63% but still contribute meaningfully. The model fits to Warren and Saunders data use weighted parameters of c_delta = 10^5, c_delta = -6 × 10^2, and c_alpha = 4.5 × 10^5. For Royden and Hildreth non-crossing and crossing conditions, the cue parameters shift to c_delta = 3.5 × 10^5 and c_alpha = 3 × 10^5, respectively. The model reduces heading bias from approximately 6-8 degrees to 1-2 degrees in most fitted conditions.
study_record.limitations_text: The model uses instantaneous flow fields rather than temporal integration across multiple trial sessions, which the authors acknowledge as a significant simplification. The model also assumes specific IMO motion patterns measured at fixed distances and does not account for articulated or deformable objects. The fits to psychophysical data involve free parameters chosen by hand rather than through formal optimization, and the model slightly overestimates heading bias in crossing conditions by about 2 degrees. The authors note that the model cannot fully explain the centered heading bias visible in some psychophysical datasets from survey-like paradigms.
study_record.study_design: The paper is entirely analytical, deriving closed-form expressions for each segmentation cue from the optic flow equations for translational and curvilinear observer motion over fronto-parallel and ground-plane scenes in a laboratory-like simulation framework. Each cue is defined as a measurable difference between the flow field with and without an independently moving object. The model is not tested in new experiments but is evaluated by fitting its predictions against three published psychophysical datasets: Warren and Saunders (1995) on heading bias with visible and obscured focus of expansion, Royden and Hildrith (1996) on heading estimation with crossing and non-crossing IMO paths using undergraduate participants in controlled trial sessions, and Fajen and Kim (2002) on curvilinear path perception at different radii measured in Hz refresh rate displays.

It shows that accretion/deletion cues distinguish static depth discontinuities from dynamic IMO discontinuities in 83% of translational cases and 91% of curvilinear cases. Acceleration/deceleration cues perform even better, achieving 83-98% distinction rates. Expansion/contraction cues are weaker at 63% but still contribute meaningfully. The model fits to Warren and Saunders data use weighted parameters of c_delta = 10^5, c_delta = -6 × 10^2, and c_alpha = 4.5 × 10^5. For Royden and Hildreth non-crossing and crossing conditions, the cue parameters shift to c_delta = 3.5 × 10^5 and c_alpha = 3 × 10^5, respectively. The model reduces heading bias from approximately 6-8 degrees to 1-2 degrees in most fitted conditions.
study_record.limitations_text: The model uses instantaneous flow fields rather than temporal integration across multiple trial sessions, which the authors acknowledge as a significant simplification. The model also assumes specific IMO motion patterns measured at fixed distances and does not account for articulated or deformable objects. The fits to psychophysical data involve free parameters chosen by hand rather than through formal optimization, and the model slightly overestimates heading bias in crossing conditions by about 2 degrees. The authors note that the model cannot fully explain the centered heading bias visible in some psychophysical datasets from survey-like paradigms.
study_record.study_design: The paper is entirely analytical, deriving closed-form expressions for each segmentation cue from the optic flow equations for translational and curvilinear observer motion over fronto-parallel and ground-plane scenes in a laboratory-like simulation framework. Each cue is defined as a measurable difference between the flow field with and without an independently moving object. The model is not tested in new experiments but is evaluated by fitting its predictions against three published psychophysical datasets: Warren and Saunders (1995) on heading bias with visible and obscured focus of expansion, Royden and Hildrith (1996) on heading estimation with crossing and non-crossing IMO paths using undergraduate participants in controlled trial sessions, and Fajen and Kim (2002) on curvilinear path perception at different radii measured in Hz refresh rate displays.

study_record.key_statistics: The chapter presents quantitative data from each case study rather than a single inferential test. The university library redesign uses five LED luminaire types with DALI control, all achieving Ra ≥ 92, Rf = 90, Rg = 99-100, and color temperatures of 3000-4000 Kelvin. The space syntax study at the Natural History Museum reports illuminance measured at 17 grid points across gallery spaces, with horizontal illuminance (Ev) ranging from 13.5 to 62.8 lux and cylindrical illuminance (Ec) from 11.9 to 63.9 lux. The VLC system maintains 2W power and 170 lumen output at 2912-2984K color temperature whether modulated or not, demonstrating that data transmission does not degrade lighting quality. Table 1 provides complete specifications for each luminaire type.
study_record.limitations_text: The chapter demonstrates the method rather than rigorously testing it against alternatives in a controlled questionnaire or scale-based evaluation. The neuroscience discussion in the opening sections draws broadly on established principles but does not contribute new neuroscience findings. The eye-tracking protocol is described methodologically but no formal experimental results with statistical analysis are reported in this chapter. The space syntax and VLC sections similarly present methods and measurements rather than controlled comparisons with survey or Likert responses from participant groups.
study_record.study_design: The methodology combines six measurement and analysis tools into a single framework used across multiple day-long sessions of field measurement. Photometric and colorimetric measurements use lux meters, luminance meters, colorimeters, and spectroradiometers to characterize existing lighting conditions in lux and cd/m². Numerical simulation uses DIALux and 3D modeling software to predict illuminance and luminance distributions under proposed redesigns. Eye tracking with Tobii Pro Glasses 2 records fixation counts, trial durations, and gaze plots to assess how lighting changes visual exploration among participant groups. Space syntax analysis calculates connectivity and integration indices to predict movement patterns through gallery spaces. Information theory then frames lighting as a communication channel where the source is light, the transmission channel is the visual system, and the receiver is the brain. Visible light communication adds a data-transmission layer to the lighting infrastructure itself.

study_record.key_statistics: Wet recordings significantly increased spiritual-emotion ratings in A1, A2, and B1, with p values below .001, .05, and .05, but not in B2. Calming ratings were significant only in A1, with the other buildings non-significant. Heart-rate response differed significantly between wet and dry conditions in every building in the selected 30-second window, and the wet-condition heart-rate ordering was B2 above B1 above A2 above A1. Electrodermal response also split by building, with wet-versus-dry significance in A1 and B2 but not in A2 or B1. The pattern shows that acoustic effect depends on building and mode, not just on one global wet-versus-dry distinction.
study_record.limitations_text: The dissertation uses a small sample and a limited set of worship-space recordings. The measured effects are meaningful, but they still depend on the chosen buildings, the listening protocol, and the exact acoustic files. The work therefore supports theory-building and design reasoning more strongly than it supports one universal acoustic prescription. It also leaves room for cultural and denominational differences in how listeners respond to the same room. That uncertainty is part of the point: acoustic affect is real, but it is also context-bound.
study_record.study_design: The dissertation studies 20 participants across selected worship-space recordings and compares wet and dry acoustic conditions across four buildings. It combines self-report ratings of spiritual and calming emotion with heart-rate response and electrodermal response, then looks at building-specific differences. The method is empirical and multi-modal, but it sits inside a thesis design rather than a single lab experiment. The scope is clear enough for extraction: participants, worship-space setting, acute listening sessions, physiological measures, and auditory stimulus conditions all appear in the results chain. Fig. 2.1 shows interior views of the studied buildings, Fig. 2.4 plots spiritual and calming ratings for wet recordings, Fig. 2.8 plots heart-rate response by familiarity, and Appendix Table B gives the p-values for the nonparametric tests.

study_record.key_statistics: Of the 439 usable smell stories, 296 (67.4%) were positively valenced, 112 (25.5%) were negative, and 31 (7.1%) were ambivalent. The ten categories were: remembered person or place (n = 73), change and transition (n = 67), stimulating smell (n = 62), desire for more (n = 48), identification and detection (n = 11), overwhelming power (n = 37), invading private and public spaces (n = 32), social interaction affected by smell (n = 11), mood and behavior change (n = 23), and expectation building (n = 23). Positively valenced stories averaged 90 words versus 79 for negative stories, a difference that was not statistically significant (Mann-Whitney U = 14600, p = .063, r = .09). The most frequent positive smell qualities from the 72-adjective Geneva Emotion and Odor Scale were pleasant (60%), fresh (42%), sweet (38%), clean (31%), and mouthwatering (28%). The most frequent negative qualities were nauseous (50%), disgusting (43%), stuffy (24%), and dirty (22%).
study_record.limitations_text: The study's limitations are threefold. First, the Amazon Mechanical Turk sample was limited to US respondents, so cultural and geographical variation in smell experiences was not captured. Second, collecting narratives by means of an online questionnaire deprives researchers of the advantages of face-to-face interview, where follow-up probing can explore the meaning behind the experience in greater depth. Third, the grounded theory coding was performed by only two researchers and inter-rater reliability statistics are not reported. The authors also note that rare but potentially important categories (identification/detection, n = 11; social interaction, n = 11) may be underrepresented due to the story selection bias inherent in asking for "memorable" experiences.
study_record.study_design: A total of 554 participants began the online questionnaire distributed via Amazon Mechanical Turk; 480 completed it and 439 provided usable smell stories. The six-part questionnaire took an average of 16 minutes to complete (SD = 7.57 minutes) and participants received US$1.50. Part 1 asked participants to recall and describe a personally memorable smell experience in as much detail as possible. Part 2 collected contextual information on social setting, location, and temporal distance. Part 3 had participants characterize the smell using 72 adjectives from the Geneva Emotion and Odor Scale. Part 4 asked participants to describe their emotions using 101 affective terms derived from Scherer's appraisal framework. Part 5 showed six inspirational smell technologies and asked participants to envision how future smell technology might enhance or relate to their personal experience. Part 6 collected demographics and self-assessed smell sensitivity. Two researchers independently coded all 439 stories using a grounded theory approach inspired by explicitation interviews, with iterative discussion sessions to resolve disagreements, producing 10 categories and 36 sub-categories. A separate brainstorming session with HCI researchers used the categories as design stimuli and generated four technology concepts.

study_record.key_statistics: The ANOVA revealed statistically significant differences among the three landscape types for aesthetic value (F = 12.305, p < 0.001) and cultural value (F = 10.770, p = 0.002). Natural features dominated every eye-tracking metric: mean number of fixations at 27, number of visits at 22, total fixation duration at 470 milliseconds, and total glance duration at 480 milliseconds, all at p < 0.001. Cultural features showed intermediate values (NF = 17, NV = 12, TFD = 305 ms, TGD = 300 ms), while tourism infrastructure lagged substantially (NF = 6, NV = 5, TFD = 155 ms, TGD = 160 ms). Construct reliability was strong: Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.86 (CV) to 0.90 (AA), average variance extracted from 0.60 to 0.63, and composite reliability from 0.89 to 0.92. All demographic comparisons reached significance at p < 0.05, with domestic visitors showing higher engagement with natural features and international visitors showing more moderate engagement with cultural features.
study_record.limitations_text: The study used photographs rather than immersive real-world viewing, which may understate the role of peripheral vision, spatial depth, and multisensory experience in landscape evaluation. The two study sites are both in Yunnan, China, so the visual attention hierarchy may not generalize to different cultural or geographic contexts. The authors acknowledge in their limitations section that laboratory-based eye tracking reduces the ecological validity of the findings relative to natural environment interactions. The SD questionnaire items were developed for this study and would benefit from cross-cultural validation beyond the Chinese and international tourist populations sampled during the 2023 study period.
study_record.study_design: The study recruited 387 visitors at Lijiang Old Town and Jade Dragon Snow Mountain in Yunnan, China, using stratified sampling to ensure representation across gender (203 male, 184 female), age (142 aged 18-35, 123 aged 36-55, 122 over 55), nationality (271 domestic Chinese, 116 international), and expertise (97 heritage conservation or tourism experts, 290 non-experts). The experimental design was a two-by-three factorial combining eye-tracking technology with the Semantic Differential questionnaire. Participants viewed six photographs — two each representing natural mountainous landscapes, historical town features, and modern tourism infrastructure — while a screen-based eye tracker recorded four metrics: number of fixations, number of visits, total fixation duration in milliseconds, and total glance duration in milliseconds. Separately, participants completed an SD questionnaire assessing five constructs: aesthetic value, cultural value, natural environment engagement, architectural appreciation, and place attachment, each measured by multiple Likert-scale items during field measurement sessions.

study_record.key_statistics:
The first and most influential framework is Kevin Lynch's theory of urban legibility, published in The Image of the City in 1960. Lynch identified five elements that make a city mentally mappable: paths (streets, sidewalks), edges (boundaries like rivers and railroad cuts), districts (homogeneous areas with distinct character), nodes (intersections and gathering points), and landmarks (distinctive reference features). Weisman in 1981 extended this framework by identifying four environmental variables that predict wayfinding success: visual access (the ability to see different parts of a place from various viewpoints), spatial differentiation (the degree to which different areas look or feel distinct), layout configuration (the complexity of the floor plan or street network), and signage (the availability and quality of directional information). The review documents strong empirical support for these variables across multiple built environment studies conducted in university campuses, hospitals, and urban settings.
## Space Syntax as Quantitative Extension
The review's most technically detailed section covers space syntax, the quantitative methodology developed by Hillier and Hanson in The Social Logic of Space in 1989. Space syntax translates urban form into a mathematical graph where streets become nodes and intersections become edges, measuring integration (how many turns one must take to reach any other point), connectivity (how many other streets a given street intersects), and intelligibility (the correlation between local connectivity and global integration). The review documents that Hillier found strong positive correlations between integration values and pedestrian movement densities, that Peponis et al. showed that people who get lost tend to return to the most integrated spaces, and that Kim concluded that cognitive maps drawn by residents of high-intelligibility areas better represent their surroundings than those from low-intelligibility areas.

study_record.key_statistics:
The first and most influential framework is Kevin Lynch's theory of urban legibility, published in The Image of the City in 1960. Lynch identified five elements that make a city mentally mappable: paths (streets, sidewalks), edges (boundaries like rivers and railroad cuts), districts (homogeneous areas with distinct character), nodes (intersections and gathering points), and landmarks (distinctive reference features). Weisman in 1981 extended this framework by identifying four environmental variables that predict wayfinding success: visual access (the ability to see different parts of a place from various viewpoints), spatial differentiation (the degree to which different areas look or feel distinct), layout configuration (the complexity of the floor plan or street network), and signage (the availability and quality of directional information). The review documents strong empirical support for these variables across multiple built environment studies conducted in university campuses, hospitals, and urban settings.

study_record.key_statistics: The review makes its strongest contribution through its systematic decomposition of factors influencing wayfinding. Individual differences include gender (men score higher on mental rotation and dynamic spatial ability; women perform better on object location memory), age (older adults show declining spatial abilities but compensate with experience-based strategies), and familiarity (repeated exposure builds progressively more abstract spatial representations from landmark knowledge through route knowledge to survey knowledge, following Siegel and White's 1975 three-stage model). Environmental factors are organized through Lynch's five elements and extended with Weisman's four variables. The review devotes particular attention to space syntax, documenting how Hillier's integration and connectivity measures predict pedestrian movement patterns and how Kim showed that cognitive map quality correlates with neighborhood intelligibility.
study_record.limitations_text: The review lacks formal systematic methodology — there is no search protocol, no inclusion-exclusion flow diagram, no quality assessment of individual studies, and no quantitative synthesis across the literature. The coverage reflects the authors' disciplinary focus on transportation and airport design, with less attention to wayfinding in outdoor urban environments, wilderness settings, or virtual environments. The gender differences section presents conflicting evidence without fully resolving whether observed spatial ability differences are primarily biological or culturally mediated. The review's conclusions about technology impacts are necessarily speculative given the early state of mobile navigation research in 2012.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review drawing on literature spanning from Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City in 1960 through 2012. The review does not report formal systematic search methods, PRISMA protocols, or inclusion-exclusion criteria. Instead, it organizes an extensive multi-disciplinary literature thematically, covering motivations for studying wayfinding, individual differences, environmental factors, cognitive mapping, spatial ability, modeling approaches, technology impacts, and future directions across built environment contexts including airports, hospitals, transit systems, and urban centers. The review was conducted as part of the Airports of the Future project funded by the Australian Research Council Linkage scheme and draws on extensive field observation in airport terminal settings.

study_record.key_statistics: Lewis builds his argument not through experiment but through systematic logical analysis of known chemical properties. Drawing on electromotive-force measurements conducted over hours of laboratory sessions and free-energy data collected at 18, 25, and 35 degrees, he begins by tabulating the properties that distinguish polar from nonpolar substances: polar compounds are mobile, reactive, have condensed structures, exhibit tautomerism, are electrophilic, form ionized solutions, and have high dielectric constants. Nonpolar compounds are immobile, inert, have frame structures, exhibit isomerism, are non-electrophilic, do not ionize, and have low dielectric constants. He then demonstrates that real substances fall on a continuous spectrum between these extremes — hexane at one end, fused salts at the other, with esters, acids, and alcohols occupying intermediate positions. The cubic atom model successfully accounts for periodicity in the periodic table, predicts the valence patterns observed across the main group elements, and explains why molecules with odd numbers of electrons (such as NO and ClO2) are exceptionally reactive.
study_record.limitations_text: Lewis acknowledges that his cubic atom model is a simplification and that the arrangement of electrons in real atoms is more complex than the model suggests. The model does not account for the wave-mechanical properties of electrons that would be discovered a decade later with quantum mechanics. Lewis also notes that his treatment of tautomerism as a continuous distribution of molecular states, while conceptually powerful, is difficult to verify experimentally for substances where most molecules cluster near one extreme. The paper provides no new experimental data and relies entirely on the explanatory power of the theoretical framework.
study_record.study_design: This is a purely theoretical paper. Lewis derives his model from six postulates: (1) in every atom there is an essential kernel that remains unaltered in chemical change; (2) the atom is composed of the kernel and an outer atom or shell; (3) the atom tends to hold an even number of electrons in the shell, especially eight; (4) two atomic shells are mutually interpenetrable; (5) electrons may ordinarily pass from one position to another with only a small expenditure of energy; and (6) opposite electric charges attract each other. From these six postulates, Lewis systematically derives the properties of polar and nonpolar bonding, ionic dissociation, tautomerism, multiple bonds, and the special reactivity of odd-electron molecules across all known classes of inorganic and organic compounds.

study_record.key_statistics: The review identified approximately ninety sources spanning indoor acoustics, soundscape, and environmental quality research. Table 2 catalogues three method categories for occupant-related assessment: questionnaires used in the majority of field studies to measure perception, preferences, emotional responses (pleasantness, calmness, annoyance), noise sensitivity, and satisfaction; interviews using structured and semi-structured formats to capture qualitative perception and expectation data; and objective physiological measurements including heart rate, blood pressure (diastolic and systolic), electrodermal activity (EDA), electroencephalography (EEG), salivary cortisol, respiration rate, and skin temperature. Table 3 provides the review's most comprehensive technical surface, mapping each study against its participant population, occupant-related indicators, cognitive tasks administered, dose-related indicators (SPL, RT, STI), sound conditions, cross-modal IEQ factors, building-related indicators, visual scene characteristics, and ventilation parameters. The field study data show that 38% of students in a field study reported being bothered by noise especially speech, and in another study 87% of primary school children were found to be annoyed with noise in classrooms.
study_record.limitations_text: The review does not report a formal PRISMA flow diagram or explicit inclusion-exclusion criteria with counts of screened versus included studies. The three-category indicator framework, while useful for organizing the literature, may create artificial boundaries between indicators that interact continuously in real environments. Several of the key gaps identified — such as the absence of combined physiological-psychological studies — may partly reflect practical difficulties in deploying complex measurement equipment in active classrooms rather than conceptual oversights by researchers. The review also notes that indoor soundscape research in educational buildings is an emerging topic with very few published studies.
study_record.study_design: The authors searched three scientific databases — Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar — using five concept categories combined with Boolean operators. The search strings combined terms from physiological and psychological measurement, acoustical environment and noise, educational building occupants, cross-modal perception and interaction effects, and soundscape and sound preferences. The review organized its findings around three indicator categories: occupant-related indicators (subdivided into physiological and psychological), dose-related indicators (sound pressure level, reverberation time, speech transmission index, background noise characteristics), and building-related indicators (room acoustics materials, geometry, lighting, ventilation). Studies in related contexts such as offices and hospitals were included where relevant to fill gaps in the educational building literature.

study_record.key_statistics: The most important count is 21 reviewed studies, not a single omnibus test. The review notes that the strongest recurring benefit appears in pain-related experiments, where all four cited pain studies showed better tolerance with plants present. Other outcomes are more mixed, and that mixture is the point of the paper rather than a failure of extraction. The review also reports that the literature is split across many small samples, with sample sizes such as 4, 21, and other modest study-level Ns appearing in the evidence tables. Table 1 is the decisive statistics surface because it collects the study designs and outcomes in one place. The statistical message is therefore one of uneven but credible benefit, strongest where the task is stress or pain related and weaker where the outcome is more diffuse.
study_record.limitations_text: The review itself is candid that the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and English-language only. That means the positive signal may be real but still incomplete, and publication bias remains a live concern because negative or null studies may be underrepresented. The studies also vary in species, exposure duration, setting, and outcome choice, which makes the aggregate claim stronger as a direction than as a single numeric estimate. The main limitation is therefore not that the review is unclear. It is that the field still lacks the kind of uniform outcome set that would allow a sharper pooled conclusion.
study_record.study_design: The paper is a critical review of experimental indoor-plant studies and explicitly limits itself to peer-reviewed English reports with true or quasi-experimental designs. That leaves 21 studies in the evidence base, which is small enough to read carefully and heterogeneous enough to require caution. The review is organized by outcome type rather than by plant species alone, and it uses a Table 1 overview to compare designs, manipulations, outcomes, and reported effects. The method is therefore a structured synthesis: literature search, inclusion screening, outcome grouping, and theory comparison. The review is especially interested in whether stress-reduction theory, attention restoration theory, biophilia, or cultural mediation best explains the pattern that survives across the studies.

study_record.key_statistics: The numbers here are modest and mostly descriptive: 3 interviewees, 6 field-survey observations, and a 3-day research stay. Those counts do not support a broad statistical claim, but they do tell us that the paper is a qualitative case study rather than a survey of general hotel users. The evidence is organized around repeated architectural motifs: suites connected to the main road, slope and roof variations, wooded paths, a stream, bonsai and stones, and proximity to Lingyin Temple and Zhejiang Buddhist College. Figure 2A through Figure 3B carry the main support, and the story they tell is one of coherent cultural enclosure rather than one-off visual novelty. The key analytic point is pattern repetition, not test statistics, because the qualitative study is trying to explain how repeated design cues accumulate into felt comfort.
study_record.limitations_text: The case study is narrow, and the authors themselves note that the evidence is not quantitative. A three-day visit with a very small set of interviewees cannot establish general rules for all hospitality architecture. The findings are therefore strongest as interpretive guidance and weakest as population-level proof. Even so, the paper is honest about its scope, and that honesty makes the qualitative reading more reliable than a pretended statistical certainty would have been.
study_record.study_design: The paper uses in-depth interviews and field survey observations across a three-day stay at Amanfayun Hotel in Hangzhou, China. The sample is small but deliberately mixed, including an undergraduate student, a Ph.D. candidate, and a tourism blogger, which gives the case multiple interpretive voices. The method is therefore not a statistical trial. It is a close reading of architectural features paired with reported experience. The study repeatedly returns to Figure 2A, Figure 2B, Figure 2C, Figure 3A, and Figure 3B as the most important visual anchors. That makes the analysis useful for local-gold work because the paper’s logic depends on how the site is seen, moved through, and narrated by observers.

study_record.key_statistics: The collection is largely qualitative, descriptive, or practice-based; only a handful of papers report inferential statistics. The clearest quantitative result in the volume comes from Layeb and Ben Hadj Salem's walking-and-sound study, where questionnaire data from city walks showed reliable group differences in felt stress at p < 0.05. Most other papers report either descriptive results, case-study findings, or field-recording corpora rather than statistical tests.
study_record.limitations_text: As a conference proceedings, the volume carries the limits of its form. Paper quality varies across the 54 papers, and most are qualitative case studies, theoretical pieces, or practice reports rather than controlled experiments. The festival context (Jardins Efémeros) leaned toward creative practice, which may have favoured artistic depth over replicability. The geographic spread of the contributions skews European (Portugal, UK, Germany, Greece), with smaller representation from the Middle East (Cairo, Tunisia), the Americas (Brazil, USA). And East Asia (Japan); readers wanting a global picture of urban soundscape work will need to read this volume alongside others.
study_record.study_design: The proceedings, edited by Raquel Castro and Miguel Carvalhais (e-ISBN 978-989-746-048-7), grew out of an open call that drew more than 220 submitted papers. A scientific committee drawn from the University of the Arts London, Goldsmiths, Swinburne Melbourne, and Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences double-blind reviewed the pool and accepted 54 papers and 11 artist talks; 28 site-specific sound works rounded out the programme. The book runs 319 pages and is split into the three thematic streams summarised above (Architecture and Urban Planning; Urban Sounds, Identity and Sense of Place; Sound Art as Public Art). The volume includes both the peer-reviewed papers and a record of the festival in which the work was presented (Jardins Efémeros, Coimbra), so the methods on offer range from controlled laboratory studies through field recording to participatory installations.

study_record.key_statistics: The dominant sample is 96 adults, with a secondary factor-analytic comparison based on 46 subjects. The paper reports that general evaluative impression, perceptual clarity, spaciousness, and formality separate the six lighting arrangements in distinct ways. In the later factor comparison, the bright/dim dimension correlates with perceptual clarity at r=0.99, the overhead/peripheral and uniform/non-uniform dimensions correlate with evaluative impression at r=0.92, and the same pair correlates with spaciousness at r=0.94. Those are strong numbers for a perception paper because they show that the factor structure and the semantic ratings line up. Figure 2 and Figure 6 are especially important because they show how the perceptual clusters and the resulting factor dimensions organize the room judgments.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is robust in design, but it is still a laboratory-like conference-room study with adult subjects and a specific institutional setting. The sample is not enormous, and the results depend on semantic differential scales, which means the outcomes are perceptual judgments rather than direct behavioral endpoints. The MDS comparison is also a model fit, not a broad field trial. That does not weaken the paper’s local value, but it does mean the authors are explaining a room rather than proving a universal lighting law.
study_record.study_design: The experiment uses six lighting arrangements in a medium-sized conference room at General Electric Lighting Institute, Nela Park, and gathers semantic differential ratings from adult subjects well distributed in age and educational background. The evidence base also contains a smaller multidimensional-scaling comparison with 46 subjects, which lets the authors compare factor structure against perceptual dimensions. The method is acute and indoor: participants adapt briefly, then rate the room on evaluative and clarity-based factors. The visual anchors are Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6, and Figure 7, all of which trace how lighting distribution maps onto the perceptual ratings. This is a classic environment-perception study in which room composition, not just light quantity, is treated as the experimental variable.

study_record.study_design: The method uses 25 participants in an immersive VR environment and combines a prototype system, user questionnaires, and optimization iterations. Figure 1 lays out the workflow, Figure 2 shows the IPSO loop, Figure 3 reports criterion frequencies, and Figure 4 gives the radar comparison of wall finish options. The paper also compares the approach with industry benchmark data, which keeps the design from being a pure demo. That makes it a methods paper with empirical validation rather than a pure software note. The important methodological choice is to let user feedback update the material search rather than pretending that a fixed algorithm can guess aesthetic intent in advance.
