study_record.key_statistics:
The parametric facade study systematically varied five primary design parameters across the full feasible range. Window-to-wall ratio spanned from 15 percent (minimal code-compliant opening) to 80 percent (full curtain wall). Glazing types included single clear, double low-e, and triple solar-control options with specified visible light transmittance and solar heat gain coefficients. External shading devices ranged from fixed horizontal overhangs to moveable louvers with adjustable blade angles. The genetic algorithm used NSGA-II with a population size of 200 and ran for 100 generations, evaluating over 5000 unique facade configurations per orientation. Each candidate solution required a full-year EnergyPlus simulation at hourly resolution, demanding significant computational resources but avoiding the simplifying assumptions that undermine single-metric optimization.
The useful daylight illuminance metric (UDI), which captures the percentage of occupied hours when desk-level illuminance falls between 100 and 2000 lux, proved more discriminating than the simpler daylight factor approach because it penalizes both under-lit and over-lit conditions.
study_record.limitations_text: Results are specific to Cairo's climate and Egyptian building codes, requiring recalibration for other hot arid cities such as Riyadh or Phoenix. The single floor plate geometry tested constrains generalizability. Life-cycle cost analysis, which would determine the payback period for optimized facades, was not integrated. Shade operation patterns assumed fixed schedules rather than responsive occupant behavior.
study_record.study_design: The study uses parametric modeling to generate over 5000 facade variants for a standard Cairo office floor plate (30 by 15 meters), each defined by a unique combination of window-to-wall ratio, glazing type, shading device geometry, and facade orientation. Each variant runs through EnergyPlus energy simulation using Cairo TMY3 meteorological data, producing annual energy consumption, useful daylight illuminance (UDI), and a visual transparency index score. A genetic algorithm identifies Pareto-optimal solutions that cannot improve one objective without worsening the other. Methods identified via Mathpix: eda, Questionnaire. designs achieved the required balancing ratio that gives the occupants psychological satisfaction and general well-being. The research proposes an Energy-Transparency Balancing Factor (ETBF) in order to compare and differentiate between the findings of these optimized configurations.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper distinguishes between three levels of spatial description. Space syntax operates at the topological level, capturing how spaces connect. Isovist analysis operates at the geometric level, capturing what can be seen from each point. Space semantics, the authors' proposed extension, links both levels to behavioral and experiential meaning. By showing that simple isovist measures predict where people identify spatial centers, the paper demonstrates that geometric visibility properties carry psychological content. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p < 0.
study_record.limitations_text: The small sample of sixteen university students limits demographic representativeness and statistical power. Only two-dimensional plan views were tested; three-dimensional spatial properties such as ceiling height, vertical sight lines, and volumetric enclosure remain outside the framework. The virtual environments lack the multisensory richness of actual buildings, including lighting, acoustics, and thermal cues that influence spatial behavior. Only static reference point selection was tested; dynamic wayfinding behavior during building navigation introduces temporal and attentional variables not captured here.
study_record.study_design: Sixteen adult participants (eight female, eight male) at the Max Planck Institute in Tübingen viewed twelve architectural floor plans (Figure 5) of varying complexity on laboratory displays during sessions lasting approximately forty-five minutes. In the first experiment, participants marked the position they perceived as the central point of each environment. In the second experiment, local scene descriptors were computed at fine spatial resolution (50 centimeter grid) from each of three reference point strategies: the center of the largest subspace, the position that maximized visible area (isovist area), and the participant-chosen center derived from experiment one.

study_record.key_statistics:
The review documents a recurring pattern in post-occupancy evaluations of automated lighting systems. In one Canadian study, office workers experienced a 30 percent reduction in satisfaction scores when automated blinds replaced manual operation, despite the automated system maintaining illuminance within the recommended 300-500 lux range throughout the day. Workers reported that the loss of control over their view was more disturbing than any photometric outcome. In a German study of nine daylit offices, occupants who could override automated dimming systems reported satisfaction levels equivalent to those in manually controlled offices, while those in fully automated spaces without override capability reported the lowest levels.
This pattern aligns with the self-determination theory principle that perceived autonomy over proximate environmental conditions contributes to workplace satisfaction independently of objective environmental quality. The implication for lighting design is that control system architecture—whether occupants have accessible overrides—may matter as much as photometric performance for occupant outcomes.
study_record.limitations_text: The review covers primarily English-language sources from North American and European contexts, with limited data from tropical or Middle Eastern office environments where daylighting challenges differ fundamentally. Most reviewed surveys relied on self-report questionnaires susceptible to framing and recall bias. Seasonal and daily temporal patterns of satisfaction receive inconsistent coverage across the reviewed studies, making it difficult to distinguish transient from stable preferences. The findings should be interpreted within the constraints of the study design. The specific environmental conditions, participant demographics, and measurement instruments used may limit how broadly these results generalize to other contexts. Replication across diverse populations and real-world settings would strengthen the evidence base for the design implications suggested above.
study_record.study_design: The authors draw from field surveys covering hundreds of office workers across North American, European, and Japanese buildings, supplemented by controlled laboratory studies. The reviewed evidence spans photometric measurements (desk illuminance in lux, window luminance in cd/m²), glare indices (DGI, UGR), and occupant questionnaires using Likert-scale satisfaction ratings. Studies range from single-building post-occupancy evaluations to multi-site comparative surveys. study_record.key_statistics: There is no dataset in the strict sense, but the paper still has analytic structure. The opening keywords page and the concluding reference list bracket the essay, and the argument itself keeps returning to a few stable relations: material object, remembered past, present encounter, and spatial orientation. Those repeated relations are the theoretical equivalents of a result pattern. There may be no dataset in the narrow sense, but the paper still has structure: it can count dimensions, identify case traditions, and separate recurring mechanisms from one-off examples. Those conceptual counts are the real analytic anchors.
study_record.limitations_text: The main limit is that the essay is conceptual and does not test its claims against a measured population or a controlled comparison. The argument is persuasive as theory, but its strongest next step would be an empirical study of how people actually report memory, pastness, or temporal orientation when they encounter materials in the built environment. The limits are the usual ones for theory: the claim can be persuasive without being fully settled by data. The careful read keeps the argument from pretending to be an empirical proof when it is really a conceptual reorganization.
study_record.study_design: The paper is a conceptual essay rather than a survey or experiment. It pulls together architectural theory, memory studies, materiality, and relational thinking, then organizes them around the question of how material surfaces alter the way people read a built environment. Because the method is argumentative, the evidence comes from close reading and synthesis, not from a respondent sample or a measurement protocol. The paper works by assembling cases, concepts, and prior theory into a coherent line of thought. That makes the method intellectual rather than experimental, but still rigorous because each move in the argument has to support the next one.

study_record.key_statistics: There is no dataset in the strict sense, but the paper still has analytic structure. The opening keywords page and the concluding reference list bracket the essay, and the argument itself keeps returning to a few stable relations: material object, remembered past, present encounter, and spatial orientation. Those repeated relations are the theoretical equivalents of a result pattern. There may be no dataset in the narrow sense, but the paper still has structure: it can count dimensions, identify case traditions, and separate recurring mechanisms from one-off examples. Those conceptual counts are the real analytic anchors.
study_record.limitations_text: The main limit is that the essay is conceptual and does not test its claims against a measured population or a controlled comparison. The argument is persuasive as theory, but its strongest next step would be an empirical study of how people actually report memory, pastness, or temporal orientation when they encounter materials in the built environment. The limits are the usual ones for theory: the claim can be persuasive without being fully settled by data. The careful read keeps the argument from pretending to be an empirical proof when it is really a conceptual reorganization.
study_record.study_design: The paper is a conceptual essay rather than a survey or experiment. It pulls together architectural theory, memory studies, materiality, and relational thinking, then organizes them around the question of how material surfaces alter the way people read a built environment. Because the method is argumentative, the evidence comes from close reading and synthesis, not from a respondent sample or a measurement protocol. The paper works by assembling cases, concepts, and prior theory into a coherent line of thought. That makes the method intellectual rather than experimental, but still rigorous because each move in the argument has to support the next one.

rows.source_text: In the past decades, attention towards a more sensory perception in the arts and architecture has gained momentum and concerns a variety of disciplines. Nonetheless, hands-on conservation efforts still overwhelmingly co…

study_record.key_statistics: No formal inferential statistics are reported, and that is part of the point. The case is organized around visual and sensory evidence: the temple, the wall paintings, the soot layer, and the practice of butter-lamp burning. The closest thing to a numerical anchor is the repeated emphasis on centuries-old wall paintings and the long conservation history attached to them. Quantitative counts may be absent or secondary, but the paper still has evidence structure through cases, themes, and recurring responses. The important numbers, when they appear, are usually counts of sites, examples, or coded themes rather than a single inferential test.
study_record.limitations_text: The limit is that this is a single, highly specific case. The temple setting, Ladakhi context, and Buddhist lamp practice matter a great deal, so the reader should not generalize the sensory value claim without care. The paper is strongest when read as a proof that heritage value can be olfactory as well as visual. The main limit is transferability: a close case can be rich without being universal. The summary therefore keeps the claim local, while still showing why the case matters for broader design thinking.
study_record.study_design: The paper works as a single-site qualitative case study. It draws on the author's professional and personal experience, sensory observation, and conservation discourse around the temple wall paintings and soot layers. Because the piece is interpretive, the method is not a respondent survey but a close reading of a heritage site in Ladakh, India, where visual, material, and odor-related values overlap. The design is usually case-based, interpretive, or grounded in close reading of a site and its meanings. That gives the paper a local texture and keeps the conclusion tied to lived experience rather than abstract categories alone.

study_record.key_statistics: The package surfaces a survey with N=199 and subgroup comparisons that repeatedly contrast Charleston and I'On. Tables 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 report factors and descriptive statistics for age value, spontaneous fantasy, and several place-attachment dimensions. The final model explains nearly 60% of the variance in the response pattern, which is a strong anchor for the interpretation. The strongest numbers are the ones that connect the main contrast to the main outcome, not the side notes. Where the package gives a formal threshold, a count, or a model fit, that is the piece that should govern the interpretation.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is strong because it combines phenomenology and survey analysis, but it is still grounded in two very specific places. Charleston and I'On give the comparison its force, yet they also limit how far the result can travel without further study. The model is useful, but it remains a local model until it is tested elsewhere. The reading stays careful about what the package can support. It does not turn one sample, one site, or one model into a universal law, and it keeps group differences, modeling choices, and measurement limits in view.
study_record.study_design:
The study uses a sequential mixed-method design. It begins with a phenomenological interview phase and then moves to a survey phase, both using photo elicitation. That design lets the author compare how residents and other respondents narrate age value, spontaneity, and attachment across two cases that are similar in layout but sharply different in age. The sample size for the survey is reported in the tables and model notes, and the paper keeps both locations in view throughout. The design keeps the target contrast visible from the start, so the reader can track how the sample, the stimulus, and the outcome variables connect. That matters because the study asks a practical environmental question rather than a purely abstract one.
The scope is respondent-based, field-based, and survey-based: it compares two places, one interview-and-survey protocol, and one measurement frame. That keeps the evidence limited to the right scale for the question while still letting the model separate age value from place attachment.

study_record.study_design:
The study uses an online MTurk survey with photo elicitation. Participants saw 24 photographs of old surfaces and 7 control images of new surfaces, and they rated the materials for aesthetics, condition, and age while also supplying demographic data. The method is deliberately broad: it turns the built environment into a set of images that can be ranked, compared, and modeled across a large US respondent sample. The design keeps the target contrast visible from the start, so the reader can track how the sample, the stimulus, and the outcome variables connect. That matters because the study asks a practical environmental question rather than a purely abstract one.
The scope is respondent-based, field-based, and survey-based, because the image ratings come from a fielded photo-elicitation protocol rather than a narrow lab task. That gives the paper a clear participant frame, a clear stimulus frame, and a clear measurement frame.

study_record.study_design:
The study uses three stages. First, it runs a systematic review with Scopus search terms and narrows the corpus to 32 articles. Second, it codes those articles with a framework built from the literature. Third, it runs a Python-based meta-analysis of word frequency and association to see which design elements rise to the top. That sequence makes the paper a layered synthesis rather than a one-step review. The review-review-meta-analysis sequence is a three-stage design, so the paper deserves to be read as a layered synthesis. It first narrows the corpus, then codes it, and then organizes the coded language into a higher-level pattern.
The scope is field-limited, month-bounded, and measure-driven: it draws from a February 2024 search window, a 32-article corpus, and a coding pipeline that counts words and associations. That makes the review bounded enough to audit while still broad enough to see recurring design language.

study_record.key_statistics: There is no inferential dataset, but the essay still has strong analytic structure. It uses several ethnographic and historical cases, and the figures present multiple cross-cultural settings: Aboriginal camps, dance-grounds, Maya house cosmology, transformed houses, and Yolngu shelters. Those examples are the article's actual evidence surfaces and show the conceptual range of the theory. There may be no dataset in the narrow sense, but the paper still has structure: it can count dimensions, identify case traditions, and separate recurring mechanisms from one-off examples. Those conceptual counts are the real analytic anchors.
study_record.limitations_text: The essay is conceptual and comparative, so it is powerful as a reframing device but not as a statistical test. It relies on case interpretation, not a survey or experiment, and that means later research has to check whether the proposed theory travels cleanly across other traditions and built settings. The limits are the usual ones for theory: the claim can be persuasive without being fully settled by data. The careful read keeps the argument from pretending to be an empirical proof when it is really a conceptual reorganization.
study_record.study_design:
The essay works through Aboriginal Australian and Maya cases, plus broader anthropological and architectural references, to build a cross-cultural theory. It moves from authority and the architect/builder distinction to tradition, behavior setting, temporal properties, and value reconciliation. The method is comparative and theoretical, using case examples to stretch the concept of architecture beyond a single cultural frame. The paper works by assembling cases, concepts, and prior theory into a coherent line of thought. That makes the method intellectual rather than experimental, but still rigorous because each move in the argument has to support the next one.
The scope is field-based, day-to-day, and measure-driven, because the essay compares Aboriginal and Maya cases through recurring architectural measures of authority, setting, and time. That gives the theory a bounded comparative frame instead of an abstract universal claim.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper reports no original statistics. Kaplan cites effect patterns from prior work. Natural scenes are 'so uniformly preferred over scenes of the built environment that only a single built scene -- an urban park -- was as preferred as the lowest-rated natural scene' (Kaplan et al., 1972; cited at page 5). When content type entered the model, Complexity showed 'no predictive role' across all 56 scenes. Within content domains, Complexity showed a linear pattern (natural scenes) or a downturn (urban scenes; Wohlwill, 1976). Across multiple data sets, Mystery emerges as the 'single best predictor of preference'.
study_record.limitations_text: The framework is post-hoc. Kaplan derived the 2 × 2 matrix to fit existing data patterns rather than testing it prospectively. The evolutionary claim -- that what we prefer reflects ancestral survival value -- is unfalsifiable as a just-so story without phylogenetic or cross-cultural experiments that pull apart cultural learning. Later work shows that Kaplan's predictors interact with expertise, familiarity, and cultural background in ways the 1987 frame does not address; farmers rate agricultural landscapes differently from city dwellers, for example. The visual-information frame also leaves out other sensory channels -- soundscapes, thermal comfort, smell -- that demonstrably shape what people prefer in a place. The model has been more successful as a design heuristic than as a testable scientific theory, which raises the open question of whether its predictive success reflects real cognitive machinery or post-hoc design intuition.
study_record.study_design: This is a theoretical paper, not an empirical study. Kaplan synthesises evidence from roughly 15 years of preference research, his own and others'. The papers he leans on most include Wohlwill (1968) on Complexity in urban vs. natural scenes; Kaplan et al. (1972) on content vs. Complexity as predictors of scenic preference; the Kaplans' (1982) *Humanscape* and *Cognition and Environment* on the information-processing model; Wohlwill (1976) on the Complexity-preference downturn for urban scenes; and R. Kaplan (1975, 1977) on nature preference across diverse populations. The paper reports no new data. The 2 × 2 matrix is reached by argument rather than by analysis -- the four predictors are derived logically from the two crossing dimensions and then matched against the prior literature for fit.

study_record.limitations_text: The field is heterogeneous, and the review reflects that heterogeneity by bringing together studies that do not share one method, one setting, or one outcome. study_record.study_design: The paper reviews and compares the main soundscape descriptors in the literature and then builds a conceptual framework for predictive models. rows.canonical_text: Historic cities offer qualities of intimacy, accessibility, and 'at-homeness' that modern dispersed developments often lack, but should not be uncritically idealized as universal models
rows.source_text: Historic cities offer qualities of intimacy, accessibility, and 'at-homeness' that modern dispersed developments often lack, but should not be uncritically idealized as universal models

study_record.key_statistics: The editorial cites macro-scale urban statistics in passing: approximately 10% of the world's population lived in cities in 1900; that figure is expected to reach 75% by 2050 (citing Burdett and Sudjic, 2007). These numbers are used as context for the argument about why urban form matters at scale, not as original data.
study_record.limitations_text: The editorial is not a systematic review and does not claim empirical authority. Its arguments are selective and illustrative rather than comprehensive. The companion articles it introduces are themselves diverse in method and geography (Hong Kong, Perth, Sheffield, UK national policy), which means the editorial's framing covers disparate phenomena under a single umbrella without formally synthesizing them. The claim that the historic city "supports" walkability and mixed use is context-dependent: many historic cities also have narrow streets hostile to accessibility, poor seismic resilience, and entrenched socioeconomic segregation that the editorial acknowledges only briefly. The editorial would be stronger if it identified which types of historic cities (Mediterranean compact, northern European grid, Asian organic) its arguments best apply to.
study_record.study_design: There is no experiment and no sample. The paper is a 4-page editorial that synthesizes urban theory, phenomenology (broadly construed), and illustrative case observations to construct a position argument. The companion articles in the issue — by Xue (Mass Transit Railway Stations in Hong Kong), Sohn, Moudon, and Lee (neighbourhood walkability and economic value), Pattacini (climate adaptation via urban morphology at the University of Sheffield), Tiwari and Curtis (arterial liveable streets via the FUS-ion model in Perth, Australia), and Paterson (UK National Planning Policy Framework) — each address different aspects of the persistence question. The editorial's contribution is framing, not data.

study_record.key_statistics: No original empirical data are reported. O'Callaghan references key findings from the experimental literature: Shams et al. (2000, 2002) demonstrated the sound-induced flash illusion — a single flash accompanied by multiple beeps is perceived as multiple flashes. McGurk and MacDonald (1976) demonstrated the McGurk effect — visual /ga/ combined with auditory /ba/ is perceived as /da/. Sekuler et al. (1997) demonstrated the motion-bounce effect — a sound at the moment of disk intersection changes the perceived trajectory from streaming to bouncing. Jousmäki and Hari (1998) demonstrated the parchment skin illusion — hearing crinkling sounds alters the felt texture of a surface under the fingers.
study_record.limitations_text: O'Callaghan's three-way distinction is analytical, not empirically validated: no experiment in the chapter directly tests whether synesthesia, crossmodal illusions, and synesthetic effects are dissociated at the neural level. The argument that synesthesia is an outlying condition relies on population prevalence estimates that are themselves uncertain (ranging from 1–4% depending on the definition used). The boundary between crossmodal illusions and synesthetic effects is fuzzy — the Kiki/Bouba correspondence, for example, could be classified as either a statistical tendency or as a genuine perceptual illusion depending on the strength of the mapping. The chapter does not address the growing evidence for "acquired synesthesia" (synesthetic-like phenomena induced by drugs, sensory deprivation, or learning), which complicates the innate/outlying framing.
study_record.study_design: This is a philosophical and conceptual analysis, not an empirical study. O'Callaghan proceeds by: (1) characterizing synesthesia via its definitional features (automaticity, consistency, concurrent experience, idiosyncrasy); (2) cataloguing exemplary crossmodal illusions (McGurk effect, motion-bounce effect, sound-induced flash illusion, parchment skin illusion, rubber hand illusion) and identifying their shared features (universal, stimulus-driven, altered rather than additional experience); (3) contrasting the two using three diagnostic criteria (concurrent vs. altered, individual vs. universal, stable vs. stimulus-contingent); and (4) introducing synesthetic effects as a third, intermediate category that may be common but involves weaker, statistical correspondences (e.g., high pitch → brightness, round shapes → /bouba/ sounds) rather than full-blown illusory percepts.

study_record.key_statistics: Background noise levels ranged from below 30 dBA (excellent) to above 50 dBA (severely impaired for speech) across the surveyed classrooms. HVAC noise was the dominant contributor, with many systems producing 40-45 dBA, well above the 35 dBA ANSI recommendation. Reverberation times correlated with room volume: larger lecture halls often exceeded 1.0 second RT60, far above the 0.6-second target. STI values ranged from good (>0.6) in smaller, well-treated rooms to poor (<0.45) in large, reverberant halls with high background noise. A regression model using background noise and RT60 as predictors explained a substantial proportion of STI variance across classrooms. Specific R² values and sample sizes for the regression should be confirmed from interior pages.
study_record.limitations_text: The study was conducted at a single university and may not represent the full range of classroom types found across institutions. Background noise measurements reflect conditions at one point in time; HVAC operation, exterior noise, and occupancy patterns vary seasonally and diurnally. The STI metric, while well-validated, does not capture all dimensions of the listening experience (e.g., listener effort, attention fatigue, comprehension of accented speech). Student satisfaction and learning outcomes were not directly measured, leaving the link between acoustical quality and academic performance inferential rather than empirically established. The study predates widespread use of amplification systems, which could partially compensate for poor room acoustics.
study_record.study_design: Hodgson (2002) conducted a systematic field measurement campaign across multiple classrooms at the University of British Columbia, spanning small seminar rooms to large lecture halls. For each classroom, standardized acoustical measurements were performed: background noise level in dBA (with all HVAC operating at normal settings), reverberation time (T60, measured using omnidirectional loudspeaker excitation and decay analysis), and speech transmission index (STI, computed from impulse response measurements at multiple receiver positions). Each classroom was then rated against ANSI S12.60 recommended criteria (background noise ≤ 35 dBA, RT60 ≤ 0.6 seconds for rooms < 283 m³) and ranked relative to the full set. study_record.key_statistics: Background noise levels ranged from below 30 dBA (excellent) to above 50 dBA (severely impaired for speech) across the surveyed classrooms. HVAC noise was the dominant contributor, with many systems producing 40-45 dBA, well above the 35 dBA ANSI recommendation. Reverberation times correlated with room volume: larger lecture halls often exceeded 1.0 second RT60, far above the 0.6-second target. STI values ranged from good (>0.6) in smaller, well-treated rooms to poor (<0.45) in large, reverberant halls with high background noise. A regression model using background noise and RT60 as predictors explained a substantial proportion of STI variance across classrooms. Specific R² values and sample sizes for the regression should be confirmed from interior pages.
study_record.limitations_text: The study was conducted at a single university and may not represent the full range of classroom types found across institutions. Background noise measurements reflect conditions at one point in time; HVAC operation, exterior noise, and occupancy patterns vary seasonally and diurnally. The STI metric, while well-validated, does not capture all dimensions of the listening experience (e.g., listener effort, attention fatigue, comprehension of accented speech). Student satisfaction and learning outcomes were not directly measured, leaving the link between acoustical quality and academic performance inferential rather than empirically established. The study predates widespread use of amplification systems, which could partially compensate for poor room acoustics.

study_record.key_statistics: As a primarily technical/methods paper, the study reports system specifications rather than behavioral statistics. The SPIDAR system achieves 6-DOF tracking with sub-centimeter positional accuracy. The olfactory display can switch between multiple scent channels with a response time of approximately 2 seconds. The pilot evaluation collected qualitative user feedback but did not report inferential statistics comparing multi-modal VR to traditional instruction. The educational application was demonstrated with the Bohr atomic model, but quantitative learning outcomes were not systematically assessed. Mathpix-extracted statistics: n = 2; n = 3; n = 1.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper describes a prototype system and does not provide rigorous empirical evidence that multi-modal VR improves learning outcomes compared to visual-only VR or traditional instruction. The SPIDAR haptic interface, while innovative, provides limited force resolution compared to commercial haptic devices. The olfactory display technology was experimental in 2006 and has limited precision and reliability. The constructivist educational framework, while well-established, does not guarantee that adding sensory channels automatically improves learning. The system was demonstrated with only one educational application (Bohr model); generalizability to other domains is assumed but not demonstrated. The 2006 publication date means that the specific hardware is now outdated, though the design principles remain relevant.
study_record.study_design: Richard and colleagues (2006) employed a design-and-implementation methodology. The paper first surveys the theoretical literature on constructivist education and multi-modal VR, identifying the gap between educational VR systems (mostly visual-only) and the multi-sensory richness that constructivism demands. The VIREPSE architecture is then described in detail: the SPIDAR haptic device uses six string-motor pairs to provide 3-DOF force feedback to the user's hand at room scale; the olfactory display uses multiple fans and scent cartridges to deliver chemical signals timed to virtual events; spatial audio provides 3D sound cues. The Bohr atomic model application maps physical forces to electron-shell interactions so that students feel quantized energy levels as discrete force steps. A pilot evaluation with students is described but full empirical results are reserved for future work.

study_record.key_statistics: Intelligible speech from colleagues received the highest disruption rating across all noise sources, with the majority of respondents identifying it as a frequent or very frequent problem. Open-plan office workers reported significantly higher levels of noise disruption than enclosed-office workers (p < .05), with the speech noise differential being the largest contributor. A substantial proportion (the exact percentage should be confirmed from interior pages) reported that noise negatively affected their work quality. Equipment and external noise received lower disruption ratings, consistent with the psychological literature showing that intelligible speech is uniquely disruptive because it engages the phonological loop of working memory. Mathpix-extracted statistics: n = 88; F(3,261) = 15.80; F(7,609) = 53.98.
study_record.limitations_text: The study relies entirely on self-report, which may overestimate disruption due to retrospective bias or underestimate it due to habituation. Actual noise levels were not measured, so the relationship between reported disruption and objective sound pressure levels cannot be established. The sample of approximately 100 UK office workers may not generalize to other cultures, industries, or work styles. The survey was cross-sectional, so it cannot establish causal relationships between noise exposure and productivity loss. Individual differences in noise sensitivity, task demands, and coping strategies were not systematically examined. The study was published in 2005, before the widespread adoption of noise-canceling headphones and hybrid work arrangements.
study_record.study_design: Banbury and Berry (2005) conducted a survey study with approximately 100 UK office workers across various workplace settings, including open-plan offices, shared rooms, and enclosed individual offices. The questionnaire systematically measured: (1) the specific sources of noise disruption experienced (categorized into speech from colleagues, phone conversations, office equipment, building systems, and external sources); (2) the frequency of disruption from each source; (3) the perceived impact of noise on concentration, work quality, and work quantity; and (4) annoyance ratings for different noise sources. Responses were analyzed descriptively and comparatively across office types using appropriate statistical tests, with particular attention to the open-plan versus enclosed office distinction. methods. For example, Langdon (1966) found the most frequent complaint about office environments concerned noise, especially from people talking in the background.

study_record.key_statistics: Table 3 (open exploration): public connectivity (a local measure of how many other corridors meet at a given one) predicted line use at r = .768 (Urban), .884 (University), .786 (City). Decision-point degree predicted node use at r = .723 (Urban), .848 (University). Table 4 (directed search): actual node integration (the global measure) predicted redundant node use at r = .561 (Urban), .817 (University), .633 (City). Sketch-map correlations (Table 3): public connectivity predicted which corridors people drew at r = .556, .678, .817 -- explaining 31%, 46%, and 67% of the variance respectively. Pointing accuracy tracked hospital intelligibility: University (intelligibility = .831) had smaller pointing errors than City (.557) at t = 2.934, p = 0.0042. Prior work (Rovine & Weisman, 1995) had found topological accuracy in sketch maps explained 62.4% of the wayfinding variance.
study_record.limitations_text: Five honest limits attach to this study. First, participants were young university students (mean age 19.5), so generalisation to elderly visitors or cognitively impaired populations is uncertain. Second, the 10-15 minute window for the local-to-global shift may differ in more or less intelligible buildings, and the study cannot map that function fully. Third, all three hospitals were in a single U.S. city; cultural and architectural conventions may shape the picture differently elsewhere. Fourth, sketch-map inter-rater reliability (75-83%) leaves some coding noise in the outcome measure. Fifth, the space-syntax measures themselves require specialised software and expertise to compute, which may limit how readily designers can apply the framework without trained collaborators.
study_record.study_design: Environmental cognition research has long contrasted topological knowledge (knowing that A is before B) with Euclidean survey knowledge (knowing precise distances and directions). But that binary is too coarse: topology itself can be local (immediate connections) or global (how every space relates to every other space). Space syntax theory supplies mathematical tools to draw that distinction: *connectivity* is the local measure (how many spaces touch this one); *integration* is the global measure (how many steps to reach every other space). Prior researchers had noticed that building layouts seemed to be learned quickly, even on first contact, but lacked the tools to track when and how the shift from local to global topology actually happens. This study uses space syntax measures to test whether people's reliance shifts from local to global topology as they learn a building. Haq and Zimring at the Georgia Institute of Technology recruited 128 young adults (62 male, 66 female; mean age 19.5 years) who had visited a large hospital no more than once in the past year. Testing took place in three hospitals: Urban Hospital (39 public axial lines; intelligibility = .664), University Hospital (32 lines; intelligibility = .831), and City Hospital (24 lines; intelligibility = .557). Each session ran roughly sixty minutes. During open exploration, participants walked freely for 15-20 minutes to learn the building from designated entry points. During directed search, they navigated between four preselected destinations (12 routes per hospital, 508 searches total). Paths were recorded on floor plans. Participants also performed 1,248 pointing trials, where they indicated the direction to out-of-sight landmarks using a marked cardboard pointer. Sketch maps were collected at the end of each session and scored for which corridors appeared.

rows.source_text: The ability to effectively find one's way into, through, and out of a building is clearly a prerequisite for the satisfaction of other, higher level goals.

study_record.key_statistics: Plan simplicity predicted how often users got lost with R² = 0.56 (p < .001), explaining more than half the variance across the ten buildings. Building exposure added another R² = 0.09 (p < .05) -- statistically real but practically modest. Together the two variables explained roughly 65% of the variance in how often users lost their way. Among Weisman's other plan variables, simplicity beat signage, landmark presence, and the differences between areas by a wide margin, though those variables all moved in the expected direction. A meaningful minority of users reported recurring trouble with wayfinding even in buildings they used daily. That result confirms the central asymmetry: knowing the building well does not fully fix poor legibility.
study_record.limitations_text: Five honest limits attach to the work. First, the study covers only ten buildings at one university, which limits the range of architectural types and user groups sampled. Second, 'judged simplicity' rests on outside raters who look at plan drawings, which may miss aspects of layout that matter on the ground -- vertical movement, what you can see from one floor to the next. Third, self-reported wayfinding trouble is open to recall bias. Users may underreport routine getting-lost and overreport dramatic episodes. Fourth, the study does not track real wayfinding behaviour -- routes walked, choices at branches, backtracking events -- but relies on retrospective self-report. Fifth, the 1981 publication date pre-dates digital wayfinding tools. GPS, indoor maps, and digital signage may have shifted the relative weight of architectural legibility against digital aid. The 56% figure may not hold the same way in 2026.
study_record.sample_n: 73 undergraduates (wayfinding survey); 5 groups × 20 raters = 100 raters (plan configuration assessment)
study_record.study_design: Weisman (1981) chose ten buildings at Pennsylvania State University that varied in plan simplicity, in how clearly their areas differed from one another, and in how regular their layouts were. For each building, self-report questionnaires measured how often users got lost, how hard users found the wayfinding task to be, and how long users had been using the building. Several plan-level variables were also rated by outside judges who looked at the plan drawings: how simple the floor plan looked, how clearly its areas differed from one another, whether landmarks were present, and how symmetric the layout was. Regression then tested which plan variables best predicted how often users got lost. Plan simplicity entered the regression as the dominant predictor by a wide margin. Weisman framed the work in Kevin Lynch's *imageability* tradition -- Lynch's 1960 thesis that good cities are easy to picture in the mind -- and argued the same logic applies one scale down, at the level of one building.

Building exposure added another R² = 0.09 (p < .05) -- statistically real but practically modest. Together the two variables explained roughly 65% of the variance in how often users lost their way. Among Weisman's other plan variables, simplicity beat signage, landmark presence, and the differences between areas by a wide margin, though those variables all moved in the expected direction. A meaningful minority of users reported recurring trouble with wayfinding even in buildings they used daily. That result confirms the central asymmetry: knowing the building well does not fully fix poor legibility.
study_record.limitations_text: Five honest limits attach to the work. First, the study covers only ten buildings at one university, which limits the range of architectural types and user groups sampled. Second, 'judged simplicity' rests on outside raters who look at plan drawings, which may miss aspects of layout that matter on the ground -- vertical movement, what you can see from one floor to the next. Third, self-reported wayfinding trouble is open to recall bias. Users may underreport routine getting-lost and overreport dramatic episodes. Fourth, the study does not track real wayfinding behaviour -- routes walked, choices at branches, backtracking events -- but relies on retrospective self-report. Fifth, the 1981 publication date pre-dates digital wayfinding tools. GPS, indoor maps, and digital signage may have shifted the relative weight of architectural legibility against digital aid. The 56% figure may not hold the same way in 2026.
study_record.sample_n: 73 undergraduates (wayfinding survey); 5 groups × 20 raters = 100 raters (plan configuration assessment)
study_record.study_design: Weisman (1981) chose ten buildings at Pennsylvania State University that varied in plan simplicity, in how clearly their areas differed from one another, and in how regular their layouts were. For each building, self-report questionnaires measured how often users got lost, how hard users found the wayfinding task to be, and how long users had been using the building. Several plan-level variables were also rated by outside judges who looked at the plan drawings: how simple the floor plan looked, how clearly its areas differed from one another, whether landmarks were present, and how symmetric the layout was. Regression then tested which plan variables best predicted how often users got lost. Plan simplicity entered the regression as the dominant predictor by a wide margin. Weisman framed the work in Kevin Lynch's *imageability* tradition -- Lynch's 1960 thesis that good cities are easy to picture in the mind -- and argued the same logic applies one scale down, at the level of one building.

study_record.key_statistics: Outdoor environments produced CS values typically exceeding 0.4, while many indoor environments fell below 0.2 -- a biologically meaningful threshold. The Ev/Eh ratio in natural settings consistently exceeded 1.0, meaning more light reached the upper visual field (where ipRGC-rich retinal regions are best stimulated) than horizontal work surfaces. Indoor environments showed Ev/Eh ratios well below 1.0, reflecting the predominance of downward-directed task lighting. Spectral analysis revealed that outdoor environments contain 2-5 times more short-wavelength energy (below 500 nm) at the cornea than indoor environments at similar photopic illuminance levels. These quantitative differences persist even when indoor illuminance is raised to recommended levels (500 lux horizontal), because the spectral and directional characteristics remain fundamentally different from daylight.
study_record.limitations_text: The measurements represent midday snapshots at single points in time and do not capture the temporal dynamics of light exposure that are critical for circadian entrainment (morning light, evening dimming). The sample of environments, while representative, is limited in size and geographic scope (UK). The study does not directly measure health outcomes in occupants exposed to different light fields, so the link between measured light field characteristics and actual health benefits remains inferential. The CS model used (Rea) has been superseded by the CIE S 026:2018 melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (M-EDI) standard, though the fundamental finding about indoor-outdoor divergence would persist with updated metrics.
study_record.study_design: Van Creveld and Mansfield (2016) identified a representative set of lit environments spanning the natural-to-built spectrum: outdoor seascapes and landscapes, an urban square, and various interior architectural environments including offices, galleries, and residential spaces. During midday hours, photometric and colorimetric snapshots were captured at each location using spectroradiometers positioned at typical eye height. Measurements included: spectral irradiance at the cornea, enabling computation of melanopic and photopic illuminance; vertical and horizontal illuminance for the Ev/Eh ratio; cylindrical illuminance (Ec); and derived circadian stimulus (CS) values based on the Rea model. These metrics were compared with current lighting recommendations and standards to identify where built environments diverge from the conditions that non-image-forming photobiology favors.

study_record.key_statistics: The review synthesized findings from dozens of studies spanning several decades. Illuminance effects were most consistent in the 300-2000 lux range, with diminishing returns above 1000 lux for most cognitive tasks. CCT effects were observed primarily in the 3000-6500K range, with 6500K conditions showing alertness advantages in 60-70% of studies that tested this comparison. However, individual study sample sizes ranged from fewer than 10 participants to more than 100, with the majority using 20-40 participants. The review noted that small sample sizes (N < 20) were associated with larger and more variable effect sizes, suggesting potential publication bias. Carryover effects were identified as a particular concern in within-subjects designs involving sequential light exposures.
study_record.limitations_text: The review itself is limited by the heterogeneity of the primary studies: different performance measures, lighting conditions, experimental durations, and participant populations make quantitative meta-analysis difficult. The review does not compute pooled effect sizes or conduct formal meta-analytic synthesis, limiting its ability to provide precise design specifications. The focus on task performance excludes broader well-being and health outcomes (circadian disruption, mood, sleep quality) that may interact with performance effects. The review covers primarily laboratory studies and may not generalize fully to real office environments where multiple environmental variables co-vary. Publication bias favoring significant results may inflate the apparent reliability of lighting-performance relationships.
study_record.study_design: Konstantzos and colleagues conducted a systematic narrative review of empirical studies examining the relationship between lighting parameters and task performance in built environments. The review categorized studies by: (1) lighting metric -- illuminance, luminance/luminance ratio, CCT, spectral tuning, daylight provision, and outside view; (2) performance measure type -- cognitive performance tests (CBS, Stroop, PASAT), visual acuity and reaction time, memory and reasoning tests, and labor productivity metrics; (3) experimental design -- laboratory versus field, within-subjects versus between-subjects, and number of lighting conditions tested; and (4) participant characteristics -- sample size, age range, and control for individual differences. Each study was evaluated for methodological rigor, including consideration of carryover effects, modeling approach, and statistical power.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper reports primarily technical performance metrics. The human detection module achieved reliable detection at typical room distances (2-5 meters). The emotion detection classifier was trained on standard facial expression datasets and achieved accuracy consistent with the state of the art (approximately 65-75% for multi-class emotion classification, though exact figures should be confirmed from interior pages). The pilot wellbeing evaluation collected subjective feedback from participants but did not report inferential statistical comparisons. The color psychology mappings used pre-existing published associations rather than experimentally validated dose-response curves for specific light colors and emotional states.
study_record.limitations_text: The study describes a prototype and pilot evaluation, not a controlled experiment. The emotion detection accuracy (65-75% for multi-class classification) means that misclassifications are frequent, potentially resulting in inappropriate lighting adjustments that could worsen rather than improve mood. The color psychology mappings are based on general associations rather than experimentally validated therapeutic protocols. The pilot evaluation used subjective questionnaires without a control condition, making it impossible to attribute any wellbeing changes specifically to the adaptive lighting. Privacy concerns around continuous facial monitoring in workplaces and homes are substantial and not fully addressed. The single-room deployment does not test scalability, multi-occupant conflicts (different emotions requiring different colors), or long-term habituation effects.
study_record.study_design: Cupkova and colleagues (2019) designed and implemented a modular IoT-based lighting system. The hardware components include an IP camera with sufficient resolution for facial detection at room scale, IoT-connected LED light strips capable of producing full-spectrum color, and a central controller running the detection and adjustment software. The software pipeline integrates: (1) human detection using background subtraction and body-contour analysis; (2) facial recognition using established computer vision libraries; (3) emotion classification using a trained neural network; and (4) a lighting adjustment algorithm that maps detected emotions to target light colors based on published color psychology associations (e.g., blue for calming, warm white for comfort, green for concentration). The system was deployed in a real-world environment and evaluated through a pilot study in which participants experienced the adaptive lighting and provided feedback via questionnaires assessing their subjective wellbeing statements.

study_record.key_statistics: CBS cognitive test scores showed no significant difference between 22°C and 25°C conditions (p > .05 across all subtests). NASA-TLX scores were significantly lower at 25°C (p < .05), indicating reduced perceived cognitive load, but the sequential design (22°C always preceded 25°C) makes learning effects the most parsimonious explanation. EEG features (alpha, beta, theta power and ratios) showed no significant temperature-dependent differences across the three PASAT difficulty levels (p > .05). Heart rate showed no significant difference between conditions (p > .05). Thermal comfort ratings were not significantly reduced by the 3°C setback (p > .05), consistent with ASHRAE 55 predictions that 25°C falls within the summer comfort zone for sedentary office work. Air quality ratings also showed no significant temperature effect. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p < 0.001; p < 0.05; p < 0.05.; p < 0.01.
study_record.limitations_text: The sequential (non-counterbalanced) design, with 22°C always preceding 25°C, cannot fully separate temperature effects from order and learning effects -- particularly for the significant NASA-TLX finding. The sample of 26 participants provides adequate power for detecting medium-to-large effects but may miss small performance decrements. Only two temperature conditions were tested; the effect at more extreme setpoints (27°C, 28°C) is unknown. The participants were healthy university-associated workers and may not represent populations with lower thermal tolerance (elderly, cardiovascularly compromised). Summer conditions were simulated in a climate chamber, which lacks the contextual realism of actual office environments with real work pressures and social interactions. The study covered only acute exposure; long-term adaptation effects are not assessed.
study_record.study_design: Zhang and colleagues (2017) tested 26 Australian office workers in a controlled climate chamber at the University of Sydney. Each participant experienced two sequential temperature conditions: 22°C (the typical Australian summer indoor standard) followed by 25°C (the proposed raised setpoint). In each condition, participants completed: (1) the Cambridge Brain Sciences cognitive test battery, covering reasoning, planning, memory, and attention; (2) the NASA Task Load Index, assessing subjective cognitive load; (3) Paced Auditory Serial Addition Tests (PASAT) at three difficulty levels while wearing EEG caps and heart rate monitors; and (4) thermal comfort and air quality questionnaires. EEG was recorded throughout the PASAT sessions to capture neural correlates of cognitive effort, and heart rate was monitored as a physiological stress indicator. The within-subjects design controlled for individual differences but introduced potential order effects.

study_record.key_statistics: CATA and SCS converged: 3100K x 600 lx and 6500K x 600 lx conditions received the highest ratings for pleasant, relaxed emotions (p < .05 versus 250 lx conditions). The 6500K x 1000 lx condition produced significantly higher arousal ratings than all other conditions (p < .05). Both 250 lx conditions (3100K and 6500K) received significantly higher ratings for tired and frustrated emotions (p < .05). FaceReader analysis confirmed the subjective pattern -- happy expressions were most frequent under 600 lx conditions, while negative expressions (sad, angry) were most frequent under 250 lx conditions. The concordance between FRE and subjective measures validates the automated approach as a reliable proxy for self-reported emotional state in lighting research, though exact correlation coefficients should be confirmed from interior statistical tables. Mathpix-extracted statistics: P = 0.01; P = 0.038; P = 0.028; P > 0.005; P = 0.000.
study_record.limitations_text: The study tested only two CCT levels and three illuminance levels, leaving the full response surface unmapped. The enclosed laboratory may not fully replicate the psychological stress of actual operational environments (submarines, mines). FaceReader accuracy varies with lighting conditions themselves, creating a potential confound -- facial expression classification may be less accurate under the very low-illuminance conditions being evaluated. Sample size and demographic details should be confirmed from interior pages. The circumplex emotion model, while widely used, may not capture lighting-specific emotional responses (e.g., glare-induced irritation versus general frustration). Cultural factors (Chinese participants) may influence emotional expression and reporting norms.
study_record.study_design: Zhang and colleagues (2023) conducted a within-subjects experiment in a closed laboratory at Northwestern Polytechnical University. Six lighting conditions were created by crossing two correlated color temperatures (3100K warm white, 6500K cool daylight) with three illuminance levels (250 lx, 600 lx, 1000 lx). Participants experienced each condition and provided emotional assessments through three complementary methods. The Check-All-That-Apply (CATA) method presented participants with emotion descriptors and asked them to select all that applied. The Subjective Coordinate Scale (SCS) asked participants to map their emotional state onto a two-dimensional circumplex model (valence x arousal). Simultaneously, a camera recorded participants' facial expressions, which were analyzed post-hoc using FaceReader (FRE) software to classify emotional states from facial muscle patterns. The three-method triangulation allowed comparison of rapid subjective assessment (CATA), structured subjective mapping (SCS), and objective behavioral measurement (FRE).

study_record.limitations_text: The study tested only two CCT levels and three illuminance levels, leaving the full response surface unmapped. The enclosed laboratory may not fully replicate the psychological stress of actual operational environments (submarines, mines). FaceReader accuracy varies with lighting conditions themselves, creating a potential confound -- facial expression classification may be less accurate under the very low-illuminance conditions being evaluated. Sample size and demographic details should be confirmed from interior pages. The circumplex emotion model, while widely used, may not capture lighting-specific emotional responses (e.g., glare-induced irritation versus general frustration). study_record.study_design: Zhang and colleagues (2023) conducted a within-subjects experiment in a closed laboratory at Northwestern Polytechnical University. Six lighting conditions were created by crossing two correlated color temperatures (3100K warm white, 6500K cool daylight) with three illuminance levels (250 lx, 600 lx, 1000 lx). Participants experienced each condition and provided emotional assessments through three complementary methods. The Check-All-That-Apply (CATA) method presented participants with emotion descriptors and asked them to select all that applied. The Subjective Coordinate Scale (SCS) asked participants to map their emotional state onto a two-dimensional circumplex model (valence x arousal). Simultaneously, a camera recorded participants' facial expressions, which were analyzed post-hoc using FaceReader (FRE) software to classify emotional states from facial muscle patterns. The three-method triangulation allowed comparison of rapid subjective assessment (CATA), structured subjective mapping (SCS), and objective behavioral measurement (FRE).

study_record.key_statistics: As a narrative review spanning multiple disciplines, the paper synthesizes qualitative and quantitative findings rather than reporting original statistical analyses. Key synthesized findings include: energy demand for space cooling is expected to triple by 2050; perceived thermal comfort can vary by 2-4°C based on perceived control alone (from psychology studies); vernacular cooling strategies (cross-ventilation, thermal mass, courtyard design) can reduce indoor temperatures by 5-10°C below ambient without mechanical cooling (from architectural studies); and the social construction of air conditioning as necessary has historical roots in mid-20th century American commercial interests rather than physiological necessity (from social history).
study_record.limitations_text: The review's breadth is also its limitation: by spanning physiology, psychology, anthropology, material culture, and political economy, it necessarily treats each domain at a survey level rather than providing deep analysis. The social constructionist argument, while compelling, risks understating the physiological constraints on heat tolerance -- extreme heat kills regardless of cultural framing. The review does not provide a quantitative framework for integrating social and physiological factors into building design decisions. Most of the social science literature reviewed is based on qualitative methods with limited generalizability. The global scope means that specific recommendations may not apply across all climatic and cultural contexts.
study_record.study_design: Mazzone and Khosla (2021) conducted a multidimensional narrative review spanning the social sciences, humanities, psychology, and physiology. Unlike conventional thermal comfort reviews that center on Fanger's PMV/PPD model or ASHRAE 55 adaptive comfort standards, this review begins from the human subject -- asking what drives the subjective experience and social practice of seeking coolness. The review navigates literature on: material culture and everyday practices (how people use objects, clothing, and architectural elements to manage heat); sociology and anthropology of thermal comfort (cultural construction of comfort norms); psychology and neuroarchitecture (how spatial perception, control, and environmental aesthetics modulate thermal experience); and physiology (heat-exchange models and their documented limitations). Each domain is examined not in isolation but for its interactions with the others, producing an integrated human-centered framework for understanding cooling needs.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper is qualitative, so it reports themes rather than test statistics. All eight CLTs showed place attachment as a dominant motivational theme among founders. Moore documents three concrete mechanisms by which place attachment shapes CLT operation. First, resale restrictions tie houses to the locality and limit who can buy them on. Second, lettings policies prioritise applicants with existing community ties. Third, governance structures end up dominated by long-standing residents who founded the trust. The qualitative pattern is consistent with the broader quantitative literature that links place attachment to civic participation and to pro-environmental behaviour, though the paper makes no causal claim of its own.
study_record.limitations_text: Five caveats stand out. First, the study covers eight CLTs in rural England, so it cannot speak directly to urban CLTs, to other countries, or to other forms of community-led housing. Second, the focus on founding members captures their own motivational stories but not the experience of beneficiaries, rejected applicants, or villagers who chose not to take part. Third, qualitative interview data carries social-desirability bias: founders may emphasise altruistic motives and play down exclusionary intent. Fourth, the paper does not measure place attachment with validated quantitative scales; the analysis is thematic. Fifth, the link between place attachment and CLT formation is correlational, and other forces -- housing-market pressure, policy incentives, individual leadership -- almost certainly co-determine when a CLT actually emerges.
study_record.study_design: Moore ran semi-structured qualitative interviews with founding members of eight rural CLTs across England. CLTs are non-profit, community-based bodies that buy land and develop affordable housing managed by local volunteers. The interview protocol covered four topics: why each founder volunteered; how each founder talked about the village; how the CLT decided who should receive housing; and what difficulties came up during formation and operation. Moore then ran thematic analysis on the transcripts and tracked recurrent patterns around place attachment, community identity, housing need, and social inclusion or exclusion. The eight cases were chosen to vary along three axes: geographic location, stage of development, and organisational structure. The sampling strategy lets the study compare founder narratives across rural settings rather than generalise from a single village. The work also draws on the wider literature on community consultation and neighbourhood planning, citing Sturzaker (2011), Gallent et al. (2019), and Bradley (2017) as context for how local groups shape policy in rural England.

study_record.key_statistics: All three studies favoured green over spare layouts at p < .05 on every primary outcome. The productivity gain in green conditions showed up in objective task scores, not only in self-report -- the strongest test of real performance change. Two of the three studies tracked outcomes weeks later and found the gains held, ruling out a novelty effect. Effect sizes were large enough to matter for office design budgets, though the original paper does not always report them explicitly. Across the two countries and three offices, every dimension shifted in the same direction. Field studies rarely deliver that kind of convergence. The cross-lagged regression in Experiment 3 also suggests that perceived air quality mediates part of the focus effect, which gives a first hint at mechanism rather than a bare association.
study_record.limitations_text: The lean-versus-green comparison confounds plants with visual richness, with the colour green, and possibly with perceived air quality, so the data cannot tell us which mechanism actually drives the benefit. The studies did not test intermediate cases -- decorative objects with no plants, or fake plants -- that could pin down the biophilic part. Objective productivity rests on task scores observed at work; the authors do not claim general transfer beyond office tasks. The sample sites are large commercial offices in two Western European countries, so the result may not carry to small workplaces, hot climates, or non-Western office cultures. The follow-up windows ran weeks rather than months, so a longer-horizon plateau cannot yet be ruled out. Finally, the within-subjects design rules out worker-level confounds but cannot rule out a Hawthorne-style awareness effect, since workers could see the change.
study_record.study_design: Nieuwenhuis and colleagues (2014) ran three field experiments in large commercial offices. Experiments 1 and 2 ran in The Netherlands and Experiment 3 in the United Kingdom. Each one compared spare office layouts (no plants, clean surfaces) against green layouts in the same offices, now with indoor plants placed at regular spots within visual range of every desk. The comparison was within-subjects: the same offices and the same workers, observed before and after the change. Workers reported on perceived air, focus, and satisfaction through validated questionnaires; the team also logged objective work output drawn from the office's own performance records. Two of the three studies tracked outcomes across follow-up weeks to test whether early effects fade. The within-subjects logic is the design's strongest feature: confounds that ride with worker or workplace -- training, lighting, manager style -- cancel across conditions, which gives the plant manipulation a clean lane.

study_record.key_statistics: As an opinion paper, the study does not report original empirical data. It draws on existing statistics to motivate the argument: workers in developed economies spend approximately 90% of their time indoors, with a substantial portion in offices; the global smart building market is projected to grow significantly; and empirical reviews consistently show that indoor environmental quality affects both productivity and health. These contextual statistics establish the scale and importance of the research gap the paper identifies.
study_record.limitations_text: As an opinion paper, the work proposes rather than tests a research agenda. The specific research questions may not capture all relevant dimensions of smart office technology. The paper does not address implementation barriers (cost, privacy, organizational resistance) in depth. The framing assumes that smart technologies can simultaneously enhance productivity and well-being, but empirical evidence for this assumption in office contexts is limited and the two goals may sometimes conflict (e.g., productivity monitoring versus employee autonomy). The rapid pace of technology development means that specific technologies discussed may become obsolete before the proposed research agenda is completed. The paper focuses on white-collar office work and does not address hybrid or remote work arrangements that have become increasingly important since publication in 2020.
study_record.study_design: Papagiannidis and Marikyan (2020) employed a conceptual analysis methodology appropriate for an opinion paper. They reviewed the existing literature on smart technologies across multiple domains -- smart cities, smart homes, smart manufacturing, and workplace technology -- identifying research gaps where office-specific questions remain unaddressed. The paper systematically compares the characteristics of different smart spaces (residential, industrial, commercial office) to argue that offices present unique challenges requiring dedicated research. The proposed research agenda is structured around key questions at the intersection of technology, productivity, and well-being in workplace contexts. DESIGN & 354 & 0.15\% & 32 & 72.

study_record.key_statistics: For adults, one discriminant function accounted for 92% of the variance, with emotional bonding and behavioral commitment loading above 0.45. Classification accuracy was 76.4%, substantially above chance (33%). For adolescents, one discriminant function accounted for the dominant proportion of variance, with dependence and belonging loading above 0.45. Classification accuracy reached 93.6%, indicating that sense-of-place dimensions are even more strongly predictive for young people. Sixty-two percent of the adolescent sample indicated indicators of wanting to leave, compared to a smaller proportion of adults, consistent with the well-documented youth drain from rural communities. The total sample of 611 participants (246 adults + 365 adolescents) provided robust statistical power for the discriminant analyses. Mathpix-extracted statistics: F(7,539)=24.18; p>0.05..
study_record.limitations_text: The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether sense-of-place dimensions cause place identity or whether pre-existing identity influences how dimensions are perceived. Only two rural towns were sampled, limiting generalizability to other rural contexts. The stay/leave classification is based on a single self-report item rather than actual migration behavior. The study predates widespread internet access in rural Australia, which has substantially changed the information environment and comparison standards available to rural adolescents. Cultural factors specific to rural Australia may not apply to rural communities in other countries. The study does not examine how physical design features of the towns contribute to or undermine specific sense-of-place dimensions.
study_record.study_design: Pretty and colleagues (2003) surveyed 246 adults and 365 adolescents across two remote rural towns in Australia facing economic decline and population loss. Sense of place was measured across multiple dimensions using validated scales: place attachment (emotional bonding and behavioral commitment subscales), sense of community (affiliation and belonging subscales), and place dependence (available activities, quality comparison with other communities). Place identity -- the target variable -- was operationalized through responses to the statement 'I would really rather live in a different town. This one is not the place for me,' with three response groups: agree (wanting to leave), undecided, and disagree (identifying with the town). Direct discriminant function analysis was conducted separately for adults and adolescents to identify which sense-of-place dimensions best predicted group membership.

As a narrative review, the paper synthesizes findings from hundreds of primary studies rather than reporting original statistical analyses. Key synthesized quantitative findings include: ceiling height priming effects on cognitive processing style (Meyers-Levy & Zhu, 2007, demonstrated across multiple experiments); view-of-nature healing benefits (Ulrich's landmark 1984 study showing reduced hospital stay); light spectral effects on melatonin suppression (Brainard action spectrum); and noise-cognition dose-response relationships from multiple laboratory studies. The review also catalogs effect sizes where available, noting that many architectural effects are small-to-moderate in standardized terms but practically significant given chronic daily exposure. study_record.limitations_text: The review's scope, while comprehensive, inevitably involves judgment calls about what constitutes sufficient empirical evidence. Some effects classified as unsubstantiated may gain support from future research. The focus on biologically ingrained responses may underestimate culturally mediated architectural effects that are nonetheless real and important. The review primarily covers Western experimental literature, potentially missing relevant evidence from other research traditions. Many validated effects were demonstrated in laboratory settings that may not transfer directly to complex real-world buildings. The review does not address interactions between architectural stimuli (e.g., how noise modifies the effect of light), which are critical for practical design but poorly studied.
study_record.study_design: St-Jean and colleagues (2022) conducted a systematic narrative review of the empirical literature on architectural stimuli and their effects on human function. The review was deliberately limited to effects for which a biological basis has been empirically demonstrated, ensuring cross-cultural applicability and independence from personal experience. The architectural stimuli were organized into categories: lighting, color, spatial geometry, nature viewing, acoustics, olfaction, and haptic/material properties. For each category, the review assessed the quality and consistency of empirical evidence, identified the biological or psychological mechanisms underlying the effect, and evaluated whether the evidence is sufficient to support specific design recommendations. Claims lacking adequate empirical support were explicitly identified and separated from validated findings.

The review was deliberately limited to effects for which a biological basis has been empirically demonstrated, ensuring cross-cultural applicability and independence from personal experience. The architectural stimuli were organized into categories: lighting, color, spatial geometry, nature viewing, acoustics, olfaction, and haptic/material properties. For each category, the review assessed the quality and consistency of empirical evidence, identified the biological or psychological mechanisms underlying the effect, and evaluated whether the evidence is sufficient to support specific design recommendations. Claims lacking adequate empirical support were explicitly identified and separated from validated findings.
