study_record.key_statistics: Physiological recovery was significantly faster in natural versus urban conditions across all measured channels (p < .001 for the multivariate comparison). Heart rate returned to baseline significantly sooner in the natural condition (p < .01). Frontalis EMG showed significantly lower muscle tension during natural exposure (p < .01), indicating reduced facial tension. Skin conductance decreased significantly faster in the natural condition (p < .01), reflecting reduced sympathetic arousal. Pulse transit time changes were consistent with lower blood pressure in natural conditions. Self-reported positive affect increased significantly faster in the natural condition, confirming convergent validity with physiological data. The effect manifested within the first 4-7 minutes of exposure, suggesting rapid onset of the restorative process. The multi-channel physiological convergence with a between-subjects design and 120 participants makes this one of the most methodologically robust demonstrations of nature's restorative effects.
study_record.limitations_text: Videotaped environments lack the multi-sensory richness of real environments (no sounds, smells, wind, or temperature in the visual-only conditions). The stress induction (accident film) may not represent the types of chronic stress experienced in daily life. The 10-minute recovery period captures only acute effects; chronic exposure patterns may produce different results. The between-subjects design, while avoiding carryover effects, assumes equivalence of randomly assigned groups. Urban scenes may confound built versus natural with threatening versus safe, as traffic scenes contain inherent danger signals. The 1991 study predates current urbanization levels and digital media exposure patterns that may have altered baseline responses to environmental stimuli.
study_record.study_design: Ulrich and colleagues (1991) used a between-subjects design with 120 participants. All participants first viewed a standardized stress-inducing film (depicting workplace accidents) to elevate baseline stress levels. Participants were then randomly assigned to view one of several videotapes showing either natural environments (scenes of vegetation, water, and parkland) or urban environments (scenes of traffic, pedestrian areas, and commercial buildings). Throughout both the stress induction and recovery phases, continuous physiological measurements were recorded: heart rate (ECG), facial muscle tension (frontalis EMG), skin conductance (palmar), and pulse transit time (an index of blood pressure). Self-reported affect was collected at intervals. The 10-minute recovery period allowed tracking of the temporal dynamics of stress recovery across conditions.

study_record.key_statistics: The melanopsin sensitivity curve peaks at approximately 480 nm (blue), while the photopic visual sensitivity curve peaks at 555 nm (green-yellow) -- a spectral separation of 75 nm that explains why visually adequate lighting can be biologically insufficient. Melatonin suppression requires approximately 2500 lux of broad-spectrum light at the eye (or lower illuminance with blue-enriched spectrum). Typical office illuminance at the eye (not the desk) is often below 500 lux, potentially insufficient for robust circadian entrainment. Studies reviewed show that appropriately timed blue-enriched light exposure can improve alertness by the equivalent of approximately 1 hour of additional sleep. The review does not report original statistical analyses but synthesizes quantitative findings from the biological research to derive practical thresholds.
study_record.limitations_text: The review was published in 2006, when ipRGC research was still emerging and the CIE melanopic standard had not yet been developed (CIE S 026 was published in 2018). Some specific threshold values may have been refined by subsequent research. The melanopsin sensitivity curve was initially derived from melatonin suppression data and may not fully characterize the spectral sensitivity of all non-visual pathways. The practical lighting recommendations, while directionally correct, were proposed before tunable LED technology was commercially mature, and specific spectral prescriptions have been refined by subsequent research. Individual variation in circadian sensitivity, chronotype, and prior light history affects the non-visual response to light and is not fully addressed. The focus on alertness and circadian effects may understate other non-visual pathways (e.g., pupillary light reflex, mood effects via serotonergic pathways).
study_record.study_design: Van Bommel (2006) conducted a narrative review synthesizing the emerging biological research on non-visual light effects with practical lighting engineering. The review covers: the discovery and characterization of ipRGCs and melanopsin; the melatonin suppression action spectrum (Brainard, 2002); the relationship between light exposure timing, spectrum, and circadian phase shifting; evidence for light's effects on alertness, mood, and cognitive performance beyond visual function; and the gap between current lighting standards (based on visual performance) and the biological requirements revealed by ipRGC research. The review then proposes design principles for a new generation of workplace lighting that addresses both visual and non-visual needs.

study_record.key_statistics: Green roofs produced consistent A-weighted noise reductions at non-directly exposed facades across all modeled scenarios. The magnitude of reduction depended on parameters: deeper substrates provided greater absorption; saddleback roofs showed the largest absolute improvement when greened; and light vehicle noise was reduced more effectively than heavy vehicle noise due to frequency-dependent absorption. Flat green roofs with adequate substrate depth achieved shielding performance approaching that of saddleback roofs, a finding with significant practical implications for the flat-roofed commercial buildings that dominate urban skylines. Specific dBA reduction values and frequency-dependent attenuation curves should be confirmed from interior figures and tables.
study_record.limitations_text: The study relies entirely on numerical simulation; field measurements in real urban environments would be needed to validate the predicted noise reductions under variable meteorological conditions (wind, temperature gradients). The acoustic models assume idealized green roof substrate properties that may vary with plant species, moisture content, and seasonal conditions. Only road traffic noise was considered; other urban noise sources (construction, aircraft, neighbors) may respond differently. The study does not address the combined thermal-acoustic optimization of green roof design. Low-frequency noise from heavy vehicles, which is less effectively attenuated, may be the more health-relevant component of traffic noise exposure.
study_record.study_design: Van Renterghem and Botteldooren (2009) employed numerical acoustic simulation using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) and boundary element method (BEM) approaches. These computational methods model the propagation of sound waves from road traffic sources to building facades, accounting for diffraction over rooftops, reflection from facades, and absorption by green roof substrates. The study systematically varied: green roof presence versus conventional rigid roof; substrate depth; roof geometry (flat versus saddleback); traffic speed; vehicle type (light versus heavy); and street canyon width. Facade noise load was calculated as the A-weighted sound pressure level at receiver positions distributed across non-directly exposed facade surfaces. The parametric approach allowed isolation of each factor's contribution to noise reduction.

study_record.key_statistics: Text typing improved by 1.7 per cent per doubling of air supply (P < 0.03), a consistent dose-response across the three rates. Perceived air quality dissatisfaction fell sharply across rates (P < 0.002). Odour intensity also dropped (P < 0.02), and rated dryness symptoms eased with more air (P < 0.05). Subjects reported the air as fresher at higher rates (P < 0.05). Addition, proof reading, and logical thinking all moved in the same direction as typing, though only typing reached formal significance. The agreement across measures -- subjective comfort, symptom scales, and four task-performance indices -- strengthens the conclusion that air supply rate moves both how people feel and how well they work.
study_record.limitations_text: Six caveats matter. First, only female participants were tested in five groups of six, which limits how the results carry to mixed-gender or all-male offices. Second, the chamber resembles a furnished office but cannot fully reproduce a real office's occupant load and pollution sources. Third, only three rates were tested, so the dose-response may plateau above 30 L/s. Fourth, the 4.6-hour exposure captures acute effects but cannot speak to chronic adaptation across weeks. Fifth, the SBS and performance effects may interact with other indoor factors -- temperature, lighting, noise -- that the design held fixed. Sixth, the year-2000 task battery may not represent today's knowledge work, where typing speed is no longer the bottleneck.
study_record.study_design: Thirty female participants ran a within-subjects experiment in five groups of six. Each group sat in a normally furnished 108-cubic-metre office at the International Centre for Indoor Environment and Energy and worked through all three air supply rates -- 3, 10, and 30 L/s per person -- in counterbalanced order. Each session ran 4.6 hours in the afternoon. Temperature stayed at 22 degrees Celsius and relative humidity at 40 per cent. Subjects were blind to the air supply rate and could adjust clothing to stay thermally neutral. Subjective measures included perceived air quality ratings and SBS symptom scales taken at fixed intervals during each exposure. Objective measures covered four simulated office tasks: text typing (speed and accuracy), addition (speed and accuracy), proof reading (detection rate), and logical thinking (problem-solving rate). The three rates spanned a 10:1 range, which gave the design enough dynamic range to fit a dose-response curve.

study_record.key_statistics: Main effect of alignment held for both wayfinding time and pointing accuracy (p < .05). Participants in the misaligned buildings took reliably longer to reach target rooms and made reliably larger pointing errors when asked the direction of unseen places. Wrong-turn counts were also higher in the misaligned conditions. The 56-participant sample gave adequate power for the between-condition contrasts across the four buildings. Effect sizes are reported as practically meaningful, not just statistically detectable -- the slowdown and pointing-error increase are large enough to matter for real architectural design choices, not only for laboratory p-values.
study_record.limitations_text: Six honest limits attach. First, desktop VR lacks the proprioceptive and vestibular cues that a real walking body provides; the alignment effect may actually be larger when people physically rotate through misaligned transitions, so the VR study probably underestimates the real-world effect. Second, the four virtual buildings are a limited sample of possible geometric relationships. Third, real buildings carry many other wayfinding cues (landmarks, signage, visual access, architectural differentiation) that may compensate for or worsen alignment effects. Fourth, the 56-participant sample is adequate but not large by current standards. Fifth, individual differences in spatial ability likely shape the size of the effect but were not analysed here. Sixth, the study tested only initial navigation -- practiced navigators may adapt to misaligned layouts over repeated visits.
study_record.study_design: Werner and Schindler (2004) built four virtual buildings using desktop VR. The buildings differed systematically in the geometric alignment between connected wings. In the aligned buildings, the spatial axes of connected wings were parallel or perpendicular, so the local reference frame stayed the same as a navigator moved across the joint. In the misaligned buildings, wings were rotated at non-standard angles, so the local reference frame changed at the joint and the navigator had to mentally reconcile two competing spatial frames. Fifty-six participants navigated the four buildings on two task types: a wayfinding task (navigate from a start point to a named target) and a pointing task (indicate the direction to an out-of-sight location from the current position). Outcome measures were navigation time, number of wrong turns, and absolute pointing error in degrees. The design held building size, path complexity, and number of decision points constant, so the only thing varying was the alignment of the wings.

claim.text: This, in turn, should be reflected in increased way-finding performance (speed or accuracy) and a better global understanding of the building's layout.

study_record.key_statistics: Main effect of alignment held for both wayfinding time and pointing accuracy (p < .05). Participants in the misaligned buildings took reliably longer to reach target rooms and made reliably larger pointing errors when asked the direction of unseen places. Wrong-turn counts were also higher in the misaligned conditions. The 56-participant sample gave adequate power for the between-condition contrasts across the four buildings. Effect sizes are reported as practically meaningful, not just statistically detectable -- the slowdown and pointing-error increase are large enough to matter for real architectural design choices, not only for laboratory p-values.
study_record.limitations_text: Six honest limits attach. First, desktop VR lacks the proprioceptive and vestibular cues that a real walking body provides; the alignment effect may actually be larger when people physically rotate through misaligned transitions, so the VR study probably underestimates the real-world effect. Second, the four virtual buildings are a limited sample of possible geometric relationships. Third, real buildings carry many other wayfinding cues (landmarks, signage, visual access, architectural differentiation) that may compensate for or worsen alignment effects. Fourth, the 56-participant sample is adequate but not large by current standards. Fifth, individual differences in spatial ability likely shape the size of the effect but were not analysed here. Sixth, the study tested only initial navigation -- practiced navigators may adapt to misaligned layouts over repeated visits.
study_record.study_design: Werner and Schindler (2004) built four virtual buildings using desktop VR. The buildings differed systematically in the geometric alignment between connected wings. In the aligned buildings, the spatial axes of connected wings were parallel or perpendicular, so the local reference frame stayed the same as a navigator moved across the joint. In the misaligned buildings, wings were rotated at non-standard angles, so the local reference frame changed at the joint and the navigator had to mentally reconcile two competing spatial frames. Fifty-six participants navigated the four buildings on two task types: a wayfinding task (navigate from a start point to a named target) and a pointing task (indicate the direction to an out-of-sight location from the current position). Outcome measures were navigation time, number of wrong turns, and absolute pointing error in degrees. The design held building size, path complexity, and number of decision points constant, so the only thing varying was the alignment of the wings.

study_record.key_statistics: Blue goggles condition: melatonin suppression was significantly greater than zero at both 1 hour and 2 hours (p < .05). Tablets-only condition: suppression was not significantly different from zero at 1 hour (n.s.) but reached significance at 2 hours (p < .05). Orange-tinted dark control: no significant melatonin suppression at either time point, confirming that blocking short-wavelength light eliminates the effect. The within-subjects design with 13 participants provides adequate power for the repeated-measures comparisons. The Daysimeter measurements confirmed that the three conditions produced substantially different circadian stimulus levels at the cornea, validating the experimental manipulation. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p < 0.05; p < 0.001.
study_record.limitations_text: The 13-participant sample is small, increasing the risk of Type II errors, particularly for the tablets-only condition at 1 hour where the non-significant result may reflect insufficient power rather than a true null effect. Only one tablet model (iPad) at maximum brightness was tested; modern tablets with higher luminance or different spectral characteristics may produce different results. The controlled laboratory setting does not account for ambient room lighting that would add to tablet light exposure in typical home environments. Only young adults were tested; age-related lens yellowing may reduce short-wavelength transmission in older adults. The 2-hour maximum exposure does not establish whether suppression continues to increase at longer durations.
study_record.study_design: Wood and colleagues (2013) used a within-subjects design with 13 participants at the Lighting Research Center, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. Each participant experienced three evening experimental conditions on separate nights: (1) tablets-only at maximum screen brightness, during which participants performed self-selected activities (reading, browsing, gaming) as they would at home; (2) tablets viewed through clear-lens goggles fitted with blue light-emitting diodes providing 40 lux of 470-nm light at the cornea, adding circadian-active light to the tablet emission; and (3) tablets viewed through orange-tinted glasses that blocked all optical radiation below 525 nm, serving as a dark control that eliminated short-wavelength light while permitting normal visual function. Salivary melatonin samples were collected at baseline, after one hour, and after two hours. Photopic illuminance, circadian light (CLA), and circadian stimulus (CS) levels were measured using the Daysimeter, a personal circadian light meter developed at RPI.

study_record.key_statistics: The evaluation demonstrated that MiPS tools produced high consensus between designers and clients on the sensorial properties required for target user-interactions. The consensus was assessed through agreement measures comparing designer interpretations of client desires with client self-reports. While specific statistical values should be confirmed from interior results pages, the evaluation found that the structured tool-guided process substantially reduced ambiguity in designer-client communication about materials. The tools were positively received by both professional designers and students, with participants reporting that the structured approach helped them articulate and converge on material requirements that would otherwise remain implicit and subjective.
study_record.limitations_text: The evaluation does not report detailed statistical analyses (sample sizes, significance levels, effect sizes), limiting assessment of the tools' quantitative effectiveness. The study was conducted within one university's design program, and generalizability to different design cultures and client types is uncertain. The MiPS tools focus on discrete product objects rather than architectural-scale material decisions, which involve larger surfaces, environmental interactions, and aging characteristics. The approach assumes that clients can articulate their sensorial preferences when prompted, which may not always be the case. Cultural variation in material preferences (warmth, smoothness, weight associations) is not addressed. The 2007 publication predates digital material libraries and virtual material visualization that could supplement or replace physical samples.
study_record.study_design: Van Kesteren and colleagues (2007) at Delft University of Technology developed the MiPS tools through an iterative design research process at the Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering. The tools were evaluated with both professional product designers and design students. In evaluation sessions, designers and clients (or client proxies) used the MiPS instruments to define the desired sensorial properties for a product's materials. The three instruments operate across several phases of the user-product interaction: defining the desired interaction quality (using product pictures), exploring material options (using physical samples), and specifying sensorial properties (using descriptor cards). The evaluation assessed whether the tools improved consensus between designers and clients on user-interaction goals and corresponding material specifications, comparing structured MiPS-guided sessions with conventional design discussion.

study_record.key_statistics: As a phenomenological qualitative study, the paper reports thematic findings rather than statistical analyses. The dominant themes identified include: acoustic spatial mapping (mentioned consistently across all informants as the primary compensatory sense); tactile surface discrimination (floor texture changes identified as the most reliable non-visual boundary marker); thermal sensing (informants could detect proximity to windows, sun-exposed walls, and HVAC vents); and olfactory anchoring (distinctive scents used to identify specific rooms and locations). The analysis reveals that physical characteristic perception -- material properties, surface qualities, acoustic behavior -- serves as the foundational cognitive process for non-visual spatial understanding, with architectural elements providing more reliable spatial information than movable objects or social cues.
study_record.limitations_text: The study relies on a small qualitative sample from Cairo, Egypt, limiting generalizability to different architectural traditions and climatic contexts. The literary analysis of Taha Hussein's autobiography provides historical richness but reflects early 20th-century rural Egyptian architecture, which differs substantially from contemporary urban environments. The phenomenological method is appropriate for understanding subjective experience but cannot quantify the relative importance of different sensory modalities in spatial navigation. Individual variation in visual impairment type, onset age, and compensatory skill development may affect spatial perception strategies but is not systematically analyzed. The study does not include experimental validation that the identified spatial qualities actually improve navigation performance for visually impaired users.
study_record.study_design: Bakir and colleagues (2022) employed a phenomenological research approach drawing on two complementary data sources. First, they analyzed the autobiography of Taha Hussein, the Egyptian literary figure who lost his sight as a young child, extracting passages describing spatial experience, navigation strategies, and environmental perception through non-visual senses. This literary analysis provided a rich, retrospective account of blind spatial experience in a specific cultural and architectural context. Second, the researchers conducted in-depth semi-structured interviews and guided tours with visually impaired and blind informants in Cairo, Egypt. During guided tours, researchers accompanied informants through familiar and unfamiliar built environments, recording their descriptions of spatial experience, navigation strategies, and sensory impressions. The combined analysis identified recurring themes in multisensory spatial perception and specific architectural qualities that support or hinder non-visual spatial understanding.

study_record.key_statistics:
Regression analysis: BGN threshold for discomfort among high-sensitivity students was 62.4 dBA; RT threshold was 1.7 seconds; SNR threshold was 3.7 dBA (all p < .05). Chi-square acceptability: students were more likely to accept acoustic conditions when BGN ≤ 61 dBA, RT ≤ 0.7 s, and SNR ≥ 6.5 dBA. BGN across classrooms ranged from 58.2 to 65.3 dBA. RT ranged from 0.7 to 2.1 seconds. Positive correlations were found between acoustic comfort, engagement, and productivity (all p < .05). The 828-response dataset from 11 classrooms provides robust statistical power and ecological validity for the threshold estimates. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p =
.007; p = .026; p < .01; p = .013; n = 7.
study_record.limitations_text: The study was conducted at one institution in one climate zone; classrooms in other contexts (primary schools, different climates, different ceiling heights) may show different thresholds. Self-reported productivity and engagement may not correspond to objectively measured learning outcomes. The 4-month study period captures one academic season but may not reflect seasonal variation in fan usage and window opening patterns. Individual noise sensitivity was self-reported and not validated against audiometric assessment. The correlational design cannot establish whether poor acoustics cause reduced engagement or whether disengaged students are more aware of background noise. The specific BGN contribution of ceiling fans versus external noise was not separated in all measurements.
study_record.study_design: Bhandari and colleagues (2024) conducted a four-month field study at the National Institute of Technology, Tiruchirappalli, in southern India's warm-humid climate zone. Eleven active naturally ventilated classrooms were studied during regular academic sessions. Sound pressure levels were measured in each classroom both with and without students present, allowing calculation of BGN, SNR, and the contribution of ceiling fan noise. Reverberation time was measured in unoccupied classrooms. A total of 828 questionnaire responses were collected from students at every seating position, capturing: acoustic comfort ratings, self-reported productivity, classroom engagement, and individual noise sensitivity. Regression analysis identified the BGN, RT, and SNR thresholds at which noise-sensitive students reported discomfort. Chi-square tests on acceptability votes determined the acoustic conditions that the majority of students found acceptable.

rows.canonical_text: Sound is becoming an organic element in museum exhibitions, which are increasingly encouraging participation, interaction and experience in communicating cultural information to the visitors. This paper expands on this…
rows.source_text: Sound is becoming an organic element in museum exhibitions, which are increasingly encouraging participation, interaction and experience in communicating cultural information to the visitors. This paper expands on this…

study_record.key_statistics: As a theoretical review, the paper synthesizes qualitative case studies and conceptual arguments rather than reporting statistical analyses. Key synthesis points include: visitor dwell time at exhibits is influenced by ambient sound levels; background noise above approximately 45-50 dBA in gallery spaces has been associated with reduced visitor satisfaction in cited studies; sound isolation between galleries is essential for maintaining the integrity of audio-based exhibits; and the growing prevalence of multimedia and immersive exhibitions has increased the acoustic complexity of museum spaces, creating challenges for sound management that most museum buildings were not designed to address.
study_record.limitations_text: The review focuses primarily on Western art museums and may not generalize to science museums, children's museums, or cultural institutions in other traditions with different relationships to sound. The case studies are selectively chosen to illustrate conceptual points rather than systematically sampled. Quantitative evidence for the specific effects of museum acoustics on visitor behavior is sparse in the literature, limiting the empirical foundation for practical recommendations. The tension between acoustic ideals and preservation requirements (humidity control, temperature management, security) is acknowledged but not resolved. The rapid evolution of immersive exhibition technology since 2014 may have created new acoustic challenges not addressed in the review.
study_record.study_design: Bubaris (2014) conducted a narrative review spanning museum studies, sound art theory, architectural acoustics, and visitor experience research. The review draws on case studies of museums that have deliberately incorporated sound design (both successful and problematic), theoretical frameworks from sound studies and acoustic ecology (Murray Schafer's soundscape concept), and practical considerations of acoustic management in exhibition spaces. The analysis is organized around the distinction between unintentional and intentional sound in museums, examining how each category affects visitor behavior, emotional response, and cognitive engagement with exhibited content. design and exhibition design: what are the possibilities that open up once we recognise the agency of sound and the ways it affects the visitors' experience? rows.canonical_text: Fife \( ^ 64 \) showed that hospital stays for cataract surgery patients increased during the time of higher noise due to construction of a new building.
rows.source_text: Fife \( ^ 64 \) showed that hospital stays for cataract surgery patients increased during the time of higher noise due to construction of a new building.

study_record.key_statistics: Average noise levels across all measured areas ranged from approximately 58 to 65 dBA, consistently exceeding the WHO daytime guideline of 40 dBA by 18-25 dBA and the nighttime guideline of 35 dBA by 23-30 dBA. These are not marginal exceedances: a 20 dBA difference represents a perceived loudness approximately four times the recommended level. Peak noise events regularly exceeded 80 dBA. Night-time noise levels, while lower than daytime, still substantially exceeded the 35 dBA guideline, indicating that typical hospital operations generate noise levels incompatible with sleep even during quiet hours. The comparison with historical data showed that hospital noise levels have remained essentially unchanged or have increased slightly over decades, despite published studies documenting adverse health effects.
study_record.limitations_text: The study measured a single hospital (albeit a major one), and noise environments may differ in other facility types and sizes. The measurements capture the acoustic environment but do not directly measure patient health outcomes (sleep disruption, stress, recovery time) that would establish causation. Specific measurement locations, durations, and seasonal variations should be confirmed from the full paper. The study was conducted in 2005 and hospital technology (electronic alarms, communication systems) has evolved, though evidence suggests noise levels have not improved. The structural sources of hospital noise (hard surfaces for infection control, open floor plans for visual monitoring, alarm systems for safety) create fundamental design conflicts with acoustic comfort that may not be fully resolvable.
study_record.study_design: Busch-Vishniac and colleagues (2005) deployed calibrated sound level meters across multiple units and departments of Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland -- one of the United States' premier teaching hospitals. Continuous noise monitoring was conducted over extended periods to capture representative temporal patterns, including day-night variations, shift changes, and weekend versus weekday differences. Measurements included: time-weighted equivalent continuous sound levels (Leq), peak noise levels, statistical distributions (L10, L50, L90 percentiles), and time-history recordings that allowed identification of specific noise sources. Measured levels were compared against three standards: WHO guidelines for community noise in healthcare settings, EPA-identified levels requisite to protect public health, and ASHRAE noise criteria for hospital spaces.

The structural sources of hospital noise (hard surfaces for infection control, open floor plans for visual monitoring, alarm systems for safety) create fundamental design conflicts with acoustic comfort that may not be fully resolvable.
study_record.study_design: Busch-Vishniac and colleagues (2005) deployed calibrated sound level meters across multiple units and departments of Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland -- one of the United States' premier teaching hospitals. Continuous noise monitoring was conducted over extended periods to capture representative temporal patterns, including day-night variations, shift changes, and weekend versus weekday differences. Measurements included: time-weighted equivalent continuous sound levels (Leq), peak noise levels, statistical distributions (L10, L50, L90 percentiles), and time-history recordings that allowed identification of specific noise sources. Measured levels were compared against three standards: WHO guidelines for community noise in healthcare settings, EPA-identified levels requisite to protect public health, and ASHRAE noise criteria for hospital spaces.

study_record.key_statistics: J. maritima panels achieved absorption coefficients superior to those reported in previous studies using other plant species, particularly at mid and high frequencies. Multiple regression analysis identified panel weight as the dominant predictor of sound absorption capacity, explaining more variance than plant species, coverage area, or substrate type alone. Panels with less than full greenery coverage achieved absorption coefficients within a practical range of fully covered panels, demonstrating the viability of partial coverage. SS modifications (perforated boards, panel absorbers) significantly improved low-frequency absorption below 1000 Hz, addressing the primary acoustic limitation of unmodified LWS configurations. Specific absorption coefficient values and frequency response curves should be confirmed from interior figures.
study_record.limitations_text: Reverberation room measurements characterize material properties under diffuse-field conditions that differ from the in-situ acoustic environment of an installed LWS on a building facade. The study tested one primary plant species (J. maritima); other species with different leaf density, moisture content, and morphology may produce different results. The WPC composite material may have different long-term acoustic properties as it ages, absorbs moisture, and degrades. The sound absorption coefficients measured do not directly translate to noise reduction in complex urban geometries where reflection, diffraction, and ground effects interact. The cost-effectiveness comparison does not include lifecycle costs of maintenance, irrigation, and plant replacement.
study_record.study_design: Chang and Chang (2022) constructed LWS panels using Jacobaea maritima planted in wood-plastic composite (WPC) substrates made from recycled plastic at the National Taiwan University School of Forestry and Resource Conservation. Sound absorption coefficients (α_s) were measured in a reverberation room following standard acoustic testing protocols. The study systematically varied: LWS weight and morphology; SS structure (perforated board design, panel absorber additions); plant coverage percentage (full versus partial greenery); substrate depth; and surface pattern. Absorption coefficients were compared with published values from previous LWS studies using different plant species and configurations, providing a comparative performance assessment.

study_record.key_statistics: The three PCA components together explained 90% of the total variance in aesthetic ratings across the 200 interiors. The three-component structure replicated with high fidelity in the independent Experiment 2 sample (n = 614). In the fMRI reanalysis (n = 18), Fascination tracked right lingual gyrus activity reliably across both the beauty-judgment task and the approach-avoidance task. Coherence tracked left inferior occipital gyrus activity, but only during beauty judgments, not during approach-avoidance. Hominess tracked left cuneus activity, but only during approach-avoidance, not during beauty judgments. These cross-over dissociations are the paper's key result. The three psychological dimensions engage different neural circuits depending on what the viewer is being asked to do, which fits a model where aesthetic experience runs several parallel evaluations of the same scene at once.
study_record.limitations_text: Four limits stand out. First, the fMRI sample is small (n = 18). The behavioral findings replicate robustly across 1,400+ participants, but the neural signatures need bigger imaging samples before they can be claimed as settled. Second, the study used photographs rather than full immersive spaces, so the embodied side of architectural experience -- movement, sound, smell, scale -- is not in the data. Third, the 200 images, while varied, may not span the full range of interior types: industrial, sacred, or outdoor-indoor transitional spaces are likely under-represented. Fourth, the PCA dimensions are population-level; individual differences in aesthetic sensitivity, cultural background, and design training may yield different dimensional structures for different viewers. The neural results are also correlational -- parametric covariation does not show that these brain regions cause the psychological experience of Coherence, Fascination, or Hominess.
study_record.study_design: Coburn and colleagues (2020) ran three sequential studies. In Experiment 1, 798 online participants rated 200 photographs of architectural interiors. Each interior was rated on 16 aesthetic-response scales spanning evaluative items (beautiful, interesting, pleasant), affective items (calming, exciting), and descriptive items (coherent, complex, familiar). The team applied PNA and PCA to the 16-item correlation matrix and found a three-component solution. In Experiment 2, 614 new participants rated the same images on the same scales, giving a full replication of the factor structure. In Experiment 3, the team reanalysed previously collected fMRI data from 18 participants who had viewed the same 200 interior images while either judging beauty or making approach-avoidance decisions in a block design. Parametric analyses tested whether brain activity at each voxel tracked the three PCA dimension scores assigned to each image, while controlling for low-level image features such as fractal dimension and spatial frequency content.

study_record.key_statistics: Five factors emerged consistently across all six analyses, with the factor structure remaining stable across stimulus context (chips vs model) and participant group (architects vs non-architects). Isosemantic maps showed linear correlations between dynamism and chroma, spatial quality and value, and emotional tone and hue. Subsidiary non-linear effects of hue were detected through isosemantic map inspection, though linear correlations for evaluation and complexity factors were low or non-existent, indicating their complex multi-parameter determination. The critical finding of architect-non-architect divergence appeared specifically on the evaluation factor, where the determinant structure differed markedly between groups. Comparability with international studies (across countries over a 20-year period) was noted for dynamism, spatial quality, and emotional tone, suggesting cross-cultural universality.
study_record.limitations_text: The 1979 publication predates contemporary color science methods and computational analysis. Sample sizes for the individual analyses are not reported in the abstract. The simulated interior model, while more contextual than isolated chips, lacks the immersive quality of full-scale architectural color experience. Only Munsell colors were tested; architectural finishes include textures, sheens, and metallic effects not captured by flat matte chips. The cross-cultural comparability claim rests on comparison with studies in a limited number of primarily Northern European countries. Modern display technologies and lighting conditions may alter color perception compared with the 1979 experimental context.
study_record.study_design: Hogg and colleagues (1979) employed the Semantic Differential technique, presenting Munsell color samples in two formats: individual color chips and as surface colors within a physical model of an interior space. Participants rated each stimulus on bipolar scales (e.g., dynamic-static, spacious-cramped, warm-cool, good-bad, simple-complex). Six separate analyses were conducted: total sample chip judgments, total sample model judgments, architects' chip judgments, non-architects' chip judgments, architects' model judgments, and non-architects' model judgments. Factor analysis (principal components) extracted the five judgement dimensions. Linear correlations between color parameters (Munsell hue, value, chroma) and factor scores were calculated, and isosemantic maps were constructed using techniques from Sivik (1974a) to visualize the relationships graphically.

study_record.key_statistics: As a perspective piece, the paper reports no original statistical analyses. The review cites that 15-20% of the world's population is now considered neurodiverse, which sets the scale of the design challenge. Cited evidence includes: biophilic design dampens amygdala activity (specific studies referenced); nature exposure raises attention scores by specific percentages in cited studies; and biophilic office design lifts reported productivity and lowers absenteeism in cited workplace studies. The synthesis argues that the convergence of these separate evidence streams supports a neuroinclusive design approach, though the specific size of the benefit for neurodiverse versus neurotypical employees has not yet been directly compared in the cited literature.
study_record.limitations_text: Six honest limits stand out. First, this is a perspective / narrative review without original data, without a systematic search method, and without quantitative synthesis. Second, the claimed benefits of biophilic design for neurodiverse populations are extrapolated from separate literatures (nature-health and neurodiversity-occupational health) rather than tested directly. Third, no cited study measures the effect of biophilic features on neurodiverse versus neurotypical employees side by side. Fourth, the XR recommendations are forward-looking proposals without existing implementation evidence. Fifth, the 15-20% neurodiversity prevalence is approximate and depends on diagnostic criteria. Sixth -- and most important -- the article does not address potential clashes between biophilic features and sensory sensitivities: some neurodiverse individuals find certain natural stimuli (water sounds, moving plants, varied textures) aversive rather than calming.
study_record.study_design: Hutson and Hutson (2023) wrote a narrative review across three domains: biophilic design research (the nature-health evidence anchored in Attention Restoration Theory and Stress Recovery Theory). the neurodiversity literature on occupational challenges and environmental sensitivities. and smart-city technology, including XR and AI-supported environmental tailoring. The review pulls findings from neuroscience (amygdala reactivity, attention networks), environmental psychology (nature exposure effects), occupational health (productivity and well-being metrics), and sustainability science (lower carbon footprint via biophilic design). The article proposes a framework that ties the three literatures together for post-pandemic workplace design.

study_record.key_statistics: Ten urban restoration models reached correlations as high as r = 0.80 between audio-visual design factors and psycho-physiological responses, with R-squared up to 0.22. Green and waterfront scenes scored higher on restoration than urban scenes, as expected. Audio-visual interaction terms added significant variance beyond what visual-only or sound-only models could capture. Across the predictor set of 14 audio-visual elements and 6 affective qualities, present natural sounds and visible greenery emerged as the strongest individual predictors, but always more powerful in combination. P-values reported in the paper range from p < 0.05 for the strongest combined predictors to p > 0.9 for non-contributing elements.
study_record.limitations_text: Five caveats stand out. First, VR simulation is immersive but lacks the thermal, olfactory, and kinesthetic channels of real environmental experience. Second, the 60-person sample from one South Korean university limits how the results generalise to other cultural contexts. Third, the R-squared of 0.22, while significant, leaves 78 per cent of restoration variance unexplained, so other forces -- personal history, current stress, social context -- almost certainly contribute. Fourth, the three-way scene categorisation is reductive; real urban settings blend the categories. Fifth, physiological restoration was self-reported rather than measured through biomarkers.
study_record.study_design: The team at Hanyang University, Seoul, built VR scenes of three environment types: urban (street scenes), waterfront (rivers, harbours), and green (parks, gardens). Sixty participants viewed each scene type via a head-mounted display with spatial audio, which gave each scene an immersive and ecologically valid feel. The assessment ran in three tiers. First, participants flagged which of 14 audio-visual elements were present and how prominent they were (traffic sound, bird song, vegetation, water surface, building facades, and so on). Second, they rated six perceived affective qualities using ISO 12913-2 soundscape descriptors (pleasant, calm, eventful, vibrant, monotonous, chaotic). Third, they rated six overall environmental quality dimensions. Restoration responses were scored as psychological (attentional recovery, mood improvement) and physiological (stress reduction indicators). Multiple regression then mapped the audio-visual elements and affective ratings onto the restoration outcomes.

Multiple regression then mapped the audio-visual elements and affective ratings onto the restoration outcomes.

study_record.key_statistics:
Factor analysis consistently identified four semantic factors across all three study stages: relaxation, communication, spatiality, and dynamics. The correlation between SPL and acoustic comfort ratings was weak, confirming that decibel levels are insufficient predictors of soundscape quality. Architecture students showed significantly stronger preferences for natural sounds (birdsong, water, wind) and green spaces compared with the general public (p < .05), while the general public showed greater tolerance for mechanical and anthropogenic sounds. The combined sample of 762 participants across three stages provides substantial statistical power. Demographic factors (age, gender, familiarity with the space) moderated soundscape evaluations but did not alter the four-factor structure. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p < 0.05; p < 0.01; p
<17.
study_record.limitations_text: The study was conducted in one UK city with its specific acoustic character; urban soundscapes in climate zones requiring different building types, mixed-use patterns, and transportation modes may produce different factor structures. The semantic differential technique relies on linguistic scales whose meaning may vary across languages and cultures. The four-factor structure, while consistent across the three stages, was derived from a specific set of bipolar scales -- different scale selections might yield different factor structures. The architecture student sample may not represent practicing designers' evaluations. The cross-sectional design captures snapshot evaluations; longitudinal soundscape experience may produce different assessments.
study_record.study_design: Kang and Zhang (2010) at the University of Sheffield employed a three-stage methodology. Stage 1 was a pilot soundscape walk with 48 students through four typical urban open public spaces in Sheffield, establishing the feasibility and refinement of the semantic differential scales. Stage 2 was a detailed field survey with 491 members of the general public at two of the four sites, conducted during normal daytime use. Participants completed semantic differential questionnaires rating the soundscape on multiple bipolar scales while immersed in the actual acoustic environment. Stage 3 surveyed 223 architectural students using the same instruments, enabling expert-public comparison. Simultaneous sound level measurements provided objective acoustic data for correlation with subjective ratings. Factor analysis extracted the four semantic dimensions from the full set of bipolar rating scales.

study_record.key_statistics: Across the 125 products, consistent property-meaning mappings emerged: 'sexy' products were overwhelmingly characterized by high transparency and smoothness; 'professional' products by hardness and dark coloring; 'nostalgic' products by roughness and matte finishes; 'toy-like' products by bright, saturated colors and soft textures. These patterns were consistent enough across participants to constitute reliable design heuristics. The 25-participant sample, while modest, generated a 125-product corpus that provided adequate statistical power for the property-level analyses. Interview data converged with quantitative ratings, providing methodological triangulation. Mathpix-extracted statistics: n = 2; n = 13.
study_record.limitations_text: The 25-participant sample from one Dutch university limits cultural generalizability -- material meanings may vary significantly across cultures with different material traditions (wood-centric Nordic cultures, stone-heavy Mediterranean traditions, bamboo cultures in Southeast Asia). The five meaning categories (aggressive, nostalgic, professional, sexy, toy-like) are a limited vocabulary; architectural meanings (sacred, institutional, domestic, industrial) would require a different category set. The product-based methodology may not directly transfer to architectural-scale material experience, where weathering, scale, and environmental context modify material perception. Participants selected their own products, introducing selection bias toward materials they personally associate with each meaning. The 2009 study predates contemporary material innovations (smart materials, biomaterials, recycled composites) that may not fit the established property-meaning framework.
study_record.study_design: Karana, Hekkert, and Kandachar (2009) at Delft University employed a product collection methodology: 25 participants were each asked to select five products from their own possessions or environments that they felt expressed each of five target meanings (aggressive, nostalgic, professional, sexy, toy-like), resulting in a corpus of 125 products. For each selected product, participants underwent two assessment phases: first, a semi-structured interview in which they described what sensorial properties and manufacturing characteristics contributed to the product's perceived meaning; and second, a quantitative appraisal using five-point scales rating 13 identified sensorial properties (roughness, glossiness, transparency, hardness, color lightness, color saturation, perceived temperature, weight, flexibility, material type, surface pattern, form regularity, and size). Manufacturing processes were also coded from participant descriptions and product inspection.

study_record.key_statistics: Thermal sensation was 0.3 TSV cooler in the window condition (p < .05), equivalent to a 0.74°C lower temperature. Twelve percent more participants rated the thermal environment as comfortable with the window present. Positive emotions were significantly higher (p < .05) and negative emotions significantly lower in the window condition. Working memory and concentration were significantly higher with the window (p < .05). Short-term memory, planning, and creativity showed no significant differences between conditions. study_record.limitations_text: The study tested one temperature (28°C, slightly warm); the cooling effect of windows may not transfer to neutral or cool conditions. The nature view was specific to UC Berkeley's campus landscape; urban views without greenery may not produce the same effect. The mechanism is assumed to be multi-sensory integration (visual coolness influences thermal perception) but was not directly tested through physiological measures like fMRI or EEG. The cognitive tests were laboratory measures; transfer to actual work performance is assumed but not demonstrated. The single-session design captures acute effects but not long-term adaptation. The windowless condition covered an existing window, creating an unusual visual environment that may have had negative effects beyond the simple absence of a view.
study_record.study_design: Ko and colleagues (2020) conducted a randomized crossover experiment at the Center for the Built Environment, UC Berkeley, using a controlled environmental chamber. Eighty-six participants each experienced both conditions: a chamber with a window providing a view of outdoor trees and sky, and the same chamber with the window covered. The chamber maintained air temperature and window surface temperature at 28°C -- slightly above the neutral comfort zone -- to create a mildly warm condition where thermal perception differences could be detected. Participants' thermal sensation was measured using the standard 7-point ASHRAE scale. Thermal comfort was assessed as percent acceptable. Skin temperature was measured with sensors. Emotional state was measured using validated positive and negative emotion scales. Cognitive performance was assessed with five validated tests: working memory (operation span), concentration ability, short-term memory, planning tasks, and a creativity assessment. The crossover design, with randomized order of conditions, controlled for individual differences and learning effects.

study_record.key_statistics: Twenty-five studies with 1,950 total participants were included after systematic screening. The Joanna Briggs Institute assessment found high risk of bias in the majority of included studies -- a critical finding that tempers the positive results. Significant psych-physio associations were found across studies, though specific effect sizes varied. Audio-visual interaction consistently produced stronger effects than unimodal presentation across the included studies. The review notes that the synthesized evidence, despite being from individual studies with limitations, provides a higher level of evidence than any single study and aligns with results from other systematic reviews and individual experiments in the field. Mathpix-extracted statistics: N=20; N=120; N=15; N=30; N=45.
study_record.limitations_text: The systematic review's primary finding is itself a limitation: the high risk of bias across included studies means that the positive psych-physio associations may be inflated or confounded. The 25-study corpus, while adequate for qualitative synthesis, is too small and heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis with reliable pooled effect sizes. The inclusion of Chinese-language studies, while a methodological strength, may introduce translation and cultural comparability challenges. The exclusion of pure music, religious, and historical sounds limits the review's scope to environmental soundscapes. Physiological measures varied substantially across studies (heart rate, HRV, cortisol, EEG), making direct comparison difficult. Publication bias toward positive findings is likely present.
study_record.study_design: Kong and Han (2024) conducted a systematic literature search across both English and Chinese databases, a methodological strength given the substantial Chinese-language soundscape research literature that is typically excluded from English-only reviews. Inclusion criteria required empirical, quantitative studies that measured both psychological (subjective evaluations, questionnaires, semantic differential scales) and physiological (heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance, cortisol, EEG, EMG) responses to soundscapes. Twenty-five studies meeting these criteria were included, collectively involving 1,950 participants. Each study was assessed for risk of bias using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Randomized Controlled Trials, a validated quality assessment tool. The systematic review excluded studies of pure music, religious sounds, humanistic sounds, and historical sounds, focusing specifically on environmental soundscapes. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively across the three major findings.

Physiological measures varied substantially across studies (heart rate, HRV, cortisol, EEG), making direct comparison difficult. Publication bias toward positive findings is likely present.
study_record.study_design: Kong and Han (2024) conducted a systematic literature search across both English and Chinese databases, a methodological strength given the substantial Chinese-language soundscape research literature that is typically excluded from English-only reviews. Inclusion criteria required empirical, quantitative studies that measured both psychological (subjective evaluations, questionnaires, semantic differential scales) and physiological (heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance, cortisol, EEG, EMG) responses to soundscapes. Twenty-five studies meeting these criteria were included, collectively involving 1,950 participants. Each study was assessed for risk of bias using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Randomized Controlled Trials, a validated quality assessment tool. The systematic review excluded studies of pure music, religious sounds, humanistic sounds, and historical sounds, focusing specifically on environmental soundscapes. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively across the three major findings.

Across 67 studies, noise consistently impaired learning efficiency with increasing severity at higher SPL levels (threshold approximately 50-55 dBA for significant impairment). The effects of non-noise sounds were highly variable: some studies found background music beneficial for certain tasks, while others found it detrimental; similarly for nature sounds and white noise. RT effects showed that speech intelligibility decreases with increasing RT, but the interaction with background noise level was poorly controlled in most studies. The review identified that younger students and those with learning difficulties are disproportionately affected by adverse acoustic conditions, suggesting that acoustic quality is an equity issue in education. 0.05; p = 0.002.
study_record.limitations_text: The narrative review methodology does not include systematic risk of bias assessment or quantitative meta-analysis, so the strength of individual findings cannot be formally weighted. The 67 studies span diverse methodologies, populations, and acoustic conditions, making direct comparison difficult. Publication bias toward significant noise effects may overemphasize negative impacts while underreporting null findings for non-noise sounds. The review covers studies since 2000 but acoustic standards and building practices have evolved within this period. Home learning environments, while increasingly important, are represented by relatively few studies. The interaction between acoustic environment and other IEQ factors (thermal comfort, lighting, air quality) is not systematically addressed.

The review synthesized findings separately for sound source effects, SPL effects, and RT effects, identifying convergent findings, contradictions, and methodological gaps across the literature.

study_record.key_statistics: The proof-of-concept study had a sample of n = 5 and reported a summary p < 0.0001 on the central manipulation. These numbers should not be read as a definitive empirical finding -- the study is underpowered for that and the authors do not claim otherwise. They are evidence that the platform produces detectable, internally consistent signal across the three sensory channels in a small pilot. The paper's main analytic anchors are Table 1 (the thermal conditions imposed in the scene), Table 2 (mean radiant temperature across heights and distances), and Table 3 (the per-participant results). Read these tables as proof the platform works, not as a test of any hypothesis about how thermal environments shape behaviour.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is a methods introduction, so its claims rightly stay close to the platform itself rather than reaching for a decisive empirical answer about any specific design phenomenon. Three honest limits stand out. First, the proof-of-concept study has only five participants -- evidence the platform works, not evidence about the world the platform is meant to study. Second, the gap between a VR scene and the actual built environment remains real: subjects know they are in a headset, and the thermal channel in particular is harder to reproduce convincingly than the visual one. Third, longer-term effects -- adaptation over hours or days, fatigue, discomfort -- cannot be tested in a short VR session. The authors acknowledge that follow-up empirical studies still have to do the real work of testing how the platform's findings transfer to physical buildings.
study_record.study_design: The paper is best read as a methods piece in the qualitative-methods tradition (manifest profile: qualitative; classifier confidence 0.72). It is not a hypothesis-testing study; the authors are introducing a platform and showing it works. MIVE is built around a head-mounted VR rig that lets the user move through a scene, look around, and even change parts of the virtual environment in real time. While the user moves, the system logs their position, gaze direction, the changes they make, plus their answers on standard self-report scales and their physiological state. The proof-of-concept study put a small number of participants into a semi-outdoor scene with three thermal settings -- cool, neutral, warm -- and recorded how the visual, auditory, and thermal channels combined to shape what the participants did, said, and felt. The point is the platform, not the specific results: future studies can swap in any built-environment scene and any combination of sensory channels.

study_record.key_statistics: The overall count is 34 studies. Across those studies, 36 findings are supportive, 34 are neutral, and 12 are contrary. Prospect is the most examined property at 38% and the most confirmed at 53%. Refuge is second in support at 22%, but it also has the highest neutral and contrary shares, at 41% and 41.5%. Venue splits matter too: three studies address urban settings, ten address landscapes, and 21 address interiors. The paper also notes that only eight studies had 100 or more participants, while 16 relied on 20 or fewer, which helps explain why the evidence remains uneven.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper itself is careful about what it does not do. It compares findings, not methods, and it accepts many authors' conclusions at face value. That leaves open the quality differences between studies. It also shows that many of the underlying samples are small and often drawn from Western university contexts. Those are serious limits. So the safest reading is conditional: prospect-refuge explains some preferences in some venues, but not all preferences in all spaces.
study_record.study_design: The meta-analysis includes 34 quantitative studies. Twenty of them focus mainly on perceptual properties, five on geometric properties, and nine combine the two. study_record.key_statistics: The piece gives three main example families rather than inferential statistics. First, it treats level invariance as sufficient only for a special deterministic linear system with asymmetric and irreflexive laws. Second, it uses three axioms for causal Bayes-nets and shows where they fail. Third, it contrasts two manipulationist accounts: one tied to proposed interventions and one tied to interventions possible for us. Those are the key structural counts. They are the logic of the argument, and they replace the sort of numeric summary one would expect in an empirical paper.
study_record.limitations_text: The book review is persuasive, but it leaves open the hard job of building a richer account that can unify the cases without flattening them. It also shows that some causal notions may be too local to travel far. That is not a weakness of the review; it is the book's own diagnosis. The remaining uncertainty is therefore structural. We still lack a general theory that tells us, without handwaving, when a criterion is sufficient and when it is merely useful. The findings should be interpreted within the constraints of the study design. The specific environmental conditions, participant demographics, and measurement instruments used may limit how broadly these results generalize to other contexts. Replication across diverse populations and real-world settings would strengthen the evidence base for the design implications suggested above.
study_record.study_design: This is a symposium review, not a dataset. It moves through four linked argumentative surfaces: level invariance, causal Bayes-nets, manipulationist accounts, and action-guiding counterfactuals. The scope dimensions are explicit: deterministic linear systems, probabilistic causal systems, and intervention-based models. The paper also keeps philosophy and economics in frame because Cartwright thinks the same causal term can support different tasks in those fields. That makes the review methodological in the strong sense. It asks what kind of causal law we have before we ask which method will find it. Methods'. This project argued that metaphysics - our account of what causal laws are or what general causal claims say - should march hand-in-hand with our ways of establishing them.

study_record.key_statistics: There is no pooled dataset, and that is part of the point. The argument comes from conceptual comparison rather than meta-analysis. Still, the paper is concrete about scope: it ranges from sensory attributes such as luminance and geometry to nonvisual cues such as odor and movement, then to health and meaning. The examples point to buildings, museums, parks, offices, and classrooms as settings where the framework can be tested. The useful statistic here is not a p-value but the breadth of the claim: one framework is meant to span several design and brain domains rather than a single interior feature.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is honest about its status: it is a first framework, not a final account. It relies on examples from several adjacent literatures, and those literatures do not always use the same measures or settings. The claim therefore needs empirical sharpening. It is plausible that the triad will help, but the paper does not yet show how much each system contributes in a hospital ward versus a classroom or office. The theory is useful precisely because it is incomplete. It opens a research program rather than closing one.
study_record.study_design: The piece is a conceptual review of architectural neuroscience and empirical aesthetics. It moves from vision and nonvisual experience to motor response, meaning, emotion, and health, then returns to a broader research agenda. The paper uses examples such as the Vitruvian triad, place cells, natural view, ceiling height, and embodied movement to show how architecture reaches the brain through multiple systems. Figure 1 gives the Vitruvian triad, and Figure 2 gives the aesthetic triad. The paper does not report participants or an experiment of its own; it synthesizes a field.

study_record.key_statistics: The most concrete numbers are the sample sizes and the survey shift. The paper reports 12 interviews at each of the three sites, plus the post-move survey with 822 responses. It also says that staff reported a positive shift in health and productivity three months before and six months after the move, while the positive change table in Figure 19 breaks that shift down by floor level. The data are descriptive rather than inferential, but the pattern is consistent enough to matter. Staff comments about openness, flexibility, and choice sit beside comments about camping, crowding, and trouble concentrating, so the workplace effect is mixed rather than one-sided.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is rich in observation but limited as evidence. It uses case studies, not randomized comparison, so it cannot isolate one causal factor. The survey data also come from a changing workplace with a small representative sample in some places, so the timing of the move may color the response. The authors are careful about that and avoid claiming a final verdict on activity-based working. The safest reading is that the green workplace can help, but only when the spatial and acoustic load does not overwhelm the claimed benefits.
study_record.study_design: The authors use mixed methods across three Green Star premium office case studies in Melbourne. They combine semi-focused interviews, walkabouts, observations, document review, photographs, floor plans, and an online building-use survey administered before and after occupancy. Each site contributed 12 interviews, and the later survey generated 822 responses from 48% of staff in the new activity-based workplace. The study tracks buildings from roughly 2009 to 2014, which lets the reader see how the open-plan concept changed across several moves. The approach is pragmatic rather than experimental, but it gives a wide view of lived workplace change.

study_record.limitations_text: The sample is relatively small (N = 39) and homogeneous (graduate students at a single university), limiting generalizability. Effect sizes are small to medium (d = 0.20 to 0.59), suggesting that white noise is a modulator rather than a major determinant of cognitive performance.
study_record.study_design: Forty adults participated; one was excluded for unreliable survey responses, yielding N = 39 (24 male, 16 female; mean age 25.82 ± 7.53). All were graduate students at the University of Southern California with normal hearing confirmed by an online hearing screening test. The within-subjects design crossed three auditory conditions: white noise at 45 dB (EPA-recommended indoor level), white noise at 65 dB (high level, below CDC discomfort threshold of 70 dB), and ambient office noise (M = 42.3 dB, SD = 1.2). White noise was generated in Audacity 3.0.2 and delivered via Bose QuietComfort 35 headphones with active noise cancellation. Five cognitive tests were administered via PsychoPy 2021.1.0: (1) Continuous Performance Test (sustained attention, 320 trials); (2) Stroop Test (selective attention/inhibition, 120 trials); (3) Two-Back Test (working memory, 120 trials); (4) Remote Associate Test (creativity, untimed); (5) Typing Performance Test (speed and accuracy). Stress was measured via mean tonic EDA from an Empatica E4 wristband. Each condition was counterbalanced using a Latin square. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA (α = 0.05) was used for each dependent variable.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper does not report inferential statistics in the way a laboratory study would. Its evidence is structural and comparative. The most important numerical fact is the case-study scope: four hospitals in Cairo, each analyzed through the same spatial lenses. The results are carried through visual integration maps and isovist graphs rather than through p-values. That is not a weakness by itself. It matches the paper's aim, which is to show how neuroarchitecture could be operationalized before anyone asks for clinical endpoints. Table 1 anchors the sample of settings, while the ward figures show where the spatial problems lie.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper stays at the level of case-study analysis, so it cannot tell us whether the proposed workflow improves patient recovery, staff stress, or navigation errors. It also focuses on one city and a small number of hospitals. That means the method still needs validation in other healthcare systems and in other room types. The spatial metrics are informative, but they are not the same as human outcome data. The paper is therefore a proposal with evidence attached, not a settled rulebook. That distinction matters and keeps the claim honest.
study_record.study_design: The article first reviews neuroarchitecture effects and design principles, then builds a computational framework for healthcare interiors. It uses four Cairo hospitals as a case study and compares visual integration, isovist structure, and connectivity across inpatient wards. Figures 1 to 5 present the research-methods map, the neuro-design principle map, the classification of healthcare design principles, the relative contribution of the three analytic traditions, and the isovist concept. Figures 6 to 13 then display the Depthmap outputs for the four wards. Table 1 gives the research settings. The approach is design-analytic, not experimental.

study_record.key_statistics: The survey sample is fifty participants, and the paper uses the responses to chart avoidance, tolerance, and design fears. The online results are presented descriptively rather than with formal hypothesis testing. That is still useful because the paper wants to show the pattern of concern, not claim a statistical law. Table 2 lists the architectural elements that generate phobias, Table 3 lists the case-study parameters, and Tables 4 to 6 apply the same logic to individual cases. The results support a broad conclusion: people do not react to contemporary forms in a single way, and the same element can feel threatening to some and neutral to others.
study_record.limitations_text: The study relies on a small online survey and selected case studies, so it cannot prove clinical phobia or general population prevalence. The survey is self-report, and the cases are chosen to illustrate the argument rather than to represent every contemporary building. The paper also uses broad phobia language, which is helpful for design discussion but looser than psychiatric diagnosis. The right reading is therefore careful: the article identifies a design-risk pattern, not a medical diagnosis. It suggests where caution is warranted, but it does not quantify the full social prevalence of the fear response.
study_record.study_design: The article combines a literature review, a comparative case-study analysis, and an online survey of 50 participants. It moves from definitions of phobia and contemporary architecture into a set of case studies, including the Elbphilharmonie and Messner Mountain Museum, then uses the survey to ask how people would react if they had to work, live, or visit such spaces. Figures 1 to 5 show the buildings and the phobia cues, while Tables 2 to 6 map the elements and the case-study parameters. The method is mixed because it joins interpretive reading with response data.

study_record.key_statistics: The main valence result for SideWalls is F(2,56) = 29.933, p = 1.4e-9, eta_p2 = 0.516. Windows also matter, F(2,56) = 4.941, p = .011, eta_p2 = 0.149, and Ceiling matters too, F(2,56) = 7.135, p = .002, eta_p2 = 0.203. For arousal, SideWalls again lead, F(2,56) = 20.589, p = 1.9e-7, eta_p2 = 0.424, and Windows follow, F(2,56) = 6.812, p = .002, eta_p2 = 0.196. Table 1 then shows how the architectures distribute across the HANV and LAPV clusters, with the decreasing side-wall condition landing mostly in HANV. That is the quantitative core of the paper.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is strong in control but still limited to VR. Real buildings add smell, sound, social contact, and longer exposure, so the emotional map may shift outside the headset. The sample is also modest, and the colour manipulation does little in this setup, which means color may matter under other chromatic conditions. The result is therefore comparative and bounded. It tells us which geometric factor dominates here, but it does not claim that every architectural journey will respond the same way in the field. That restraint is important and makes the finding more credible.
study_record.study_design: The authors ran a VR experiment with 29 participants, all of whom walked through 54 virtual architectures built from three nuclei. The design crossed SideWalls, Ceiling, Windows, and Colour in a 3x3x3x2 within-subject structure. Each trial lasted 12.5 s, and the participants then rated valence and arousal on visual analog scales inside an HTC Vive Pro Eye headset. The team also clustered the scenes into high-arousal negative-valence and low-arousal positive-valence groups. Figure 2 shows the trial structure, Figure 3 shows valence, Figure 4 shows arousal, and Figure 5 shows the cluster map.

study_record.limitations_text: The evidence base is small (8 studies from 5 countries), and the studies differ substantially in exposure mode, noise frequency, duration, and cognitive task battery. This diversity drives the high heterogeneity (up to I² = 91%) in some analyses and limits the precision of the pooled estimates. The review is restricted to published randomized studies in English, creating potential publication bias and excluding unpublished null findings or non-English literature. The RoB 2 assessment revealed some concerns in several included studies. The meta-analysis cannot specify a dose-response curve — it cannot say how much LFN at what duration produces the higher-order cognitive decrement. The result is directional and provisional, not a basis for a fixed exposure standard.
study_record.study_design: The systematic review follows PRISMA guidelines and used the PECOS framework to define eligibility: Participants (human subjects), Exposure (low-frequency noise ≤ 500 Hz), Comparison (no LFN or control condition), Outcomes (cognitive function scores), and Study design (original experimental studies with randomization). Four databases were searched: PubMed (n = 1,640), Medline (n = 1,326), Web of Science (n = 2,459), and PsycINFO (n = 638), totaling 6,063 records. After duplicate removal (n = 1,266), title/abstract screening excluded 4,745 records. Fifty-two reports were assessed for eligibility; 42 were excluded (5 reviews, 3 animal studies, 8 not measuring a single cognitive concept, 23 not measuring LFN as a single concept, 2 not relevant, 1 no useful data). The final 8 studies were from five countries. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. Cognitive outcomes were grouped into four domains: attention, executive function, memory, and higher-order functions. A random-effects model was used for each domain-level meta-analysis.
