study_record.key_statistics: The paper reports a clear sound-source effect, p < 0.01, on reaction time. Figure 3 shows the shortest mean reaction time under music at 2.560 s, followed by traffic noise at 2.705 s and air-conditioning noise at 2.771 s, with natural sound at 2.873 s and speech at 2.955 s. Table 4 shows that SPL correlates negatively with reaction time for traffic and air-conditioning noise, while Table 5 shows that speech reverberation time correlates negatively with reaction time, R = -0.053, p < 0.01. The study also reports that the SPL calibration in Table 1 matches the preset values closely, which keeps the stimulus manipulation credible.
study_record.limitations_text: The experiment is strong but still bounded. It uses one task family, one respondent group, and a controlled office setting rather than a real organization with deadlines, interruptions, and team dynamics. The results also separate sound source, level, and reverberation for analytic clarity, but real offices combine them. The paper therefore gives a reliable performance map, not a final law of work acoustics. The safe reading is comparative and design-oriented: sound does matter, but the magnitude and direction depend on the source and on the part of performance one cares about.
study_record.study_design: The authors test 41 respondents in an office-space experiment. They use five sound sources - speech, traffic noise, natural sound, air-conditioning noise, and music - and vary SPL from 45 to 65 dBA while also varying speech reverberation time from 0.3 to 1.5 s. Participants complete a visual cognitive task interface that measures reaction time and accuracy, plus a questionnaire on personal traits. Figure 1 shows the interface, Figure 2 the procedure, Figure 3 the reaction-time curve by sound source, Figure 4 the accuracy curve, Figure 5 the SPL curve, and Figures 7 to 8 the RT effect of reverberation.

study_record.key_statistics: The numbers that matter are structural rather than inferential. The search returned 185 articles, the review distinguishes normal and stress-induced cortisol states, and it separates acute stress elevation from chronic dysregulation and low-cortisol disease states. It also repeatedly warns against taking a single morning sample as decisive evidence, because diurnal rhythm, medication, age, and clinical state all shift the reading. The review's own tables on normal ranges, stress ranges, and disease links function as the paper's main evidentiary backbone.
study_record.limitations_text: The review is heterogeneous by design, which means it cannot give a single pooled effect with the confidence of a meta-analysis. The literature it surveys mixes ages, diagnoses, assay methods, and time windows, and the paper itself acknowledges that a single cortisol reading can mislead. The safest reading is therefore conditional: cortisol is informative, but only when the reader keeps sampling context, clinical state, and diurnal rhythm in view.
study_record.study_design: The authors conduct a systematic review by searching PubMed, Google Scholar, Sciencedirect, and Mendeley, then screening the resulting 185 articles and excluding reviews. The paper is organized around PRISMA logic and around the main measurement routes for cortisol: blood, saliva, urine, hair, and related clinical samples. Its scope spans human and animal literature, acute and chronic stress, and cognitive and psychiatric consequences, so the review has at least three clear scope dimensions: population, setting, and measurement window.

study_record.key_statistics: The strongest numerical pattern is the physiological shift after exposure. LF/HF dropped by 8.47 to 20.20 percent, RMSSD rose by 8.41 to 27.83 percent, and SDNN rose by 13.05 to 25.07 percent. EEG metrics also moved in a restorative direction, with total power falling by 0.83 to 9.10 percent and alpha relative power increasing by 2.76 to 28.51 percent. The paper reports significant differences at p < 0.05, p < 0.01, and p < 0.001 across several measures, and the walkway repeatedly gives the best recovery profile.
study_record.limitations_text: The study uses VR, so it tests restoration under controlled images rather than along an actual shoreline with wind, salt, sound, and movement. The sample is small and specific to university students, and the recovery effects are acute rather than long-term. It is therefore prudent to avoid a universal claim about all coastal spaces. The paper shows a promising pattern, not a completed theory of place-based stress recovery.
study_record.study_design: Forty-four university students took part in a laboratory experiment that paired immersive virtual reality with subjective ratings, heart-rate variability, and EEG. The four scene types were a coastal walkway, a coastal mountain park, a coastal plaza, and a coastal beach. The setting is therefore acute, controlled, and short in duration; the population is university students; and the measurements span self-report plus physiological traces. Those three dimensions are enough to make the design legible as an acute restoration study rather than a field survey.

rows.canonical_text: Chronic stress exacerbates tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive performance through a corticotropin-releasing factor receptor-dependent mechanism in a transgenic mouse model of tauopathy.
rows.source_text: Chronic stress exacerbates tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive performance through a corticotropin-releasing factor receptor-dependent mechanism in a transgenic mouse model of tauopathy.

study_record.key_statistics: The review does not report original quantitative data or pooled effect sizes. It cites landmark findings from its reviewed literature, including: (1) the inverted-U relationship between cortisol and cognitive performance (Lupien et al., 2007), (2) the role of mineralocorticoid vs. glucocorticoid receptor occupancy in determining whether cortisol enhances or impairs hippocampal function, (3) dose-dependent effects of cortisol on memory — low-to-moderate levels facilitating consolidation, high levels impairing retrieval, and (4) the measurement challenge that salivary cortisol reflects free cortisol more accurately than serum cortisol due to protein-binding variability. Mathpix-extracted statistics: N = 180; N = 12; N= 1462; N= 32715; N= 686.
study_record.limitations_text: As a narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis, the paper does not use standardized search protocols or risk-of-bias assessment. The selection of cited studies is the authors' editorial judgment, which may favor certain theoretical perspectives. The review covers an enormous literature — from rodent hippocampal models to clinical psychiatric populations — and necessarily simplifies each sub-domain. The inverted-U model of cortisol and cognition, while widely cited, has been challenged by more complex models that incorporate sex differences, age, circadian variation, and cortisol receptor subtypes. The review acknowledges these complications but does not resolve them, leaving the reader with a useful framework but not a quantitative guideline.
study_record.study_design: The paper is an integrative narrative review published in Frontiers in Endocrinology (2023). It draws on human and animal literature spanning endocrine physiology, neuropsychology, psychiatry, and clinical neuroscience. Rather than a systematic search with PRISMA reporting, the review organizes existing knowledge into thematic sections: definitions of physiological vs. psychosocial stress, the HPA axis and its negative feedback loop, cortisol measurement methods (serum, salivary, urinary, CSF, hair), the relationship between cortisol and cognitive domains (memory, attention, executive function), and clinical conditions where the stress-cortisol-cognition link is disrupted (aging, depression, PTSD, Cushing's disease, Addison's disease, traumatic brain injury).

study_record.key_statistics: The physiological effects are robust. The main effect of hue is significant at F(2,1038) = 6.93, p = .001; value-chroma is significant at F(1,1764) = 6.8, p = .009; and channel is highly significant at F(9,362) = 10.99, p < .001. Pairwise comparisons show red lower than blue at t(991) = -3.67, p < .001, and HVLC lower than LVHC at t(1764) = -2.47, p = .009. For ceiling height, the main effect is F(3,608) = 3.55, p = .014, with ceiling-channel differences at F(9,250) = 6.48, p < .001. The paper also reports strong psychological effects, including ηp2 values as high as .653 for spaciousness.
study_record.limitations_text: The experiment takes place in VR, so it controls stimulus conditions at the cost of real-world occupancy. The participants are university students, not younger pupils, and the paper does not test long-term learning outcomes. The safest interpretation is therefore local. It shows how color and ceiling height affect perception and EEG in a simulated setting, but it does not yet prove that the same combination will improve grades or behavior over a semester.
study_record.study_design: This is a within-subject VR experiment with forty undergraduate students. The authors use six color schemes, built from hue and value-chroma combinations, and four ceiling heights between 3 and 6 meters. Participants wear the VR headset, their EEG is recorded, and they also complete spatial-perception and satisfaction questionnaires. The scope dimensions are explicit: an undergraduate population, an immersive laboratory setting, a short exposure window, and dual measurement streams combining EEG with self-report.

study_record.limitations_text: Like the preprint, this study lives in VR and therefore does not test actual long-term occupancy. The paper identifies the direction of a good classroom atmosphere, but it does not prove what happens after months of daily use.

study_record.key_statistics: There are no inferential statistics here, but the argument is structured around a small number of decisive examples. Figure 1 shows the Salk Institute as a creativity-oriented research space, and Figure 2 shows the MIT Stata Center as a collaboration-oriented building. The text then distinguishes space from place, open exploration from constrained movement, and sensory cues from memory-linked orientation. Those contrasts are the real evidence in the paper, because they are what the commentary keeps returning to.
study_record.limitations_text: The commentary is persuasive, but it remains a bridge argument rather than a tested protocol. It does not measure a design intervention, and it does not quantify how much a landmark or path changes hippocampal activity in a real building. The relation between place cells and architecture is suggestive, not settled. That means the paper should be read as a disciplined invitation to research, not as a completed theory of design.
study_record.study_design: This is a commentary rather than a data paper. It draws on neuroscience findings about orientation, landmarks, memory, and navigation, then uses architectural examples to translate those findings into design language. The scope is broad enough to include research buildings, hospitals, and public interiors, and it also includes animal place-cell studies that explain why movement paths matter. The paper therefore has three scope dimensions at once: the human navigator, the built setting, and the time spent moving through or remembering that setting.

study_record.key_statistics: The most useful counts are structural. Mostafa's ASPECTSS index is organized around seven criteria: acoustics, spatial sequence, escape, compartmentalization, transition, sensory zone, and safety. The general design guidance also resolves into five aims: safety, health and well-being, sensory comfort, social integration, and privacy. The paper then proposes two steps for intervention: first balance the home for the whole family, then tune the space for the autistic individual. Those lists are the paper's core evidence.
study_record.limitations_text: The guidance is persuasive, but it is still literature-driven and normative. It does not test the home proposals against post-occupancy outcomes or compare one family against another in a controlled way. The paper also assumes that sensory regulation is always the right priority, which may not hold equally across all households. So the safe reading is that the article provides a disciplined starting framework, not a completed universal code for autism-sensitive housing.

study_record.key_statistics: The review does not report original quantitative data. It organizes and reinterprets established findings, including: (1) evidence that urban street grids vs. organic layouts produce different spatial orientation behaviors linked to distinct SMRs, (2) findings that planned rectangular grids inherit specific EF-SMR signatures from designers' intentions, while unplanned districts emerge from accumulated spontaneous feature-action couplings, (3) neurophysiological evidence that the pulvinar and thalamus mediate transthalamic sensory-to-motor transmission in response to environmental features, and (4) the argument that the default mode network's responses to short environmental features (objects) vs. long environmental features (spaces) reflect different SMR predictions.
study_record.limitations_text: The review is entirely theoretical and does not report new data. The EF-SMR coupling, while conceptually compelling, has not been validated as a predictive model: no study has yet shown that manipulating a specific EF (e.g., doorway width) produces a specific, predicted SMR (e.g., a change in approach velocity) that in turn produces a predicted behavioral outcome (e.g., route choice). The framework relies on enactivism and predictive processing, which are themselves debated theoretical positions in cognitive science. The review acknowledges that MoBi studies are needed to test the framework but does not specify the experimental designs or effect sizes that would constitute confirmation or refutation. The connection between thalamocortical processing and building-scale features is plausible but leaps several levels of analysis.
study_record.study_design: This is a narrative review published in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews (Volume 138, Article 104715). The paper organizes literature from four domains: (1) exogenous attention and environmental feature perception, (2) thalamocortical processing and the pulvinar's role in transthalamic transmission, (3) sensorimotor contingencies and enactivism, and (4) behavioral and neurophysiological evidence from built and natural environments. It is structured in five sections: definitions of EFs and SMRs, a psychobiological framework for EF-SMR coupling, evidence from urban morphology and building design, and a methodological proposal for Mobile Brain/Body Imaging (MoBi). The authors are from Aalborg University (Denmark) and Technical University Berlin (Germany), drawing on the Gramann Lab's established MoBi methodology.

study_record.key_statistics: The article does not report inferential statistics, but it does structure the argument around recurring examples. Schools should support cognition and memorization, hospitals should support recovery, workspaces should support collaboration and creativity, and cities should support social life. It also leans on the classic B = f(P, E) frame to show that behavior is a function of the person and the environment. Those examples and contrasts are the paper's real working numbers.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is broad and persuasive, but it remains more of a synthesis essay than a testable intervention study. It does not quantify how much one design change alters behavior, and it does not compare competing interventions in a controlled way. That means its claims should be treated as programmatic guidance. The logical direction is sound, but the exact magnitude of the effect is still an open question.
study_record.study_design: This is an argumentative essay built from neuroscience examples, architecture examples, and broad reflection on human behavior. It draws on the person-environment relation, System 1 and System 2 thinking, and practical cases such as schools, hospitals, and workplaces. The scope dimensions are clear even without a sample: user groups differ by age, gender, and culture; settings differ by function; and the time horizon matters because long-occupation spaces need different treatment from brief-use spaces. That gives the paper a planning logic rather than an experimental one.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper is not statistically driven in the usual sense, so the important technical details are structural rather than inferential. It distinguishes two major methodological families, stationary and mobile, and it uses a small set of representative studies to illustrate each side. Those examples include work on curvilinear spaces, ceiling height, enclosure, window shapes, restorative interiors, and door-width affordances. The key analytical contrast is between high-control but low-ecology scanner or image studies and more naturalistic but noisier mobile paradigms. That contrast is the paper's main quantitative logic.
study_record.limitations_text: The authors are careful about the trade-off they propose. Stationary methods offer control, but they can flatten architectural experience into two-dimensional snapshots. Mobile methods improve ecological validity, but they introduce movement artifacts and more complex data analysis. The review therefore does not claim that mobile imaging is a complete replacement. It claims that the field needs a broader method mix and that embodied exploration cannot be treated as optional if the goal is to understand architecture as experienced in the world.
study_record.study_design: This is a methodological review, not a new experiment. It synthesizes the historical development of neuro-architecture, then separates the field into stationary paradigms and mobile paradigms before arguing for ecological psychology and Mobile Brain/Body Imaging as the way forward. The paper does not recruit a fresh participant sample; instead it uses prior work on architectural aesthetics, affordances, and embodied movement to make a programmatic claim. Its scope is therefore conceptual and field-building, but it is anchored in a concrete set of studies on contour, ceiling height, enclosure, window shapes, and moving through spaces.

study_record.key_statistics: The review's most important counts are simple but useful. It screened 1,334 records and included 9 studies. The biomarker table shows repeated use of EEG, fMRI, HRV, GSR, pupil dilation, salivary cortisol, and other physiological measures. The geometry table shows the same concentration of evidence around curvature, enclosure, and proportion. The review also highlights specific studies: 112 participants in one virtual geometry study, 49 healthy men in a virtual TSST study, 18 participants in a ceiling-height and enclosure fMRI study, 32 participants in an enclosure-restoration study, and 33 female participants in a postpartum-room VR study.
study_record.limitations_text: The review is clear about its own limits. Many studies use small samples, inconsistent definitions, and short exposures. The field also relies heavily on virtual or 2D proxies, which may not capture the multisensory character of lived interiors. Because the biomarker and geometry definitions differ from study to study, the paper cannot honestly claim a universal architectural law. It can only say that the evidence is converging enough to justify better standardization and stronger longitudinal testing.
study_record.study_design: The paper is a PRISMA-P-guided systematic review. It searched three major databases, plus Google Scholar and reference lists, and screened English-language studies from 2013 to 2023. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, the review identified 1,334 potentially relevant records and included 9 sources for extraction. Its design is a controlled evidence map rather than a pooled statistical meta-analysis, because the studies vary too much in their definition of form, their exposure setting, and their outcome biomarker.

study_record.key_statistics: The headline numbers are strong. Classroom parameters explain 16% of the total variation in learning progress in the final model, compared with 25% in phase 1. The pupil-level variables reduce variance by 18% and the classroom variables by 26%, and the final R-squared fit reaches 58%. Naturalness contributes about 49-50% of the classroom effect, individualization about 28%, and stimulation about 23%. The seven retained design parameters are light, temperature, air quality, ownership, flexibility, complexity, and colour. The school-level variance is only about 3%, so the classroom is the key built layer here.
study_record.limitations_text: The sample is large, but it is still a specific sample: primary schools in England with a particular curriculum and climate. The findings also concern formal academic progress, not every possible educational outcome. The authors are honest that teacher effects were not fully measured, and that some single-factor correlations dropped out in the multilevel model once all factors were considered together. The study therefore supports classroom design as a real influence, but it does not support the idea that any single building factor acts in isolation or that the same weighting will hold in every country.
study_record.study_design: This is a large multilevel school study in England. The authors assessed 153 classrooms in 27 schools and linked classroom features to the academic progress of 3,766 pupils. They used the HEAD environmental-behaviour model, which turns naturalness, individualization, and stimulation into ten design parameters and then into measurable classroom factors. The analysis used multilevel regression so that pupil-level and classroom-level variance could be separated. That design matters because it avoids confusing individual pupil differences with the built environment.

study_record.key_statistics: The review reports 11 attention studies and 7 memory studies, with substantial overlap between the two domains. Seven studies were simulation-based and eight were performed in real learning environments. The review also notes an average sample of roughly 81 participants and the frequent absence of standardized protocols. On the substantive side, it identifies a coherent pattern: attention improves in cool, quiet, bright spaces; memory improves in warm, moderately bright spaces and in some cases with cold-hued walls, narrower rooms, and optimal ceiling or enclosure conditions.
study_record.limitations_text: The authors are explicit that the literature is heterogeneous and that a meta-analysis is not yet feasible. They also note weak standardization in data reporting, inconsistent measurement tools, and limited control of indoor environmental quality variables. Many studies involve small samples or narrow age groups, which makes replication and comparison difficult. The safest reading is therefore conservative: there is meaningful evidence for design effects, but the field still lacks the cross-validated protocol needed to turn that evidence into a single general rule.
study_record.study_design: The review searched multiple databases, screened 164 documents, and reduced the literature to 14 included papers. It used PRISMA, the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, and explicit inclusion criteria for human studies in real or simulated learning environments. The authors required a cognitive endpoint in attention or memory, not merely a general academic outcome. That is important because it keeps the review focused on processes rather than outcomes alone. The study mix includes controlled classroom studies, VR studies, fMRI studies, and EEG studies.

study_record.key_statistics: The numerical pattern is clear. In Study 1, face-to-face interaction fell 72% after the redesign, while emails sent increased 56% and instant messages sent increased 67%. In Study 2, the same pattern held at a slightly different level: F2F interaction fell between 67% and 71%, while email activity rose between 22% and 50%. The paper also reports 643 dyads that decreased F2F interaction and 141 that increased it in Study 2, reinforcing the direction of the effect across many pairs.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is still limited to two headquarters and two redesign episodes. It is quasi-experimental, not randomized, and it measures communication in a specific corporate setting with a specific technology mix. The authors are careful not to generalize beyond what the field sites support. Even so, the pattern is strong enough that it should be treated as a warning against assuming that open space is automatically collaborative.
study_record.study_design: The authors ran two quasi-field studies in large corporate headquarters that were transitioning from cubicles to open offices. They used sociometric badges to measure face-to-face interactions and server data to measure email and instant messaging. study_record.key_statistics: The numerical pattern is clear. In Study 1, face-to-face interaction fell 72% after the redesign, while emails sent increased 56% and instant messages sent increased 67%. In Study 2, the same pattern held at a slightly different level: F2F interaction fell between 67% and 71%, while email activity rose between 22% and 50%. The paper also reports 643 dyads that decreased F2F interaction and 141 that increased it in Study 2, reinforcing the direction of the effect across many pairs.
study_record.limitations_text: The study is still limited to two headquarters and two redesign episodes. It is quasi-experimental, not randomized, and it measures communication in a specific corporate setting with a specific technology mix. The authors are careful not to generalize beyond what the field sites support. Even so, the pattern is strong enough that it should be treated as a warning against assuming that open space is automatically collaborative.

study_record.key_statistics: The preference differences are statistically sharp. Window size differs by style at Pearson chi-square p = 0.001 and Fisher's exact p = 0.0001; indoor greenery also differs at p = 0.001; flooring and desk/chair materials at p = 0.001; color scheme at p = 0.002; and classroom width at p = 0.044. study_record.limitations_text: The evidence is still limited by the VR format, which cannot fully reproduce long-term use, social noise, or the ordinary pressure of a real school year. The sample comes from one national context, so cultural and pedagogical differences may change the weighting of the design features. The study also measures preference, attention, and stress, not achievement over a term. So the paper is strongest as a design map, not as a proof that the suggested templates will automatically raise grades in every classroom.
study_record.study_design: The study surveyed 107 high school students in Taiwan using the Kolb Learning Style Inventory and classroom-preference questionnaires. Students then evaluated VR classroom scenes built from a fixed set of design factors: spatial layout, ceiling height, window size, indoor greenery, flooring and furniture materials, and wall color. The authors used chi-square tests to compare preference distributions and MANOVA to test interaction effects on attention and stress. That design is clean because it holds the room constant while varying the environmental features and the learning-style grouping.

study_record.key_statistics: Set I used weak, medium, and strong stimuli of about 125, 300, and 500 units, and the medium stimulus produced the fastest habit acquisition. Set II used a stronger discrimination contrast and found that learning speed increased with stimulus strength up to the strongest usable level. Set III, where discrimination was hardest, again showed an intermediate optimum, with 195 units most favorable. The paper also notes that males responded to a stimulus about 10% lower than the threshold for females, and that the experiment used ten tests per morning until a perfect three-day run was reached.
study_record.limitations_text: The paper is historically important, but it also has obvious limits. The apparatus is invasive, the sample is small by modern standards, and the findings are embedded in a specific animal-learning setup. The shock measures and units are tied to the inductorium and to the authors' calibration assumptions. So the safest reading is structural rather than literal: the study is evidence for an inverted-U relation between arousal and task difficulty, but not a model for modern experimental ethics or translational generalization without modification.
study_record.study_design: The authors studied 40 mice trained on a white-black discrimination habit in electric boxes. They varied both the brightness difference between the boxes and the strength of the shock, creating three sets of conditions with different discriminability. Each mouse received repeated tests and the authors tracked how many trials were needed before the animal reached a stable correct habit. Although the apparatus and terminology are historical, the experimental logic is precise: control the task difficulty, vary the aversive stimulus, and compare the rate of learning.

study_record.key_statistics: The most important counts are straightforward. The review includes 22 studies, with sample sizes ranging from 8 to 207 participants. Twelve studies had fewer than 30 participants, eleven reported 31-92, and one had 207. Most studies were laboratory-based, and most of the samples were healthy, although clinical groups with depression, anxiety, or gambling disorder were also represented. The review reports that benefits are often associated with changes in prefrontal activity, while stress and anxiety outcomes vary more by exposure type and setting.
study_record.limitations_text: The authors are transparent about the limits: small samples, cross-sectional designs, varied exposure types, and inconsistent definitions of nature exposure. They also note that the screening and quality appraisal process used a single reviewer with a second reviewer only when clarification was needed. That does not invalidate the review, but it does mean the field still needs stronger standardization and more longitudinal evidence. The honest conclusion is that nature helps, but we do not yet know precisely which form, dose, or rhythm helps most.
study_record.study_design: The authors followed PRISMA and PECOS, searched seven databases plus Google Scholar, and reviewed literature from 2014 to 2025. They identified 3,557 studies, then screened them down to 22 that met the inclusion criteria. Quality was assessed with GRADE and risk of bias with NICE. The review includes both laboratory and naturalistic exposures, and it includes healthy and clinical samples. That range makes the paper broad but also heterogeneous, so its design is best understood as a structured evidence synthesis rather than a pooled causal estimate.

study_record.key_statistics: The chapter's useful numbers are the ones associated with its cited studies. The IPAR work included 40 highly creative architects, 43 age- and sex-matched architects from the same firms, and 41 architect controls from other firms. The review also highlights a later sample of architects in which fluid intelligence predicted originality and trait creativity, and it cites fMRI studies showing that architecture-related design tasks engage the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. These counts and contrasts provide the chapter's empirical scaffolding even though the chapter itself is not an original experiment.
study_record.limitations_text: Because this is a synthesis chapter, it cannot establish direct causal effects on its own. It mainly organizes prior evidence and uses that evidence to argue for a richer neuroscience of architecture. The chapter also leans on studies with different methods, different populations, and different levels of ecological realism. That means the claims are strongest as a conceptual map. They are weaker as a single quantitative rule, which is exactly why the summary should stay close to the cited cases rather than overgeneralize them.
study_record.study_design: This is a chapter-length synthesis rather than a participant-based study. The author draws on archival creativity work, neuroimaging, neuropsychology, and case studies such as Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater and later fMRI research on architectural judgment. The evidence base includes the IPAR architect sample, later divergence-thought studies, and scanner work on design tasks and aesthetic choices. The paper is therefore interpretive and comparative, but it is still anchored in concrete examples and a clear historical arc.

study_record.key_statistics: The paper is not statistically driven in the usual sense, so the important technical details are structural rather than inferential. It distinguishes two major methodological families, stationary and mobile, and it uses a small set of representative studies to illustrate each side. Those examples include work on curvilinear spaces, ceiling height, enclosure, window shapes, restorative interiors, and door-width affordances. The key analytical contrast is between high-control but low-ecology scanner or image studies and more naturalistic but noisier mobile paradigms. That contrast is the paper's main quantitative logic.
study_record.limitations_text: The authors are careful about the trade-off they propose. Stationary methods offer control, but they can flatten architectural experience into two-dimensional snapshots. Mobile methods improve ecological validity, but they introduce movement artifacts and more complex data analysis. The review therefore does not claim that mobile imaging is a complete replacement. It claims that the field needs a broader method mix and that embodied exploration cannot be treated as optional if the goal is to understand architecture as experienced in the world.
study_record.study_design: This is a methodological review, not a new experiment. It synthesizes the historical development of neuro-architecture, then separates the field into stationary paradigms and mobile paradigms before arguing for ecological psychology and Mobile Brain/Body Imaging as the way forward. The paper does not recruit a fresh participant sample; instead it uses prior work on architectural aesthetics, affordances, and embodied movement to make a programmatic claim. Its scope is therefore conceptual and field-building, but it is anchored in a concrete set of studies on contour, ceiling height, enclosure, window shapes, and moving through spaces.
